# Book 2 of the Hieroglyphics

...having been carried across the Hellespont by the ram, he arrived in Colchis, sacrificed the ram to Mercury <note>The Roman god of commerce and communication, associated with the Greek Hermes; in alchemical texts, he often represents the element mercury or the "quick-silver" of the philosophers.</note>, and hung the fleece in the grove of Mars. <margin>Mercury gilded the fleece.</margin> This fleece, which Mercury had covered in gold, was sought in vain by many. But now, let us approach those things that are noteworthy concerning what has been narrated so far. Here, we should first consider how these things have been explained by others.

<margin>The explanation of others.</margin> Many people, and the simpler sort among them, believe that these things truly happened: that Jason was sent, went forth, fought with monsters, and having defeated them, returned home. Yet by the "Golden Fleece" they understand either live sheep of a golden color, or sheep that had been gilded; or perhaps not sheep at all, but rather gold-bearing minerals that were customarily cleaned and collected using sheepskins <note>A historical technique where gold-rich river sands were washed over sheepskins to trap the heavy gold flakes in the wool.</note>. Others believe it refers to a book fashioned from sheepskin (which they call *parchment*), in which the chemical art of making gold had been written.

Others admit these stories as fables, but they twist them toward some moral teaching, as if such great and complex "coverings" <note>original: "involucra" — a common term in Renaissance scholarship for the allegorical "veils" that hide deeper truths.</note> were fashioned merely to shape morals or were of use for that purpose. 

There are still others who accept all these things as hieroglyphs and allegories—not for morals, nor for common physics, but as containing and involving the most occult secrets of nature: the Philosopher's Stone <term>Philosopher's Stone: The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life.</term> and the method and art of crafting it. They explain that the myth hides the truth just as a nut hides its kernel within its shells. As over a hundred supporters of Chemistry <note>Here referring to Alchemical chemistry.</note> attest to this, even the fiercest hater of this art, Natalis Comes <note>Natale Conti (1520–1582), a famous mythographer whose "Mythologiae" sought to explain myths through natural and moral philosophy.</note>, affirms it—though based on the judgment of others. 

<margin>Why was this opinion not refuted by Natalis, like most others? Perhaps because it is too clear?</margin> For thus he says in Book 6, Chapter 8 of his *Mythologies*: *"There were those,"* he says, *"who thought that the deeds done in Jason's voyage were the transformations of chemical bodies, and that the Golden Fleece, finally captured after so many labors, was called the Philosopher's Stone, which is produced at last after so many transformations of those bodies."* 

We, not being led astray by the prejudices of others, will not presume to believe this or that, or to deny one thing or the other; instead, we shall weigh the opinions of each of these in the balance of reason and experience, so that we may finally reach the equilibrium of truth. 

<margin>Response: History is not hidden beneath the Golden Fleece.</margin> Regarding those who support the history of the first sort, who think that Jason truly went and returned: let them take this response. There are indeed places in the nature of things that such heroes are said to have sought...

# Book 2 of the Egyptian-Greeks

<margin>
A real location does not imply the truth of the event imagined to have taken place there.
</margin>
...are said; because since these things are perpetual and not as changeable as the rest of the world, they have always been attached to allegories—lest they seem like mere fables—as is clear in almost all the fictions concerning *Phrygia*, *Colchis*, *Delos*, *Cyprus*, *Rhodes*, and other places brought forth in the past. For if some fable were presented without a fixed location, it would lose its charm and immediately reveal itself as a fable. However, the time, the people, and their deeds, along with the other circumstances of Jason's expedition, do not agree with the truth at all. If the time is considered, it is undefined, nor was it truly bounded by any writer who lived then, so that it might be recognized in histories. It does not escape me, however, that this time is precisely placed in chronologies and historical collections, but on the foundation that *Troy* is said to have been destroyed three hundred years before the founding of Rome, and that Jason’s expedition preceded the fall of *Troy* by nearly 100 years, because the sons of the Argonauts participated in the Trojan expedition. But both are assumed rather than proven, as will be more broadly evident below under the section on *Troy*.

<margin>
Fictional characters imply fictional events and not history.
</margin>
But if one may conclude from the persons—because an event cannot be done without persons—once the persons are removed, the event itself is taken away. Since, therefore, all the Argonauts are fictional characters, just as there are characters in Comedies or Tragedies, or as they are found in the poetry of <term>Amadis</term> <note>Referring to *Amadis de Gaula*, a famous chivalric romance popular in the Renaissance, which the author uses as an example of pure, sprawling fiction.</note> (which acknowledges neither head nor foot and produces and confirms events from events, persons from persons, fictions from fictions in a continuous series),

<margin>
All Argonauts are fictional characters and descended from gods.
</margin>
since nearly all of them trace their origin from gods who never existed as either men or gods, how can the deeds believed to have been performed by them be true? If anyone should excuse these in any way, how is it that *Hercules*—who is said to have lived in *Egypt* in the time of *Osiris* <note>The Egyptian god of the afterlife. Early modern scholars often tried to sync Greek heroes with Egyptian history to find a "true" origin for myths.</note> and was appointed governor of *Egypt* by him when he was about to travel abroad, which they fabulously claim happened 20,000 years ago—also participated in this Argonautic expedition? Or if it is permitted through distinctions to create many *Herculeses* (as also Saturns, Suns, Apollos, Mercuries, and those like them), how, I ask, did *Pollux* take part with the Argonauts, while *Helen* was born from the same egg with him <note>According to myth, Leda was visited by Zeus in the form of a swan; she produced eggs from which Helen, Clytemnestra, and the Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux) were born.</note>...

# Hieroglyphics, Book 2

<margin>
Literal or historical absurdities.
</margin>
...of the Trojan expedition; if you claim these figures were Gods, I cannot argue with you; but if you claim they were men, they seem far too long-lived. For Helen would be, at the very least, a 120-year-old toothless hag <note>original: "anus edentula"</note> by the time all of Greece waged the Trojan War for the sake of her return. These stories hold together like sand tossed by the wind;

<margin>
Incredible things contrary to nature.
</margin>
indeed, if the matter is considered as historical fact, only children, not grown men, should be convinced that there are bulls that vomit fire, or that armed ranks of men could spring from the earth faster than mushrooms or gourds—warriors who, when struck by a single stone, would slaughter one another to the last man. What shall we say of the ever-watchful dragon, said to be the offspring of Typhon and Echidna, or the sowing of its teeth? What of Medea’s potions, her schemes, and countless other wonders? Shall we fashion a history out of these?

<margin>
The explanation of others.
</margin>
Therefore, it is a tasteless fable <note>The author uses "insulsa" (unsalted/tasteless) to describe the lack of intellectual "flavor" in a literal reading.</note> to suggest that those sheep actually had golden or lemon-colored wool, or were gilded, and that Jason undertook such labor just to obtain them. Those who understood these "fleece" as gold mines—among whom Strabo is cited in his *Geography*—came closer to the truth. Even closer were those who interpreted it as a book or a parchment containing <term>Chrysopoeia<note>original: "Chrysopœam"; the alchemical art of making gold.</note></term>, such as Suidas. But no one would undergo such varied and immense dangers for such things, nor would they have any need for Medea’s magical drugs; nor would Jason—whose name signifies "Healer" <note>Jason's name (Iason) shares a root with the Greek word for healing, *iasthai*.</note> and who was trained in practical skills by the centaur Chiron—be required for the task; any other man would have sufficed. Nor, in that case, would Aeson have been restored to youth by Medea.

<margin>
The truest allegorical interpretation.
</margin>
It remains, then, for us to apply an allegorical interpretation to the entire matter from beginning to end. We do not apply it to mere moral lessons—at least not primarily—unless we wish to be mad ourselves, or to accuse those who invented such grand tales of madness for doing so merely to teach manners. We do not deny that these stories can be bent toward morality secondarily, as all things can. But the true meaning refers neither to history nor to the common works of nature known to peasants, but to the most secret works belonging to philosophers: namely, the **Golden Medicine**, which treats the golden remedy of the soul and the body. In this, those who preceded us (such as Luigi Marliani) agree with our view.

### Book 2. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.

...lianus <note>Likely referring to Claudius Aelianus or a similar commentator on ancient lore.</note> in an entire volume published under the title of the *Golden Fleece*, and those who collected so many treatises on the **Chemical art**, arranged in various volumes and published in German under that same title of the work, and countless others (whom I omit here for the sake of brevity) whose writings are held in everyone's hands and whom I shall not cite here. We will now specifically demonstrate that the aforementioned journey of Jason—with its dangers, deeds, participants, and all its circumstances—pertains to **Philosophical Medicine**, and is nothing other than the highest **Chemical craft** and the **Secret of Secrets** <note>original: "Arcanum Arcanissimum"</note> translated from the Egyptians to the Greeks and described under this most beautiful allegory.

<margin>Who Jason is.</margin> What kind of man Jason is, his name, his education, his lineage, and his deeds all prove: for his name expresses a healer, derived from the Greek word *to heal* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἰάσθαι" (apo tou iasthai)</note>; for the art of a Physician <note>original: "Ἰατρὸς" (Iatros)</note> is the art of healing. It is not enough to assert, as some do, that Jason was not a surgeon and never practiced medicine, using that as a reason to turn his story into a mere moral lesson. For even if he was not a literal physician or surgeon (since Jason himself never actually existed in the natural world), he is imagined and presupposed to be one. Indeed, all the omens agree with his name. He was educated by **Chiron**, who instructed him in medicine, and who also taught Hercules and Achilles—youths of a similar disposition and family: the latter being the invincible hero of the Trojan War, the former most fit for taming monsters.

<margin>Chiron and Medea were beneficial to Jason’s training.</margin> From Chiron, therefore, Jason drew manual experience, just as he received from Medea the counsel and the **perfect Theory** necessary for the completion of the work. From this, a point worthy of notice occurs: that manual handling of any kind, learned from Chiron, must precede the perfect Theory instilled by Medea in the investigation of this work. For perfect Theory precedes perfect practice, and not practice the theory; yet many errors precede perfect theory. For these errors are, as it were, the masters and correctors in the art.

# Hieroglyphics, Book 2.

...errors, however, are not recognized except through practice often attempted and repeated; and so it appears that **Chiron's** <note>The centaur Chiron was the traditional tutor of heroes, representing the foundational, practical knowledge of medicine and nature.</note> instruction precedes **Medea’s** most perfect counsels; these also order and dispose the labors of the craftsman. This lineage is drawn from the genealogy of the Gods: for his paternal **great-great-grandfather** is **Jupiter**; **Polymeda** is assigned as his mother—a name meaning "of many counsels"—the daughter of **Autolycus**, descending also from **Sisyphus**, **Aeolus**, and **Jupiter**. Thus, if Aeolus or Jupiter are removed, the lineage of **Jason** begins from nothing; likewise, if **Chiron** never existed, he had no teacher; and he certainly never existed in the natural world unless **Saturn**, having turned into a beast—a horse—mated with the nymph **Philyra**, or if he never lived at all.

<margin>Medea's grandfather is the Sun.</margin> Similarly **Medea**, the wife of **Jason**, is the granddaughter of the **Sun** and **Oceanus**; she had as a father **Aeetes**, named from "brightness" <note>original: "á fulgore dictum"; the name Aeetes was often linked to the Greek word for "eagle" or "shining/intense."</note>, whose sisters were **Pasiphae**, the wife of **Minos** who gave birth to the Minotaur, and **Circe**, who transformed men into beasts by her power. Her mother was **Idyia**, named from "knowing" <note>original: "á cognoscendo nominatam"; Idyia's name derives from the Greek verb 'to know.'</note>; for knowledge is the mother of counsel.

<margin>Jason the physician; Golden Medicine; the craftsman; the Argonauts as sons of the Gods.</margin> Such parents, teacher, and wife were fitting for **Jason**, the future physician and most sharp-witted investigator of natural things. Now we shall come to weigh his achievements; fifty companions are chosen for that journey, almost all born of the Gods. But why was that? Perhaps because that age produced Gods? I think not: but because it pleased the poet **Orpheus** to assign such great parents to his **Argonauts**, lest they should seem to have risen from a humble place, but rather to be of a "golden" family. For when either **Aeolus**, or **Jupiter**, or **Mercury**, or other Gods, Goddesses, or Nymphs are the progenitors of them all, who would not recognize them as true heroes? Among the Pagans it would have been a sin to deny the Gods themselves; among us it is permitted, and we add that neither Gods nor men were the ancestors of the Argonauts, such as **Jason, Hercules, Hylas, Aethalides, Amphion, Augias, Calais, Castor, Cepheus, Iphiclus, Aeson, Lynceus, Meleager, Mopsus, Peleus,**

<margin>What the ship Argo is.</margin> **Pollux, Telamon, Zetes**, and the rest. The ship **Argo** is constructed, which is said to be the first ship, made from **Dodonian** oak <note>The oaks of Dodona were sacred to Zeus and said to be oracular/prophetic.</note>, from which oracles were delivered; hence it had a talkative and prophetic mast. And that is the first thing worthy of consideration: because it was built by the poetic and prophetic pen of **Orpheus**; the second...

# Book 2. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.

...because it is said to have been built by the counsel of **Pallas**, that is, of wisdom; third, that such a great mass could be carried by fifty men through the deserts of **Libya** for twelve full days; fourth, that it was steered only by the lyre and song of **Orpheus**; fifth, that finally, collapsing from old age, it crushed **Jason** while he was sleeping beneath it; and sixth, that it was placed among the stars, where it is still seen. These individual points describe clearly enough what kind of vessel it was: namely, one <note>The text here attributes the construction to Orpheus, though earlier it mentions Pallas; this likely signifies the union of divine wisdom and harmonic "attunement" required to begin the work.</note> built by **Orpheus**, set upright, and inscribed among the stars in eternal memory of the deed.

Why was a clod of earth offered by **Eurypylus**, the son of **Neptune**? Because <term>Philosophical Earth</term> <note>The solid, fixed "salt" or "body" that remains after the initial dissolution of the raw matter.</note> given as a guest-gift, though it be cheap, is not to be rejected. It is given by a son of **Neptune** because it is fitting; for earth is made from water. But what did **Medea** prophesy from this clod dissolved in water? What kind of return there would be to the fatherland—whether prosperous or otherwise—and what the outcome of the work would be. For unless earth becomes water and from earth water again, the labor is in vain. Therefore, from the dissolution of the earth into water, many things were to be predicted by **Medea**, or by excellent reason and counsel. 

They add that not only did **Eurypylus**, son of **Neptune**, give this gift to the **Argonauts**, but it was also received and kept by another son of **Neptune**, **Euphemus**: for nature leads nature, and rejoices in its own similar nature. The Golden Fleece is indeed promised, but only after the dangers have been overcome; however, because those dangers were great, very many men had succumbed to them. A Dragon as large as a ship driven by fifty oars, ever-watchful, had to be slain. This is the task, this is the toil. <note>original: "Hoc opus, hic labor," a famous phrase from Virgil’s Aeneid regarding the difficulty of returning from the underworld.</note> Who would attack such a beast unless relying on the divine art of *Pallas* <note>Athena, representing wisdom.</note> and the counsel of *Medea*?

placed there; and in Chapter 54: *In the stinking Menstruum* <note>In alchemy, a "menstruum" is a solvent or the base matter in a state of putrefaction. original: "Menstruali foetenti"</note> *the fire is against nature, which transforms our whole stone into a certain Dragon, strong and wide-throated, which thickens and impregnates its own mother.* Thus others have very often made mention of the Dragon, which does not die unless it be killed along with its brother and sister. <margin>What do the remedies given to Jason by Medea signify?</margin>
Truly *Jason*, the Physician-Philosopher, received the most ready assistance from *Medea*, or reason: images of the *Moon* and the *Sun* to be worn around his neck, a fire-resistant ointment <note>original: "vnguentum Apyrum"</note> with which he might anoint himself, and a sleep-inducing cake with the clearest water, or "virgin’s milk," <note>A common alchemical term for a white, purified liquid, often a mercurial solvent. original: "lacte virginis"</note> which wards off and extinguishes every flame. Armed with these remedies, he slays the Dragon and pulls out its teeth; such a thing truly happens in this medicine. For it is necessary that the seed of our future harvest be obtained, which, when sown in its own proper earth, will afterwards yield fruit.

Now, this seed must be extracted from the Dragon by art, just like the teeth. Having obtained this, *Jason* proceeded to tame the Bulls; but what is understood by the Bulls, we have already advised before under the Hieroglyphic of Apis. <note>Apis was the sacred bull of Egypt; in this context, it represents the volatile and powerful "prime matter" of the alchemical process.</note> For this is the true subject of the Golden Medicine, without which nothing happens, even if the Dragon’s teeth are prepared. Therefore, the furious and fire-breathing Bulls must be tamed and put under the yoke. Why say more? The previously prepared seed is entrusted to these Bulls of their own earth, and the earth is turned over until it is sufficient; then it is capable and disposed to bear fruit. *Jason* used the same aids in subjugating the oxen as he did in overcoming the Dragon. But the most powerful remedy was that type of Pentacle <note>An amulet or talisman used for protection or to focus spiritual power.</note> with the image of the *Sun* and *Moon*, which, by a certain hidden power and property, protects against the venom of such great monsters. If anyone can acquire this, let him not doubt his victory; but how he may obtain it, the Philosophers teach in their books when they speak of the *Sun* and *Moon*, and their conjunction and natural dissolution in things...

If anyone, therefore, were to hear that golden apples grow on trees, they would desire to enjoy them by a certain innate appetite. <margin>The interpretations of others.</margin>
*Aretas* <note>Likely Aretas of Caesarea or a similar commentator on geography/myth.</note>, in his writings on Libyan affairs, perceived that there were sheep which were called "golden"; and since they had a cruel and rustic shepherd, they were said to be guarded by a dragon. However, he seems to have been misled by a word that signifies both "apples" and "sheep" <note>The Greek word *mēla* (μῆλα) is a famous homonym meaning both apples/fruit and flocks of sheep or goats.</note>. *Pherecydes* <note>An early Greek mythographer and historian.</note> related it to apples of a golden color, a view supported by *Lucian*. This is also the direction of *Virgil's* verse in his *Eclogues*: *I have sent ten golden apples; tomorrow I will send another ten* <note>original: "Aurea mala decem misi, cras altera mittam." from Virgil's Eclogue 3.</note>. Among more recent writers, some have sensed a historical reality underlying these things—namely, that there were sheep of a yellow or golden color belonging to the two brothers, *Hesperus* and *Atlas*. Others apply it to astronomy, transferring the "golden apples" to the golden stars and the "dragon" to the Sun. Some adapt it to ethics and moral teaching, as if the greedy, guarding their riches, are like serpents watching over golden apples. 

<margin>Response to the interpretations of others.</margin>
To these we shall give first a response, and then our own interpretation. Since subjects must be understood according to their own proper qualities, it is a marvel that *Aretas* turns apples into sheep. For although both are called <term>mēla <gloss>apples or sheep</gloss></term> by the Greeks, they differ greatly in their nature and attributes. The latter [sheep] carry wool that is perhaps golden, while the former [apples] are carried as gold by trees. Nor is there any reason why all authors would have put "apples" for "sheep," or would have wished "sheep" to be understood for "apples." Is there perhaps only a single author who used that equivocal word so simply that the sense is not clear—whether he meant apples or sheep—and have not many others remembered this allegory? I believe there are very many. Therefore, it is a play on words and a violent distortion from the fruit of a tree to a beast, although the latter may also be found to have provided golden wool, as was told before <note>A reference to the Golden Fleece of the Argonauts mentioned in earlier chapters.</note>. But it is altogether frivolous what he adds: that they had a cruel shepherd, and for that reason he was called a dragon. O miserable sheep, who, possessing golden wool, experienced such a rustic shepherd! Truly, they were worthy of being snatched away by *Hercules* after the shepherd was slain. Both ideas are childish: to believe that such a shepherd was called a dragon, and that the sheep truly carried golden wool. Those who admit they are apples, but of a golden color, perhaps

# Book 2: Of the Egyptian-Greeks
### 81

...what some tell in fables does not agree with the truth; much less what others say, that he was a King of Mauritania <note>In antiquity, Mauritania referred to the region of the Maghreb in Northwest Africa, home to the Atlas Mountains.</note> changed by Perseus into a mountain of such great size by the showing of Medusa’s head. For these are the fictions and emblems of poets, with which they shadowed and depicted other more secret things hidden beneath them: <margin>Why Atlas is fashioned as an astronomer.</margin> They call Atlas an astronomer because the stars can be observed most clearly on its summit, especially since it enjoys a clear sky, like Africa and Egypt, not clouded by rains. Secondly, because it is of such height that its peak seems hidden among the clouds and stars, as it appears. And thirdly, because it is thought to sustain the heaven as if on its shoulders; for it is said to represent the figure of a statue of a man, with the summit rising like a head.

This Atlas, whose daughters are said to be the Pleiades <note>A group of seven stars in the constellation Taurus, named in myth after the daughters of Atlas.</note> (from one of whom, called Maia, Mercury was born to Jove, as will be related later under the genealogy of the gods), had a brother named Hesperus, and from him three nieces, the Hesperides: *Aegle, Arethusa, and Hespertusa.* <margin>Note.</margin> Through Hesperus and his daughters, we understand the same mountainous regions of Atlas. For although "Atlas" is taken as if referring to a single mountain, yet by the same name and continuity it embraces all the other adjacent mountains. For Atlas traverses almost the entire maritime region of Africa, and thus comprises not one mountain, but many thousands. Just as it is similarly established regarding the Taurus in Asia, and the Alps, Apennines, and Pyrenees in Europe, that countless mountains and hills are contained under each: so we understand regarding the Pleiades and Hesperides, that they are parts and, as it were, daughters propagated from those great mountains of steep height, Atlas and Hesperus. 

Thus, Mercury is not without merit born of Maia, so that he is called the descendant of Atlas <note>original: *Atlantiades*</note>, and by Aegle, Arethusa, and Hespertusa the trees bearing golden apples are kept, which are therefore named after the Hesperides. <margin>Who the Dragon is.</margin> The Dragon, who was placed in charge of guarding them, born of Echidna and Typhon <note>Echidna and Typhon were the primary monsters of Greek myth, the parents of many legendary beasts.</note>, is said to have a hundred heads. Furthermore, a numerous offspring of the same parents is read to exist, and they are always poisonous and monstrous; such as the dragon at the spring of Cadmus <note>Referring to the dragon Cadmus killed before founding the city of Thebes.</note>, which was lethal to his companions; another at the Golden Fleece <note>The dragon of Colchis that guarded the fleece sought by Jason and the Argonauts.</note>; and this third one at the apples...

### 82

<margin>
Minerals concealed by the names of monsters.
</margin>
...of the *Hesperides*, the fourth to the cattle of *Geryon*; likewise *Cerberus*, the *Sphinx*, the *Chimera*, and other such horrendous and multiform monsters, which will be discussed in their proper places. *Typhon* <note>In Greek myth, a monstrous giant; here, he represents volcanic or sulfuric gases.</note> denotes a sulfurous and burning spirit, while *Echidna* denotes an aqueous, cold, and revolving substance. For from these two, diverse species of minerals sprout, which were always called and described by the ancients by the names of monsters because of the variety of their nature. Concerning the Dragon—as a general category—just as with the birthplace of the golden apples, enough is established from these facts. Now we shall see regarding the species of such great trees and their fruits. It pleases certain Physicists <note>The author refers to "Physici," or natural philosophers who studied the physical world.</note> that a tree is an "inverted animal" for this reason: because it has its roots toward the center of the earth, or toward the lower parts (which represent the mouth of the animal), while being positioned toward the upper parts. If indeed we consider the stomach and its mesenteric veins or the Liver in an animal as the starting point for the distribution of nourishment through the veins of the body, it is a different matter.

<margin>
The mineral tree.
</margin>
In the same way, the minerals from which metals are extracted and medicines are made (useful for the healing of human bodies) represent a certain tree of a vegetable kind. For their roots, which are a twofold smoke of sulfur and <term>quicksilver: mercury, often paired with sulfur in alchemical theory as the "parents" of all metals</term>, are closer to the center of the earth. From there, tending toward the upper parts, they extend their veins through the rocks and tracts of the earth wonderfully, so that they truly represent the form of some great tree propagating its branches far and wide, if they could be seen with the eyes—as is evident from the experience of those who search for those veins. If these things be so, it is clear what was meant by those trees bearing golden apples. For surely these are trees growing not in the open air, but under the earth, which bear golden apples; provided that those of a better nature are distinguished from the wild ones. For in this the whole difficulty lies: namely, to choose those which are suitable for the Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy, the practice of purifying or transforming materials.</note>. Therefore *Morienus* <note>Morienus Romanus, a semi-legendary alchemist said to have taught the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> at the end of his treatise adds these notable words:

> Likewise, know that the greatest root of this work lies in the investigation of the species which are better for this mastery: For every single mineral is of many kinds. <note>original: "Similiter scias quod maior radix huius operis est in inquisitione specierum, quæ sunt meliores ad hoc magisterium: Nam unaquaque minera multorum est generum."</note>

Concerning these mineral trees growing under the earth...

...growing, almost all authors have mentioned them in various words, implying the same thing: namely, that the **golden fruit** must be taken along with its tree and transplanted. 

As Flamel <note>original: "Fla." refers to Nicolas Flamel, the legendary 14th-century French scrivener and alchemist.</note> says: *“The fixed grain is like an apple, and Mercury is the tree; the fruit, therefore, must not be separated from the tree, because it cannot receive nourishment from anywhere else.”* And shortly after: *“whereby it may be planted again without removing the fruit, into a more fertile and noble earth, which will give more nourishment in one day than the previous field would have provided in a hundred years, because of the constant agitation of the winds.”* <note>The "agitation of the winds" likely refers to the alchemical process of sublimation or the circulation of vapors within a vessel.</note> *“The other earth, because it is closest to the Sun, makes the tree grow and flourish with continuous dew and constant Sunlight in the **Philosophical Garden**, morning and evening, day and night, and at every hour without intermission; and while it shines, the tree is sprinkled and nourished with the sweetest dew, growing more in one year than it did in the previous earth in ten thousand.”*

and gold represent the flowers and fruits. Nothing clearer could be said to declare the subject of this art <note>The "art" refers to Alchemy.</note> and to explain what the **golden apples of the Hesperides** are, and how they grow. Nor should this seem so strange, as if it were contrary to nature, when we see daily through the **grafting** of shoots from various kinds of trees into wild or common trunks, a "nobilitation" of the fruit occurs. This makes it manifest how much can be achieved with plants, which consist of different and non-similar parts. Therefore, it is reasonable—and well known from experience—that in the mineral kingdom, especially in that which is purely **homogeneous** <note>of the same kind or nature throughout</note>, this can happen much more quickly and easily. 

It has long been known that the same thing happens in the bodies of animals and even in man himself; for instance, how the nose, ears, and similar parts can be repaired and restored from living human flesh. We ourselves were eyewitnesses to this matter in Bologna, where we were personally acquainted with the excellent **Gaspare Tagliacozzi**, who performed such things. <note>Gaspare Tagliacozzi (1545–1599) was a pioneer of plastic and reconstructive surgery; his "Italian method" for nasal reconstruction involved grafting skin from the arm.</note> Innumerable examples from the works of nature and art could be produced here to attest to the same thing, but it would be unnecessary...

### 84

...we believed it would be so, since the perceptions of the craftsmen do not seek help or proof from reason, but on the contrary: 

<margin>1. An example from the vegetable kingdom</margin>
Let this one instance suffice for us in this place: In certain locations, where in the winter time everything is stiff with frost and ice, if a small branch is cut from an apple tree around the beginning of December and placed in water for several days in warm places or **hypocausts** <note>original: "Hypocaustis," referring to rooms heated from below or via stoves, common in early modern laboratories and homes.</note>, it produces leaves and flowers striking in their beauty and novelty. This is a fact known even to common people. However, from this, the Philosophers recognize the **first matter** <note>original: "materiam primam," the primal substance from which all things are made</note> lying hidden within the tree branches, and they judge similarly regarding the golden apples contained within their own branches and roots. This is enough for the intelligent. Or, if it pleases you, we shall add a rarer example of vegetable nature, which can illustrate this matter in no small way: 

<margin>2. A rarer example.</margin>
There are those who, around the 25th day of November, hide cabbage leaves in a trench a foot and a half deep under the earth; they leave them there under the open sky through the winter snows and cold until the 25th of March, and then they take out from there not cabbage leaves, but the purest seed. Sworn witnesses have affirmed to me that they have done this every year. In this transmutation, we see that through **putrefaction** <note>The process of decay which alchemists believed was necessary to release the "seed" or essence of a substance.</note> alone, that vegetable (as they assert of other plants as well) is reduced to its first matter, from which it comes—or rather to its final matter, toward which it tends. This same thing must also happen in the **Chemical Art** <note>original: "artificio Chymico," referring to alchemy</note>, but in its own specific way. And so, our golden tree bearing apples has become well enough known to rational men, as has the explanation of this allegory.

<margin>Who the Nymphs are.</margin>
Now, in order for Hercules to seek out this tree, he went to the Nymphs of Jupiter and Themis, who lived near the **Eridanus** <note>The River Po in Italy, often associated in myth with falling stars and precious resins like amber.</note>, the gold-bearing river of Italy, in caves or subterranean mines. From them, he sought counsel. But why that? Because the works of nature must be consulted first; that is, one must consider how nature proceeds in its operations. For this reason, in many places, the Philosophers send the investigator to natural works to search out the true matter, inviting them to consider these things deeply, as can be seen throughout the writings of **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy whose works emphasized systematic experimentation.</note> and others. Those Nymphs living in caves or gold mines refer Hercules back to **Nereus**, who is the truthful son of the Sea and the Earth...

### 85

<margin>M 3</margin>

<margin>Who Nereus was.</margin>
He was believed to be a prophet; he foretold the Trojan calamities to Paris; and was called the most ancient of the Gods by Orpheus. Hercules, coming to him as he tried to evade him by changing into various shapes, held him fast until he returned to his original form and revealed the matter at hand. He was the father of fifty Nereids <note>sea nymphs in Greek mythology</note>, raised and nourished by the waves, whose daughters are said to run especially around the chariot of Triton. This Nereus is the **First Being** <note>original: "primum Ens," the primary substance or "first matter" sought by alchemists</note> that the Philosophers often commanded to be sought, without which the path or passage to the golden apples <note>the "Golden Apples of the Hesperides," symbolizing the goal of the alchemical work</note> does not lie open.

<margin>Who Prometheus was.</margin>
But Prometheus, named from *prometheia* <note>Greek: προμηθείας</note>, that is, from "providence" or "forethought," to whom one is sent by Nereus for counsel, brought down fire to men. He is considered a fire-bearing Titan, a friend to the Ocean, and a contemplator of divine things, who shared a common altar with Vulcan <note>the god of fire and smithing</note> and Pallas <note>Athena, goddess of wisdom</note>. By his advice, Saturn was cast down by Jupiter into Tartarus <note>the deep abyss of the underworld</note>. From there, Saturn escaped to Italy and came to Janus, who was then reigning there, by whom he was kindly received with hospitality. Saturn taught Janus the way of living and the cultivation of fields. In return for the instruction he received, Janus is said to have rewarded him with half of his kingdom. On the coins, which were first struck by his ingenuity, there was a ship on one side and a two-faced image on the other; this was because the kingdom was governed by the shared counsel of Janus and Saturn, as Ovid records in Book 1 of the *Fasti*. 

However, we do not doubt that through Prometheus, a prior **speculation of the mind** <note>original: "mentis speculationem," the intellectual or theoretical preparation</note> concerning this work is expressed, which is why he had an altar in common with Pallas [Wisdom] and Vulcan [Fire]. Nor is he undeservedly said to have given counsel to Jupiter about imprisoning his father and thrusting him down to the underworld. For by this speculation of the mind, all this is foreseen—namely, that after the dark **blackness** <note>original: "nigredinem," referring to the *nigredo* stage of decomposition and purification</note>, the **whiteness** <note>original: "albedinem," the *albedo* stage of purification and washing</note> will follow. Ancient histories do mention the Reign of Janus and Saturn, but only through the fables of the Poets. For the heathens were persuaded that the god Saturn, son of Heaven and Earth, was expelled from his kingdom by the god Jupiter, and suffered many other things. But these are all Hieroglyphics, and handed down by the Egyptians or

...or fashioned by the Greeks for those things which they wished to wrap in such coverings: By *Two-Faced Janus* <note>original: "Ianum Bifrontem," the Roman god of beginnings and transitions, depicted with two faces looking in opposite directions</note>, we understand one matter or thing, called **Rebis** <note>a central alchemical term meaning "double thing," representing the union of opposites like spirit and body, or mercury and sulfur</note>, and containing two things—or if you prefer, a double mercurial substance. For there is no doubt that this was the emblem of that voyage, containing both the ship and the livestock whose fleece was golden. 

Besides many others, *Greverus* <note>likely Jodocus Greverus, a 16th-century German alchemist</note> among the moderns mentions these golden apples, and his works can be read for themselves. From the same Garden <margin>3. *The Golden Apple of Eris.*</margin> of the *Hesperides*, the Golden Apple of *Eris* <note>the goddess of Discord</note> was also sought, which was the primary cause of the Trojan War; we shall speak of this in the following Book 6. 

Especially significant are those three golden apples <margin>4. *The golden apples cast before Atalanta.*</margin> which are imagined to have been handed by Venus to *Hippomenes*, to be thrown before *Atalanta*. For since this royal maiden was not only most outstanding in the gift of beauty, but also most celebrated in the art of hunting and throwing the javelin, she attracted many suitors to herself. But her father, *Schoeneus*, was unwilling to give her in marriage to anyone except the man by whom she—otherwise most swift of foot—was defeated; the maiden would be granted to the victor, while death was decreed for the vanquished. 

Therefore, while many attempted this in vain and met their deaths, *Hippomenes*, by the counsel and gift of *Venus*, threw the three golden apples one after another before the running maiden; because of this, she was delayed by the desire to pick them up, was defeated, and was given as a wife to *Hippomenes*. Who, when out of an impatience of love he lay with his bride in the temple of the Mother of the Gods <note>Cybele, the ancient Phrygian earth goddess</note>, he stirred up the anger of that goddess against himself, whereupon both, marked by lion skins and wildness, took to the woods <note>according to the myth, they were transformed into lions as punishment for desecrating the temple</note>. Moreover, *Atalanta* is said to have competed with men in the hunt and [the glory] of victory...

...was given a prize because of the boar of remarkable size killed by *Meleager* <note>In Greek myth, Meleager led the hunt for the Calydonian Boar and gave the hide to the huntress Atalanta</note>. It has become known through the testimonies of many that this "Royal Virgin" is our **matter** <term>materia: the raw starting substance of the alchemical Great Work</term>; but she is fleeting and has wings on her feet—namely, the winged sandals of *Mercury*. She kills the boar because she is a second *Diana* <note>The goddess of the hunt, often associated with the moon and silver</note>; she draws a spring from the rock near the temple of *Aesculapius* because the hardest **philosophical stones** <term>petræ philosophicæ: the mineral matter used by alchemists</term> yield water. Thus *Ripley* <note>Sir George Ripley, a famous 15th-century English alchemist</note> says in his figure: *He produced water from the earth and oil from the hardest rock.*

### 88

[She] had golden horns and bronze feet, and was sacred and inviolable to *Diana* <note>The goddess of the hunt; in alchemy, she often represents the lunar, cool, or silver principle</note>; Therefore, she was not to be captured by arrows or spears, nor by dogs, but by running. For it was not fitting for blood to flow from her wounds; for in that way she would either be diminished in strength or utterly destroyed. Instead, she had to be taken alive and in perfect health; thus, she was to be exhausted by running alone. She lived on Mount *Maenalus*, where the boar and the lion and other such beasts dwell. *Hercules*, sent for her by *Eurystheus* <note>The king who imposed the twelve labors on Hercules</note> so that he might bring her to him, is said to have spent a whole year running before he was able to exhaust her. But finally, weary, she fled to Mount *Artemisius* and was captured at the river *Ladon* just as she was about to swim across, and was carried to *Mycenae* upon his shoulders. Then they say *Eurystheus* was so struck by the virtue of *Hercules* that he prepared a bronze jar as a hiding place for himself and would not admit *Hercules* into the city.

Now, the hind is among the swiftest of animals, possessing black blood and "melancholic flesh" <note>Referring to the Four Humors; melancholy was associated with the element of earth, coldness, and dryness</note>, and is therefore of innate fear. She seeks safety by running if pressed, and is most powerful in her swiftness. But since she has bronze feet and golden horns, contrary to the common nature of hinds, she is somewhat held back and slowed in flight by these, so that she can be exhausted. For unless there were that very solar light, or golden radiance, within the fleeting and volatile **philosophical matter** <term>materia Philosophica: the "First Matter" used by alchemists to begin the Great Work</term>, it would almost never be observed to be halted or fixed.

<header>Book 2. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.</header>

### 89

More recent authors also mention this hind, but they join a **Unicorn** to it when they say: *“Philosophers say boldly that there are two animals in this forest: one is laudable, beautiful, and swift—a great and robust hind; the other is a unicorn,” as the Philosopher shows.* And **Basil Valentine** <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, often cited for his allegorical descriptions of chemical processes</note> relates that a donkey, after rotting under the earth, was transformed into a hind with golden horns. It also has bronze feet, resplendent and white. This is because the thing whose head is red, eyes are black, and feet are white, is our <term>magisterium</term> <note>The "Great Work" or the completion of the alchemical process</note>. And it is well known how often the <term>philosophical bronze</term> <note>Latin: *æs philosophicum*; a symbolic metal, often referring to a purified state of matter rather than common bronze</note> is repeated; for this is the foundation and basis of the work, so it is not without merit that the animal’s feet refer to it.

The hind is sacred to **Diana** <note>The Roman goddess of the moon and nature</note>, because it was customary to sacrifice a hind to her, as is clear in the allegory of **Iphigenia** <note>In myth, Diana saved Iphigenia from sacrifice by replacing her with a hind</note>. Now, Diana represents the lunar nature; for the Sun and Moon together constitute the entire composition. The hind is exhausted by running—that is, it is shut within its vessel, and by ascending and descending <note>Refers to the process of reflux or circulation in a glass vessel</note> it is blocked from fleeing until the matter, as if tired, remains at the bottom and no longer ascends. This is achieved by a gentler fire; if the full force of the fire were applied too soon, violence would be done to this fleeting animal.

Weary, she fled to **Mount Artemisius** and was captured at the **River Ladon**. This was necessary so that the virgin <note>Representing the pure, unreacted substance</note> might remain inviolate, as she was sacred to Diana, who is called **Artemis**—a name some interpret as <term>aerotemis</term> <note>Original Greek: *ἀεροτέμις*; literally "air-cutting," implying a spirit that moves swiftly through the air</note>, or as others suggest, because she makes things whole or healthy, as **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian</note> attests in Book 14. **Ladon** is a river of **Arcadia**, from whose daughter **Metope** and the Theban river **Asopus**, the nymph **Thebe** (who gave her name to the city) is said to have been born. **Ladon** is also the name of the serpent guarding the golden apples, as previously mentioned. Whichever way one looks at it, the sense fits the subject. The hind lived on **Mount Maenalus** in Arcadia, a place abundant in minerals, where the "Maenalian verses" were composed. This location was highly celebrated by the poets.

She is carried to **Mycenae** on the shoulders of **Hercules** so that she is not harmed. But why did such great fear seize **Eurystheus** <note>The king who commanded Hercules' labors</note> upon the capture of the hind, when he had seen Hercules lay low far more monstrous beasts, such as the lion, the boar, the hydra, and the like? It seems that it is a greater feat to conquer by art than by Mars <note>By skill and nature rather than by brute force or war</note>, by patience than by haste, and by gentleness than by violence. Hence, for a whole year...

[The seeker] exhausted the beast by continuous running and pursuit; 
for thus the logic of the work requires: *For we take a whole year,* 
says **Ripley** <note>original: "Riplæus"; referring to George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a famous English alchemist and canon of Bridlington</note>, *before we prepare our <term>calx</term> <note>The powder or "ash" resulting from the calcination of a metal, a primary stage in the Great Work</note>: For in a shorter space of time our calx cannot be finished, capable of fusion with a color that does not vanish.* Mythologists, in order to explain these fables according to their own capacity, turn **Hercules** into the sun of the heavens, who runs through an entire year and chases I know not what hind with golden horns; but because these interpretations are easily recognized as being distorted from their genuine nature to a foreign one, they do not stand firm, nor do they provide any utility to the minds of readers or listeners, except for mists and darkness, which we have discussed to some extent.

<margin>6. Concerning Midas, the participant in the golden wish.</margin>
Furthermore, **Midas** holds the symbol of gold, as well as the vow [or wish]; which he obtained from **Bacchus**, because he had kindly received **Silenus** <note>The tutor and companion of Bacchus, often depicted as a wise, drunken old man</note>. Specifically, he asked that whatever he touched might be converted into gold. The wretch was almost killed by hunger, unless, led by repentance for his wish, he had again obtained a cessation of this "gold-making." The remedy was that he should wash himself in the **Pactolus** river, which transferred this "gold-sickness" <note>original: "auriginem"</note> to itself, so that from then on it threw out golden sands. It is a very pretty little tale, not unpleasant to the ears nor the eyes, since it shows nothing but gold—which is burned for and thirsted after by everyone—and it is most fit for declaring and restraining the insatiable appetite of the greedy. For it is clear that many are **Midas** in their wish, but very few in the result: because to desire an immensity of wealth is within anyone's will, but to obtain it is by the gift of God. But what god is it who granted such a harmful gift to the petitioner? A fictitious and Hieroglyphic one, not He who is truly God and is so called, who gives us goods that are more useful than they are pleasing, as a father does for his little sons. 

For **Bacchus**, who is also **Dionysus** and **Osiris**, is the primary of the "golden gods," and therefore the granter of such a great gift. But it is fitting to receive kindly **Silenus**, his teacher or companion; who, sitting on a sway-backed little donkey, though he be mocked as an old man by boys, nevertheless has more in his hidden recesses than he promises on his face. 

<margin>The Sileni of Alcibiades.</margin>
From here that saying about the **Sileni of Alcibiades** became frequent, a gibe against **Socrates**, who was most ugly on the outside, but most beautiful within <note>A reference to Plato's *Symposium*, where Socrates is compared to hollow statues of Silenus that, when opened, contain beautiful figurines of the gods</note>...

More specifically, however, this refers to the "gold-making power" impressed upon its own subject; this power is immense and always capable of being multiplied, unless it is restrained and that fiery virtue is quenched in its own water. Concerning marvelous golden things.

To these we shall add other golden symbols and hieroglyphs of antiquity which did not truly exist in the nature of things, but were invented by artists and poets to declare other matters through them. Such are the **Golden Age**, the **golden rain**, the **golden harvest**, and similar things. It is commonly accepted regarding the **Golden Age** that it once occurred under the reign of King **Saturn**, just as the Silver Age occurred under **Jupiter**, and afterwards the Bronze and Iron Ages under others.

<margin>The Golden Age</margin>
But if Saturn was neither a god, nor a man, nor a king, then in truth no "Golden Age" ever existed. Even if we grant that he was a king, was the time under him truly more "golden" than under Jupiter? Perhaps because Jupiter was impious toward his father, whom he castrated, and was an adulterer and a murderer? But is not Saturn also depicted as such—he who castrated his father **Caelus** <note>The personification of the Sky (Uranus)</note>, took his sister **Rhea** as his wife and **Philyra** as his mistress (among others), and devoured his own children? But regarding gold and its generation in the air, even if we were to read of it, we would not grant it belief. Yet there is no doubt that miraculous rains have sometimes occurred by the will of God, as in the time of **Moses** in **Egypt**, or by magical power (as in the same place), and that they can still occur, since experience testifies to this in all ages and places; but that golden rains fell in Rhodes could be held as certain if by divine fate and miracle [sent...]

<margin><unclear>Golden rain falling in Rhodes.</unclear></margin>

For theoretical science is a perfect Virgin, and is born only from the brain of Jupiter as its nursery, nor is it mixed with Vulcanian or smithing arts. Hence the same Pallas manfully repelled Vulcan when he tried to force himself upon her, and from their quarrel **Erichthonius** took his origin.

# BOOK THREE.

# ON THE GOLDEN

### Genealogy of the Gods and Goddesses, from which, as if from a Philosophical tree, countless branches of Hieroglyphic Heroes are propagated.

<image-desc>Large ornate decorative drop cap 'R' featuring stylized vines, leaves, and flowers within a square border.</image-desc>

To attempt a refutation of the pagan Gods and Goddesses—who were accepted for so many ancient centuries by Poets and Historians, and indeed by the greater part of the world—in this, our almost final age, in which the Christian religion by the grace of God shines most brightly, would be like unweaving a web that has been woven over many thousands of years, and would perhaps be a labor in vain. This is partly because such a refutation is unnecessary for Christians who are already sufficiently confirmed in their faith, and partly because it might seem impossible to the Heathen <note>original: "Ethnicis"; referring to non-Christian, particularly Greco-Roman, authors</note> writers, who filled nearly everything with the superstitious deeds of the Gods and the Heroes descended from them. Therefore, let no one think that we have compiled this treatise for the purpose of making the truth of doctrine visible now for the first time, or so that the falsehood of the Heathen deities might be detected; for that has long been known from sacred history <note>A reference to the Bible and established Church history</note>, which is beyond all exception. Nevertheless, since things that do not help when taken individually may be of great benefit when gathered together, and since it is permitted to light a lamp in private houses even when the Sun occupies the middle of the Sky, so that places which are darker...

# Hieroglyphics, Book 3

...are, they can be looked into deeply; we have not unreasonably thought that we would be doing something worthwhile if we were to make the genealogies of the Gods and Goddesses—which are quite entangled in themselves and have not yet been traced back by anyone to their true origin from which they flowed—clearer through our own modest illustration.

<margin>No knowledge arises from negative propositions.</margin>
For it does not seem that much light is added to the human intellect if one merely knows that the things or persons held as Gods—and believed to be such for very long ages—are not actually Gods, as compared to if one investigates from the fountains of truth what was understood by the wiser ancients, and what ought to be understood, through those things or persons, since they are not gods. For anyone can imagine that they were not introduced in vain or by chance. To perform this, according to the talent granted to us by the highest Giver, in the first book we unfolded the principal Egyptian matters, called Hieroglyphics; in the second, we ran through the more conspicuous Greek Allegories, marked with gold. Now we shall review the golden

<margin>The golden genealogy of the gods.</margin>
family of the Gods and Goddesses, from which, as if from a numerous Chain <note>original: "Cathena"; referring to the "Chain of Being" or a genealogical lineage</note>, the progeny of Gods and Heroes depends, with which the World has struggled until now. Homer,

<margin>Homer’s golden chain.</margin>
in the 8th book of the *Iliad*, relates that all the Gods, hanging from a golden chain, tried to drag Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, the king of the gods</note> down from Heaven, yet their attempt was in vain. For if Jupiter were removed, the greatest part of those of whom he is the Progenitor would be taken away. Thus he outweighs all others in authority and dominion, because the empire of Heaven, as they say in fables, fell to him. All the Heathens worshipped him as the greatest of the Gods; but since he is not said to have risen from himself, but from parents prior to him in time, we shall begin with them. Since even they—namely Saturn and Rhea—are not recognized as being without any origin, but are also born from others, we shall proceed to these: namely, Heaven and Earth. The Heathens, without any tradition of Sacred Scripture or presupposed knowledge, conceived various opinions about God and the parts of the world out of the thick darkness of the human mind. Some contemplated a first eternal cause, but joined to it the world as an effect co-eternal with it, such as the Peripatetics <note>original: "Peripatetici"; followers of Aristotle's philosophy, known for walking while teaching</note>...

### Book 3: Egyptian-Greek Matters
<page-num>97</page-num>

...with his **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC) famously argued that the universe was eternal, having no beginning and no end.</note>; others believed that God, as the eternal efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is a philosophical term for the agent or force that brings something into being.</note>, did not establish the World from eternity, but voluntarily in time, like the **Platonists**, along with the divine **Plato**; their opinion is more similar to that of Christians than the rest of the Philosophers. Some imagined that the world flowed together by chance from atoms; others fashioned the idea that certain smaller parts were made, or coagulated one after another, like butter from milk. Thus the **Arcadians** <note>The Arcadians of ancient Greece were nicknamed "Proselēnoi," meaning "before the moon," because they claimed their ancestors inhabited the land before the moon existed in the sky.</note> boasted that they existed
<margin>See Censorinus on these matters. <note>Censorinus was a 3rd-century Roman grammarian who wrote "De Die Natali," a work discussing the origins of humanity and the world.</note></margin>
before the Moon; and others, trying to solve that question—whether the egg was before the hen, or the hen before the egg in the nature of things—hand down stories of the miraculous births of men and animals, just as we narrated regarding Egyptian customs at the beginning of the first book. And since these people did not recognize the **Creator** of heaven and earth, who made all things from nothing <note>original: "ex nihilo"</note>, they thought that all animals, as well as plants, sprang forth of their own accord from earth and water mixed in various proportions, with air and fire joining in; and that heaven and earth had always existed without origin. Therefore, if they held them to be works made or created, they feared they would be forced to admit an efficient cause for them as well, and so progress into infinity; to avoid this, they accepted Heaven and Earth themselves as the first unbegotten gods. They encompassed the air within Heaven, and the water (or Ocean and seas) within Earth. Besides these, they established that rivers, springs, mountains, and winds were of the same age as earth and heaven—either relatives or kin; or, what is more believable, born from the first sexual union. From Heaven and Earth, therefore, the birth of all the **Gods** is derived, as well as all other things. 

But although there is no need to offer a response to such frivolous and most absurd opinions, nevertheless we shall include many things in a very few words, by which their intention is utterly destroyed: If man comes from man of double sex, and the remaining animals likewise come from their own seed—and plants, too, always arise from their like—and this occurs in time according to individual instances; then nothing of them is produced by chance, nor is anything eternal according to individuals, nor indeed according to the species. 
<margin>Reasoning against the opinions of the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum"</note> concerning individuals propagated from eternity.</margin>
And what is true of the parts, there is no reason why it should not also be most true of the whole...

### Book 3 of the Hieroglyphics
<page-num>98</page-num>

is held as certain; but first, it is confirmed by experience itself. The reason for this connection is well known: because whatever arises from the seed of its own species arises naturally and not by chance; and that which has arisen in time across all individuals cannot be said to be eternal in the past. Therefore, it follows as a truth: Thus Man and the rest of the animals, plants, and all parts, species, and contents of the earth and water, the air, and the whole of Heaven with its contents, were not from eternity, but began to exist in time. They did not come from themselves; therefore, they came from another. Who is that other? The God of Gods, the Creator of creatures. Since other arguments are well known, let us pass over them here and consider Heaven and Earth—believed to be the first and great Gods—along with their offspring. We do not deny that some of the wiser Heathens <note>original: "Ethnicorum"</note>, seeing such a great crowd of Gods which must eventually be reduced to the unity of a first cause, reduced almost all the Gods to the elements of the larger world <note>The "greater world" or macrocosm refers to the universe or nature itself.</note>, and thus silently renounced a plurality of deities. Among these, **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC) was a Roman scholar who sought to explain traditional religion through physical and social allegories.</note> is most occupied with ensuring the Gods do not appear to be entirely fables. But since this opinion harbors many absurdities and is not according to the intention of the authors who first brought this kinship of the Gods from Egypt into Greece, we reject it entirely. From

<margin>The Golden Chain of Gods, Goddesses, and Heroes, or Genealogy.</margin>
**Heaven** and **Earth**, therefore, **Saturn** and **Rhea** were born; then Titan, Iapetus, Thetis, Ceres, Themis, and others whom **Hesiod** <note>Hesiod was an ancient Greek poet whose "Theogony" describes the origins and family trees of the gods.</note> enumerates. From Saturn and Rhea came **Jupiter**, **Juno**, **Neptune**, Glauca, and Pluto. From Saturn and Philyra came **Chiron**; from the genitals of Saturn, **Venus**. From Juno alone, **Hebe**. From Jupiter alone (after he had swallowed his wife Metis), **Pallas** <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom, who was famously born fully grown from Jupiter's forehead.</note> from his head. From Jupiter and his wife Juno came **Vulcan** and **Mars**. To Jupiter from his mistress Latona, **Apollo** and **Diana**. From Maia, **Mercury**. From Semele, **Dionysius**. From Danae, **Perseus**. From Alcmena, **Hercules**. From Leda came **Pollux** and **Helen**, and **Castor** and **Clytemnestra**, from two eggs <note>According to the myth, Jupiter visited Leda in the form of a swan; she later produced eggs from which these four children hatched.</note>. From Europa came **Minos** and **Rhadamanthus**. From Antiope, **Amphion** and **Zethus**. From Thalia, the **Palici** brothers. From Ceres, **Proserpina**. And these are the most prominent among the many sons of Jupiter, of whom alone—omitting the rest—we shall treat hereafter;

### Book 1 of the Egyptian-Greeks
<page-num>99</page-num>

Next, we shall touch upon a few of the more distinguished among his grandsons and great-grandsons. We will pass over the majority of **Neptune's** eighty sons (according to the usual count) born from various Nymphs, as well as others, for the sake of brevity. 

<margin>Heaven and Earth</margin>
We do not object to the idea that **Heaven** and **Earth** <note>original: "Cælum et Terrā"</note> joined together, if this is understood naturally—insofar as Heaven is the active force and Earth the passive, the former being "form" and the latter "matter"—regarding the creation of things and whatever springs from their seed. However, if this is understood supernaturally, or as the words literally sound—as an act of generation or sexual union—then we judge this to be a hallucination that should be purged with hellebore <note>A plant used in antiquity as a remedy for madness or insanity.</note>, rather than refuted by reason or argument. 

It is a wonder that the Heathen Sages dreamed such a dream as to attribute testicles to **Heaven**, the father of **Saturn**, and to claim they were cut off by **Saturn** so that no more children would be born to him. No one in a workhouse <note>original: "ergastulis," referring to a Roman prison or slave-stable.</note> ever raved more than these so-called "sages"; no one has embraced a true opinion of God less than these men, who are called "Theologians," if it please the gods! 

But they will answer that this was done rationally—that is, that **Heaven** was castrated so that it would not generate another heaven or another earth. Yet, if everything generates its own like, then **Saturn**, **Rhea**, and the other children of **Saturn** would be new heavens and new earths. This, however, is not accepted by them. Instead, they mostly claim that **Time** comes from **Saturn**; various progenitors from **Titan** and **Iapetus**; a sea goddess from **Thetis**; a goddess of crops from **Ceres**; and a goddess of justice from **Themis**. 

Let us first look at **Saturn**, and consider the father through the son, or the following sons through this father: 

<margin>Saturn and Rhea. The Hieroglyphics of Saturn.</margin>
He was depicted by the ancients as a pale, bent old man, carrying a sickle in one hand and a dragon biting its own tail <note>The Ouroboros, a symbol of eternity and the cyclical nature of time.</note> in the other, while with his other hand he placed a small son to his mouth and devoured him. His head was covered by a helmet, over which was a cloak. He had four sons near him, from one of whom—**Jupiter**—he had his genitals cut off, from which **Venus** was born. 

They relate that although **Saturn** was younger than **Titan**, he nevertheless transferred the kingdom to himself. Because of this, a war broke out between **Titan** (and his sons, called the **Titans**) and **Saturn**. This war was settled by a law: that if any male children were born to **Saturn** from **Rhea**, they would be put out of the way <note>Literally "removed from the midst," meaning killed or hidden.</note>. And so **Saturn**...

### Book 3 of Hieroglyphics
<page-num>100</page-num>

He <note>Saturn</note> ordered the newborn **Jupiter** <note>The Roman name for Zeus.</note> to be brought to him; but, having been outwitted by **Rhea**, he received instead a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes, which he promptly devoured in place of **Jupiter**. Meanwhile, **Jupiter** was raised elsewhere in Crete by the **Corybantes** <note>Armed priests or dancers who clashed their shields to drown out the cries of the infant god.</note> until he reached the proper age. In the same manner, **Neptune** and **Pluto** are said to have been saved from the voracity of **Saturn** by **Rhea**, who was always offering him something else in their stead. 

When **Saturn** fell in love with **Philyra**, the daughter of Ocean, he was surprised by his wife **Ops** <note>Another name for Rhea.</note> and transformed himself into a horse; from this union he fathered **Chiron**, the most just and wise of the centaurs (the teacher of so many disciples, including *Jason*, *Hercules*, and *Achilles*). Afterward, **Saturn** suffered the very same fate from his son that he had inflicted upon his own father—namely, castration and being cast down from his kingdom. This followed the rule: *A man is punished by the very things through which he sins* <note>original: "Per quae quis peccat, per eadem punitur." This is a common moralizing proverb derived from the Wisdom of Solomon.</note>. 

Then, the son of Heaven is said to have come to *Italy* as a fugitive. It is a wonder that such a tiny portion of the earth could support the son of so great a father, and that it received him as an exile hiding in that very place (from which they claim the name *Latium* is derived) <note>A traditional folk etymology: the region Latium was thought to be named from the Latin verb "latere," meaning to hide.</note>. But the Heathens were pleased to trifle in this way so that they might trace the names, foundations, and governments of their regions and cities back to one of the most ancient Gods, so that they might be believed to have sprung and descended from gods rather than from men.

<margin>Note</margin>
*In ancient times, the altar of **Saturn** was honored by the lighting of wax candles, and candles were sent to one another by the wealthier citizens. This was because **Saturn** was seen to be, or to signify, the light of human life, and was considered the inventor of many comforts. When the **Saturnalia** <note>A famous Roman mid-winter festival of role-reversal and gift-giving.</note> was celebrated in honor of this God among the Romans, the masters would serve the slaves. Above all else, it is memorable that (as **Natalis** <note>Noël Conti, a famous 16th-century mythographer.</note> cites from **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure linked to alchemy and wisdom.</note>) three truly wise men flourished in the time of **Trismegistus**: namely, Heaven, Saturn, and Mercury. Most thinkers, as has been said, have explained **Saturn** as **Time**, as if he arose from the motion of the heavens. They say he is "alone" (hence Saturn), just as the heaven was despoiled of its virile members <note>An allegory: once the universe was created, the "generative" act of heaven ceased.</note>. Likewise, they say that **Time** devours all things, and consumes all its children who are generated in and by time, sparing none—except perhaps the hardest stones. For this reason, the stone was vomited up by Saturn—*

<meta>This page continues the author's philosophical and alchemical interrogation of the Saturn myth. <header>Book 3 of the Egyptian-Greeks.</header>
<page-num>101</page-num>

...said to be cast out by this action: These things are indeed similar, but as the saying goes, they "do not walk on four feet" <note>A Latin idiom meaning the argument is inconsistent or does not hold up logically.</note>. For if Heaven <note>original: "Cœlus," the personification of the sky/Uranus.</note> is the father of Time <note>Saturn/Cronus</note>, why is Earth <note>Terra/Gaia</note> the mother? Did Earth conceive time? What does the earth contribute to the production of time? What does heaven contribute, unless you are looking only at the motion of the Planets? What if heaven stood still and only the Planets moved—would time not exist for that reason? Why is the Sun not rather held to be Time or the father of time—since he causes the year, the day and night, summer and winter, and the other successions of time—rather than *Saturn* or *Heaven*? Why is *Saturn* depicted as lame, when time is most swift and possesses wings faster than the winds? Why is he established as an old man, since time does not grow old, but rather represents a youth? For just as a flame of fire is always at its newest—not enduring as the same flame for even the smallest space of time, but always succeeded by another and then another new flame—so also time, and its momentum (which they call the "Now"), is always growing young, possessing nothing of old age. Does not the Dragon, which *Saturn* carries, signify youth rather than the circle of the year, since it sheds its skin? Is its appearance not the same as those snakes assigned to **Mercury**, **Aesculapius** <note>The god of medicine, often depicted with a serpent-entwined staff.</note>, the gardens of the **Hesperides**, and other places previously assigned? Does it denote the roundness of the year in one place, the harmony of two most opposing things in another, and elsewhere the prudence of the mind or supreme vigilance? However, the true reasoning of this Hieroglyphic is that which Basilius Valentinus <note>Basil Valentine, the legendary 15th-century alchemist whose writings were highly influential in the 17th century.</note> explains in these words:

> "I, Saturn," he says, "the highest of the Planets in the Firmament, testify before all you Lords that I am the most useless and vile among you; of a weak and corruptible body, black in color, subject to the injuries of many afflictions in this vale of misery; and yet, I am the tester of you all. For I do not have a permanent dwelling, and I carry away with me one who is like me; the cause of my misery is to be blamed on no one but the inconstant **Mercury**, who by his carelessness and negligence inflicted this evil upon me."

The same author in *Occult Philosophy*, Chapter 12: *On Generation*.

<meta>This page continues the author's investigation into the symbolic and alchemical nature of Saturn. Having previously questioned the literal interpretation of Saturn as "Time," the author now explores the specific physical attributes and myths associated with the deity—such as his lameness, the scythe, and the devouring of his children—reinterpreting them as allegories for natural processes and the initial stages of the alchemical "Great Work."</meta>

### Book 3 of the Hieroglyphics

...of *Saturn*; it is handed down that, through the fault of his nurse, he was exposed to many vices and made lame in one foot. Nevertheless, he was rendered docile in intellect—wise, clever, and cautious—so that he conquered everyone in war, except for two who were superior in riches and power. For this reason, he is seen as pale and stooped, namely on account of poor digestion. He carries a scythe because he is the tester of all things <note>original: "probator est omnium," suggesting Time's role in testing the endurance of all matter</note>. He carries a Dragon because it renews things, as if renewing itself. As for why the Dragon devouring its own head and tail <note>The Ouroboros, a symbol of eternity and the cyclical nature of the universe.</note> is so often insisted upon by authors, there is another reason, which anyone may see in that context; let them consider the difference with this present matter, and notice how much copper differs from lupine seeds <note>original: "æra Lupinis," a Latin idiom from Horace referring to play-money or worthless counters used in the theater, contrasted here with true gold.</note>, and golden things from leaden ones. 

He devours his sons, born of himself—for whom, if anyone wishes to substitute the four Elements or other bodies, it is just as well. His head is covered by a helmet because he is strong in war, but a cheap cloak is added over it; hence he is judged to be of a lowlier fortune. But what does the war with the *Titans* signify? It means that from among others of his kind, *Saturn* was to be chosen for the kingship, as he excelled the *Titans* if not in age, then in wisdom and authority. 

So that *Jupiter* might remain unharmed with *Juno*, a stone is offered [to Saturn] and swallowed. This is a fine fiction about such a great God, unless some secret <note>original: "arcani," referring to hermetic or alchemical secrets.</note> lay beneath it. But this stone may be seen on Mount Helicon, where it was left as a monument. Is the cast-off lust of *Saturn* the cause of all lust in nature, since from it *Venus* is said to have been born—she who is present in all things propagating themselves? Did so much good come to the world from the viscera of *Saturn*? 

O, human madness, to be received with Democritean laughter <note>Refers to Democritus, the "laughing philosopher," who mocked the follies of mankind.</note>; O, blindness of minds, to be deplored with Heraclitean weeping <note>Refers to Heraclitus, the "weeping philosopher," who despaired over the human condition.</note>, if the Heathens truly believed such things were done to their Gods by Gods, or to a father by a son. Truly, we will hardly presume this of those who left us sufficient testimony in their writings of how great and what kind of men they were. 

By *Saturn*, authors commonly understand the "blackness" <note>term: <term>Nigredo</term> (the initial, "black" stage of the alchemical process involving decomposition or putrefaction)</note> occurring at the beginning of the "Work." They mention this in many places where they observe the sequence of the Planets. And thus, through the castration of *Saturn* performed by *Jupiter*, they interpret—not inconveniently—the removal of that blackness, followed by a dark or ashy whiteness...
