...and he is said to have left **Hercules** as the governor of Egypt, and gave **Prometheus** the first position after Hercules. In the mountains of **India**, not far from the **Ganges River**, he erected two columns in the east, just as Hercules did in the west. He conquered the whole of India and subdued the cities of the East. His army was composed of farmers and women. After three years he returned from India, and soon traveled through **Libya** and the **Spanish lands**. He kept many women in his camps who indulged in choral dances and rhythmic leaps. Here, when he had founded **Nysa**, a most flourishing city in India by the **Indus River**, he married **Ariadne**. However, driven by a madness cast upon him by **Juno** <note>In myth, Juno (Hera) often persecuted the illegitimate children of Jupiter (Zeus), such as Dionysus.</note>, he traveled across the whole world. *Ovid: Metamorphoses, Book 4:* around him, lynxes, tigers, and panthers were accustomed to be present. The magpie among birds, and the leaves of the fig tree, and a crown of **Narcissus** were not unwelcome to him; and the **Dragon** <note>original: *Draco*; often referring to a great serpent in classical texts.</note> among reptiles. His priestesses were women called **Maenads**, **Thyades**, **Bacchae**, and **Mimallones**. Having turned into a lion while being carried on a ship, he put all the pirate sailors to flight, except for the pilot himself, so that they jumped into the sea and were immediately turned into dolphins. He slept for three years with **Proserpina** <note>The queen of the Underworld; this refers to Dionysus's descent into the realm of the dead.</note>, and then, being awakened, he indulged in dances with the **Nymphs**. He returned to his homeland from the Indian expedition after three years and defeated his enemies. And since he is the same as **Osiris**, as has been said, when he had been buried, he is said to have come back to life whole. He was fashioned by the ancients not only with horns, but even with a bull’s head. ...about which we will deal later: When he <note>Bacchus/Dionysus</note> had been torn apart in the war of **Jupiter** against the **Titans**, **Pallas** <note>Athena</note> brought his still-beating heart to **Jupiter**. He was the first of all to lead a triumph, and since he wore a miter <note>original: *mitra*; a headband or turban</note> around his head, the custom later remained for kings to use a diadem in imitation of him. If we wished to examine all these things to the quick and apply them according to the dignity of the matter about which they were fashioned, we might perhaps overstep the bounds of our intended brevity; therefore, we will treat them only succinctly, since the details for the most part shine forth from what has been said before and what will be declared afterward.

We have spoken of the burning of **Semele**, the mother of Bacchus, under the birth of **Aesculapius**; because the method is similar in both cases. The former <note>Aesculapius</note> is said to have been snatched and nourished from the ashes of **Coronis**, the latter <note>Bacchus</note> from the ashes of his mother Semele; the former by **Chiron**, the latter by **Mercury**, or both were raised by nymphs, the **Hyades**, the watery parts. He is **Bimater** <note>original: *Bimater*; "two-mothered"</note> because he was twice begotten from Mercury, as all the [alchemical] philosophers report: <margin>Lull: *Theoria Testamenti*, ch. 46.</margin> *For our son, they say, has two fathers and two mothers, and because he was dearly nourished in the fire, he therefore never dies.*

He is depicted as being sewn into Jupiter’s thigh so that he might mature; for so it is appropriate in the **Art** <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy</note>; for the fixed fixes the volatile. In this place, **Jupiter**, approaching the mortal **Semele** (who is endowed with very long hair) with his lightning-bolt, is our **Fire** kindled in the glass, which burns more than the fire of hell, as we have cited from **Ripley** <note>George Ripley, a famous 15th-century English alchemist</note> under the section on **Vulcan**. This Jupiter aids and matures our offspring; who, having been torn apart by earth-born or earthy parts, lived again whole with his limbs rejoined by mother **Ceres**, the watery substance. 

We have said enough of his birthplace and parents; the miracles he performed look to the same end—that he himself has the power of uniting and resuscitating other divided and dead things. He killed the **Amphisbaena** <term>Amphisbaena: A mythical serpent with a head at each end.</term>, a serpent with a double head; because the double serpent must be killed in the Art, one with wings and one without wings. The liquors produced by him are so called because the whole composite consists of water and earth; if therefore **Dionysus** has grown into a substance reduced to earth, it is not without cause that he is said to produce liquors. He is young, bearded, beardless, old, male, and female; for so says **Agmon** in the **Crowd** <note>original: *in turba*; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: *He is beardless, he says, and he is also most bearded; featherless, not flying, and he is also endowed with feathers and flying, and whatever you call him, you speak the truth; if you deny he is water, you have not denied falsely.*

<header>Book 3 of the Hieroglyphics</header>

Regarding the Egyptian tradition—which holds that **Ammon** <note>A Libyan deity often identified by the Greeks with Zeus/Jupiter</note> took his sister **Rhea** as his wife, and makes her the father of **Dionysus** and the nymph **Amalthea** his mother—we say that the Egyptians looked to the realities of nature rather than the names. Even though they assign different parents to **Dionysus** and different ones to **Osiris**, they nevertheless establish that they are one and the same. It is clear, therefore, that they themselves deny this is a literal history, but rather a **hieroglyphic** fiction invented to signify certain things. They look simultaneously toward the **Horn of Amalthea** <note>The Cornucopia, or horn of plenty</note>, the source of all abundance, and the **Gardens of the Hesperides**. By that local description of so many circumstances, the first inventors of these stories intended to suggest nothing else

<margin>Explanation of the most complete allegory.</margin>
than to place a universal allegory of the entire Work before the eyes of those who understand, with all its variations and parts. Indeed, I hardly think there exists a more evident comparison among more recent authors by which the operation of the entire Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy</note> is more clearly overshadowed than by this one: By the **boy**, the subject <note>The raw material of the alchemical process</note> is understood; by the **city of Nysa**, the **vessel**; where the narrow **Gates of Nysa** represent the sealing and closing of the vessel. The region, pleasant with various trees, vines, winds, flowers, and the songs of birds, denotes that everything necessary for life and pleasure is present for the subject therein. **Aristaeus** <note>A minor god associated with crafts like cheesemaking and beekeeping</note>, the most prudent and excellent craftsman, is put in charge of the work. It is also required that **Pallas** <note>Athena, representing Wisdom</note>, signifying a singular wisdom and subtlety of mind, be present. What is later added regarding **Saturn**—who, at the instigation of his sister Rhea (who had left Ammon), moved to war against Dionysus—we understand as the **Saturnine blackness** <note>The *nigredo* stage, the first phase of alchemy involving decay and darkening</note> appearing at the beginning of the work. The **Amazons**, virgin warriors, are present for Dionysus; for the "milk of a virgin" <note>A term for a specific alchemical solvent or mercurial water</note> accomplishes much, as does the power of a virgin; *For his mother is a virgin, and his father did not lie with her.* Dionysus conquers Saturn because the blackness ceases, and he takes the **Titans** by surrender; that is, he halts the smoky exhalations of the material. And Dionysus is a god of healthful worship because he was born for the salvation of men, just like **Aesculapius**. He tamed many monsters because the material itself bears the name and omen of "monsters" (as we have demonstrated before) until he tames it and fills deserted regions with colonists. ### Hieroglyphics, Book 3.

<margin>Anius.</margin>
When Apollo had lain with Rhoeo <note>original: "Rhio"</note>, and her father Staphylus <note>Staphylus means "bunch of grapes" in Greek, continuing the Dionysian theme</note> discovered she was pregnant, he shut her in a chest and cast her into the sea. The chest was eventually carried to Euboea, where in a certain cave she gave birth to **Anius**, whom she named thus from her grief <note>A play on the Greek word *ania*, meaning trouble or grief</note>. Later, this Anius had three daughters by the nymph Dorippe: **Spermo**, **Oeno**, and **Elais**. Apollo granted these three the power to obtain, whenever they wished, either grain, wine, or oil, according to the meaning of their names <note>Spermo represents seed/grain, Oeno represents wine, and Elais represents oil—the three staples of ancient life, here used as alchemical symbols for the products of the Work</note>. Others have considered **Dionysus** to be the Sun, just as they think **Ceres** is the Moon; thus Virgil writes in the first book of the *Georgics*: *O you most brilliant lights of the world*, and Orpheus in his hymns: *The bright Sun, whom they call by the name Dionysus*. 

But the poets speak in this way according to the common understanding of the masses. If Dionysus is **Osiris**—as is sufficiently proven elsewhere—and Apollo and Diana are the Sun and Moon, how can Apollo be called the son of Osiris (that is, the Sun the son of the Sun), to say nothing of other absurdities? However, from what has been said so far, all the remaining myths about Dionysus are easily understood: why he slept for three years, why he brought laws, why he is the God of dances, why he turned into a lion, why he was depicted with horns, why he returned to life after death, and why his nurses are said to have been "boiled" by Medea <note>Medea’s boiling of the nurses refers to the alchemical process of rejuvenation or "cooking" the matter in a vessel to bring it to a new state</note>, and other similar stories.

<margin>Perseus, 9th son of Jupiter.</margin>
Now we shall come to **Perseus**, the son of **Jupiter** and **Danaë**. Acrisius, the father of Danaë, shut his daughter in a subterranean bronze chamber within the palace courtyard because he had learned from an oracle that he would be killed by a grandson born from his daughter. When Jupiter fell in love with her, he is said to have flowed down from the roof in the likeness of gold. When she had received this into her lap, Jupiter revealed who he was and lay with her, from which union Perseus was born. 

<margin>The birth of Perseus.</margin>
Horace described this in the third book of his *Odes* as follows:

> *A bronze tower and robust doors*
> *and the grim watches of wakeful dogs*
> *had sufficiently fortified the imprisoned Danaë*
> *from nocturnal adulterers,*
> *if Jupiter and Venus had not laughed*
> *at Acrisius, the fearful guardian of the hidden virgin;*
> *for they knew the way would be safe and open* <note>original: "fore enim tutum iter & patens"</note>

Some authors claim that Danaë gave birth in secret and that the boy <note>Perseus</note> had completed three years of age before King Acrisius discovered the situation. At that point, Danaë was brought by her father to the altar of **Jupiter Herceios** <note>Jupiter of the Courtyard, the protector of the home</note> and interrogated as to who the father of the child was. Later, when the chest arrived at the island of **Seriphus**, it was pulled out with a net by **Dictys**, the king’s brother, who happened to be fishing there. Danaë begged him to open the chest; when he had unlocked it and learned who they were, he took them to his home and treated them with great kindness as if they were his own kin.

**Polydectes**, the king, later attempted to force himself upon Danaë. Because he could not succeed due to the presence of Perseus, he imposed a task upon the young man: to bring him the head of **Medusa**, claiming he wished to give it as a dowry for Hippodamia. This Polydectes is portrayed as the King of Seriphus and the great-great-grandson of Neptune. As Perseus was compelled to obey, he prepared himself for the journey. Equipped with these tools, Perseus set out toward Medusa, one of the **Gorgons**, who had the power to turn many men into stone. The Gorgons were described as having heads entwined with scaly serpents, tusks like boars, hands made of iron, and golden wings with which they flew. ...with the help of these <note>original: "rum ope," likely "Deorum ope" meaning "with the help of the gods"</note> he approached Medusa. Therefore, when Perseus was carrying back the severed head of Medusa and was refused hospitality by Atlas (despite being a son of Jupiter), he showed Medusa's head to him, saying:

> *"But since you value our friendship so little,*
> *Accept this gift," he said. And turning his own face*
> *Away, he held out Medusa’s shaggy features from the left.*
> *As massive as he was, Atlas became a mountain.*

Afterward, as Perseus was by chance playing with a discus, he accidentally wounded his grandfather **Acrisius** (who was unknown to him at the time) in the foot. From this wound, Acrisius died, just as the oracle had predicted. From the spilled blood of Medusa, **Pegasus** and **Chrysaor** were born.

are formed; Pegasus, the winged horse, was led to Pallas <note>Athena</note>, by whom he was given to Bellerophon, the son of Glaucus (grandson of Sisyphus, great-grandson of Aeolus, and great-great-grandson of Jupiter) for the purpose of slaying the **Chimera**, a three-formed monster born of Typhon and Echidna. This Bellerophon—as Theopompus writes in the seventh book of his *Philippics* according to legendary tradition—did not pierce the Chimera with arrows while riding Pegasus, but rather attacked it with a certain spear that had lead fixed upon its tip. When Bellerophon thrust this part of the spear into the Chimera’s mouth, the lead was melted by the fire (which the monster breathed from its mouth) and flowed down into the Chimera's belly, consuming all its vitals, from which it died. This was a clever stratagem devised by Bellerophon; but if anyone takes this as a literal historical event, or fails to perceive for what reason and regarding what matter it was invented, he might be judged to have a "leaden wit" <note>original: "plumbeus ingenio," a pun on the lead used in the story and a dull or heavy intellect</note>. 

<margin>The origin of the Fountain of Helicon.</margin> It is handed down that from the hoof of this same Pegasus, the fountain **Hippocrene** <note>literally "The Horse's Fountain"</note> was struck forth on two-peaked Parnassus, from which the Muses, Apollo, poets, and all learned men drink and emerge more enlightened. Thus the erudition of poets flows from the fountain of Parnassus, the fountain from the hoof of Pegasus, Pegasus from the blood of Medusa, and Medusa was fathered by a sea monster and slain by Perseus. *Perseus comes from Jupiter, Jupiter from Saturn, and Saturn from Heaven <note>Caelum</note>, hanging down like a golden chain.* The same must be said of **Chrysaor**, who is the father of the three-bodied **Geryon**, the possessor of the purple-red oxen. But who would not recognize this allegory of Perseus from what has preceded? Nevertheless, we shall add a few points: The golden rain and Jupiter descending into the lap of **Danaë** denotes neither greed nor pleasure bought with gold (except secondarily), but rather because it is suitable for the <term>philosophic artifice</term> <note>a reference to the Alchemical "Great Work"</note>. For there, gold is mixed with gold, and from both 

*our son is born in the air, as **Ripley** <note>Sir George Ripley, a famous 15th-century English alchemist</note> has it in his sixth Gate, lest he sweat too much from the harshness of the blowing coals:* 

And the *Rosarium* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a key alchemical text</note> says: *Conception and betrothal take place in the putrefaction at the bottom of the vessel, and the generation of those begotten occurs in the air, namely in the head of the vessel, that is, the <term>alembic</term> <note>the top part of a still used for distillation</note>:* 

And **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the Arab alchemist Ibn Umail</note> says: *Just as we see the sun having two rays raining down upon the dead ash, and that which had been surrendered to death revives, like one who died after great poverty: This is the sister and this is the brother.*

# Hieroglyphics, Book 3.
<header>Book 3. Hieroglyphics.</header>

<margin>Riddle:</margin>
...[his bones] were found, because an oracle had predicted that they must be searched for and would be found in that place where the winds, the striker, the repercussion, and the ruin of men were found together. When Lychas <note>A Spartan who, according to Herodotus, discovered the bones of Orestes</note> interpreted this as a blacksmith’s shop, he understood the winds to be the bellows; the striker as the hammer; the repercussion as the anvil; and the ruin of men as iron. The bones of Orestes were found there, near the shrine of the Fates <note>original: "Parcarum fanum"</note> in the tomb of Agamemnon, and were buried there as the oracle commanded.

<margin>Note.</margin>
To those who are ignorant, nothing seems more absurd than this fiction; yet to those who understand, hardly anything seems more elegant. We have already considered who Agamemnon was during the Trojan War; here it is clear that Clytemnestra is the daughter of Jupiter <note>original: "Iovis filiam"</note>, although others might assert that the egg from which Castor and Clytemnestra were produced belonged to Tyndareus <note>The mortal King of Sparta and husband of Leda</note>. In both cases, the same truth is apparent. You might say it is a strange thing for women to lay eggs and imitate birds; but to the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicis"</note> it did not seem strange, because Jupiter had approached Leda in the form of a swan. However, outside of allegory, we know this to be monstrous and a complete lie. Nor is it enough to think that some sort of moral fiction lies beneath it; for one may invent moralities about everything, whether for good or for evil. But the genuine secrets of nature <note>The author distinguishes "moral" interpretations from "natural" or alchemical ones</note> contained and hidden within these stories are not so easily manipulated. Among the practitioners of alchemy <note>original: "chymiæ artifices"</note>, it is very frequently repeated that the "mother is devoured by the son, killed, and buried in his belly." For indeed, it must be so. *In two things,* says Flamel <note>Nicolas Flamel, the legendary French alchemist</note>, *this whole business consists: namely, that by fire you make your sulfur penetrative and attractive, so that it might devour its mother, and then you will have completed the work. Fasten the mother to the belly of the offspring she previously bore; then finally he will be a father to himself, and the son will be a perfected spirit from the two of them.* And in the same place: *Then the offspring devours the mother and suffocates his father in a single lake, in which flowers, milk, fruit, and blood are found together.* And in Riddle 6: *Place the red servant equally upon the pregnant mother; mortify the mother, cutting off her hands and feet.* And Lull <note>Raymond Lull, a Majorcan polymath and influential figure in alchemical literature</note> in the *Codicil*: *It is necessary that the mother, who first generates the son, be buried in the belly of the son and be generated by him.* Not only does the son mate with and kill his mother, but he also destroys his own father under an allegory; just as Oedipus killed his father Laius meeting him on the road and refusing to yield, and [wedded] Jocasta...

### Hieroglyphics, Book 3.

He <note>Minos, King of Crete</note> took the sister of King Aeetes <note>Aeetes was the sorcerer-king of Colchis and father of Medea; his sister was Pasiphae</note> as his wife, so that like might rejoice in like <note>original: "par pari gauderet"</note>—namely, the son of Jupiter with the daughter of the Sun <note>Minos was the son of Zeus/Jupiter; Pasiphae was the daughter of Helios/the Sun. In alchemy, this often represents the union of solar and celestial principles</note>. From her he fathered Ariadne and the Minotaur. The Minotaur, shut away in the Labyrinth built by Daedalus, was eventually slain by Theseus through the help of Ariadne. It is possible that some historical truth underlies these characters, just as they tell of the remains of the Cretan Labyrinth still standing today; however, Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> says that in his own time the Cretan Labyrinth had fallen into ruin, while the Egyptian Labyrinth, which was far older, had endured. Regarding the rest of the stories concerning Minos and Rhadamanthus, and their incorruptible judgment of souls in the underworld—since most of these were invented by the poets of a later age—we shall not speak of them here.

<margin>Amphion and Zethus, the 18th sons of Jove.</margin> From Antiope, the daughter of Nycteus—or as others believe, the daughter of Asopus—Jupiter fathered Amphion and Zethus. Amphion learned to master the lyre from his teacher Mercury, and with his song he moved wild beasts and stones, just as Orpheus the son of Calliope did. These two brothers are said to have founded Thebes and fortified it with walls and towers. It was fabled, therefore, that the stones leaped into place of their own accord and the wall was built while Amphion played the lyre sweetly, as Horace <note>The Roman poet Horace in his "Ars Poetica"</note> says:

> *Amphion too, the builder of the Theban city,*
> *Was said to move stones by the sound of his shell* <note>original: "testudinis." The first lyres were said to be made from tortoise shells</note>, *and by soft prayer*
> *To lead them wherever he wished;*

They report the same of the walls of Troy built by Apollo, and of the music of the prophet Orpheus, by which he guided the ship *Argo* and drew wild beasts and stones to himself. But anyone can see that these things are hyperbolic <note>exaggerated for symbolic effect</note>, regardless of how they are interpreted—whether they refer to the general art of poetry and its sweetness and power, or to the secret things contained within it. Amphion was the first to dedicate an altar to Mercury, because he had received the lyre from him. Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century CE Greek traveler and geographer</note>, in his later writings on Elis, thinks that Amphion and Orpheus were Egyptians and excelled in the knowledge of the Magi. However, this is not credible; for it is proven by all authors and circumstances that these men were Greeks, and that they transferred the knowledge of the Egyptians to the Greeks. Concerning the wonders enumerated thus far—

**Since** human memory is so fleeting and the mind so weak that, unless it is frequently stirred by some object striking the senses, it is easily led into forgetting things past or invisible; for this reason, in difficult and great matters that should never be set aside from the mind, the wisest men—both among the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicos"</note> and the Israelites, God’s chosen people—instituted certain perceptible <note>original: "sensibilia"</note> solemnities. By the consideration of these, anyone who is not idle might be stirred to remember those things which were performed and celebrated in the past, or which are otherwise held as secrets <note>original: "arcana"</note> not to be revealed. The goal was that they might give everlasting thanks for His gifts to God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Deo Opt: Max:"</note>, from whom alone all perfect goods descend. <header>Book 4: Of the Egypto-Greeks.</header>

...of things within them, completed in the space of six days; Because on the seventh day the Creator rested and ceased from His work of creation; 
<margin>*Passover.*</margin> Furthermore, **Passover** <note>original: "Pascha"</note> was instituted in memory of the angel of God striking the firstborn of the Egyptians and sparing those whose doorposts were marked with the blood of the spotless lamb; 
<margin>*Pentecost.*</margin> **Pentecost**, in remembrance of the divine law promulgated on Mount Sinai by God Himself; 
<margin>*Tabernacles.*</margin> and the **Feast of Tabernacles**, in remembrance of the forty years of wandering through the desert. 

With the same intention (though the former are accepted piously, as is fitting, while the latter are understood politically or civilly), in well-ordered republics, statues and images of those who provided great utility to their people, or liberation from enemies, or other benefits, were erected and always preserved. For this is a kind of **artificial memory** <note>The "Method of Loci" or "Art of Memory," a classical mnemonic technique using mental images and physical locations to recall information.</note> consisting of images and places, representing the memorable deeds of things or persons to anyone who is not ignorant, just as monuments of this kind were formerly in use among the Greeks, Romans, and other nations, and are still found everywhere. 

Thus among the Egyptians, when the highest of earthly goods had fallen—by the indulgence of God, the most kind giver—to certain most acute minds, such as **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure perceived as the author of the Hermetic Corpus and a founder of alchemy.</note> and others, they established certain ceremonies and solemnities with singular pomp, most suited to the matter in whose memory they were held. They did this lest the memory of these gifts fade for posterity, and so that thanks might be returned to God in whatever way possible. 
<margin>*Egyptian festivals for the sake of memory.*</margin> Of this kind were the selection, consecration, feeding, and worship of **Apis** (the Egyptian bull marked with specific colors) performed in the **Temple of Vulcan** <note>The author uses the Roman name "Vulcan" to refer to the Egyptian god Ptah, whose temple was at Memphis.</note>; his submersion in water, his burial, and the selection of a new bull; likewise the festivals of **Osiris**, **Ceres**, **Adonis**, and others like these, some of which we have already mentioned and others we shall discuss hereafter. 

There is no doubt that these were originally established by the priests for a good purpose, since it was not permitted to treat those secrets <note>original: "arcanis"</note> in any other way. But how they were then dragged into abuse by the ignorant common folk and changed into horrific idolatry has been made clear by experience itself. Besides these festivals, the Egyptians had two other ways of secretly handing down their mysteries, about which...

166 Book 4 of Hieroglyphics.

<margin>Allegories serve the mind, while Hieroglyphs serve the eyes, to help recall the meanings understood within them.</margin>
...as mentioned before, namely one which serves the mind, and the other which serves the eyes. That which serves the mind consists of the **allegories** of gods, goddesses, and heroes, containing their deeds and admirable things; of these we have treated quite extensively until now, especially in the second and third books of this treatise. That which serves the eyes consists of **hieroglyphs**—the painted and sculpted figures of animals and other things used in place of letters and writing; we also treated these in the first book. And these three—namely the celebration of sacred rites, the narration of allegories, and the sketching of hieroglyphs—were kept so hidden within the secrets of the initiated priests that they were not known to any of the common people or the uninitiated, but remained unknown to all others except the philosophers who were the sons of the priests. 

The reasons for hiding these things have already been explained by us, and more lengthily by others, so there is no need to repeat them. Thus these three things, being least understood by the common folk while being held everywhere by the priests as sacred and shrouded in silence, began to be worshiped more and more as divine matters every day. It became a sin <note>original: "nefas," meaning a violation of divine law</note> to inquire into what they signified, or why and by whom they were introduced. This is the single and triple-fold source of many abuses, errors, and superstitions later transferred from the Egyptians to the other nations of the world. But as we have so far discussed the gods and goddesses, as well as the heroes, their origin and worship, according to the plan of our work, we will now briefly treat in this book the festivals, games, solemnities, and competitions established for the sake of these same things.

<margin>1. The Rites of Bacchus. The Orphic Rites.</margin>
**Lucian** <note>A second-century Syrian satirist known for his witty critiques of religion and philosophy.</note> (who stood out as a mocker of pagan idolatry) says in his dialogue *On Astrology*: 
> *Orpheus, the son of Calliope and Oeagrus, was the first of all to introduce the rites of Bacchus into Greece, and he first established those sacred rites, which were called **Orphic**, on the mountain of Boeotia in Thebes.* 
As this is also passed down by others, there is no doubt about it. But why he established these, and how they were to be celebrated, must be investigated. It is established that these rites were taken from the Egyptians, who performed solemnities in honor of **Osiris** every three years, for the reason that they said Osiris (or **Dionysus**) <note>The author here follows the common Renaissance practice of "syncretism," equating the Egyptian god Osiris with the Greek god Dionysus/Bacchus.</note> had finally returned from his Indian voyage in the third year; 
<margin>Triennial Rites.</margin>
on that account they are called **Trieterica** <note>original: "Trieterica," from the Greek meaning "held every three years."</note>.

### Book 4. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.

Since all things told about the journey of Osiris into India and other parts of the world—how he taught men the method of tilling the fields and the system of planting the vine, along with many other useful inventions—are allegorical, so too must the festival be considered purely allegorical, which takes its origin from those events or is said to have been established in memory of that journey. For if, in the true **divine commonwealth** <note>original: "polytia," from the Greek "politeia," referring to the religious and civil constitution of a state</note> among the Israelites, sacred rites were celebrated proceeding from the truest causes (as was said before) to recall past deeds to memory and to allegorically foreshadow things to be done or future things concerning **Christ**, the same could have happened in its own way among the Pagans, so that they understood an allegory to be inherent in their own festivals.

<margin>The difference between the festivals of the Church and the nations.</margin>But the difference between these and those is, as the saying goes, "as wide as the whole sky" <note>original: "toto caelo," a Latin idiom meaning poles apart or diametrically opposed</note>. Those of the Israelites were ordained by the true, eternal, and one God in His honor—partly to represent past events as they truly happened, and partly to represent future events as they would follow under a figure. These Pagan rites, having proceeded from men alone, seem to have been hammered out by the cleverness of the human mind, so that monuments and silent symbols might exist for a matter as if it had happened that way, or as believed under an allegory. And just as **Moses** received those rites from God Himself, the fountain of Truth, and promulgated them by His command for the Israelite people to observe, so **Orpheus** transferred these rites from the Egyptian priests—the authors of every superstitious vanity—to the Greeks. The former rites aimed at the goal of eternal salvation; the latter, at temporal benefit. Yet both were directed toward the glory of God the Creator and the giver of all good things: the former were received by the true Church of God in both the Old and New Covenants; the latter by the crowd of unbelievers and the rest of the world.

<margin>The Gentiles wished to imitate the Israelites in many things, just as the devil mimics God.</margin>But leaving those matters aside for now and merely mentioning them (since many believe that this custom of instituting festivals and sacred rites was taken from the Israelites through a certain **perverse imitation** <note>original: "cacozylia," a Greek-derived term for a misguided or failed attempt to copy a superior model</note> and transferred to the heathens), we shall speak of these things as worldly inventions of men. What was understood by the journey of **Dionysus** or **Osiris**, we have sufficiently declared in the first book under Osiris, and in the third under Dionysus. The **Apaturia** were held for four days in October.

Just as those rituals were taken from the Egyptians, so the Romans received from both the Greeks and the Egyptians whatever deities existed among them. Hence Lucan, in Book 7, says of Egypt:

> We have received your **Isis** into Roman temples,
> Along with semi-divine dogs and sistrums <note>A metallic rattle used in Egyptian religious ceremonies, especially for Isis</note> commanding mourning,

And **Lactantius** <note>A 4th-century Christian author often called the "Christian Cicero"</note> says in Book 1 of his *Institutes*: *“The Romans,”* he says, *“held their own misfortunes as gods—namely, rust, paleness, and fever.”* For this reason, as is clear from **Ovid’s** *Fasti*, the festival of **Robigo** <note>The goddess of grain rust or blight</note> was held toward the end of April (specifically the 6th day before the Kalends of May); they worshipped her then, as Ovid says, so that she would not harm the crops or the farming tools. In the same way, they worshipped **Fever** so that she would not afflict them. Thus **Valerius** <note>Valerius Maximus, a Roman historian</note> says in Book 2: *“They worshipped other gods to do good, but they worshipped Fever to do less harm.”* He also describes the locations where there were three temples to **Fever**. Furthermore, the Romans worshipped a god of their own, **Romulus**, whom they called **Quirinus**. While they did not receive Romulus—along with Fever, Rust, and others of that kind—from other nations, but rather invented them for themselves through their own ingenuity, they did borrow **Mars**, **Jupiter**, **Saturn**, **Mercury**, **Apollo**, and **Aesculapius** <note>The god of medicine and healing</note> in great number from either the Greeks or the Egyptians.

Yet if she is the mother of all the gods, she did not merely follow certain of her sons to Rome, but even preceded others who were to follow. ...was born, his great-grandson **Aesculapius** <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing</note> may have seen it. These are his words: **Epidaurus** is, according to **Eutropius** <note>A 4th-century Roman historian</note>, the city that is now called **Dyrrachium** <note>Modern-day Durrës in Albania; the author or his source is likely confusing the Epidaurus in the Peloponnese with the one in Illyria</note>. Because Rome was a greater city than Epidaurus, **Augustine** says ironically that Aesculapius migrated to Rome. Regarding his arrival, **Livy** says in *Book 10* of *The Origin of the City* <note>original: "de vrbis origine," usually titled "Ab Urbe Condita"</note>, near the end: when Rome, he says, was suffering from a heavy plague, which was so great that although that year (specifically 455 years from the founding of the city <note>Approximately 298–293 BC</note>) was happy in many respects, it was scarcely enough to provide solace for this one evil—namely, the plague scorching the city, both as to its people and its fields. Therefore, they consulted the **Sibylline Books** <note>A collection of prophecies consulted by the Roman state during emergencies</note> for a remedy, and it was found that Aesculapius had to be brought from Epidaurus to Rome. **Orosius** tells the same story in *Book 3*. And Livy in *Book 11*, and **Valerius** <note>Valerius Maximus</note> in *Book 1*, testify that the city was afflicted by this heavy plague for three consecutive years.

<margin>An embassy established by the Romans to Epidaurus to bring back Aesculapius</margin>
Ambassadors were therefore sent as a remedy to fetch Aesculapius from Epidaurus. Upon arriving there, they were led by the people of Epidaurus into the temple of Aesculapius, which was five miles away from the city. And behold, a **serpent**, which (though rarely seen by the Epidaurians) was never seen without bringing them some benefit—and for which reason it was worshipped as a manifestation of Aesculapius—began to crawl with a gentle movement through the most famous parts of the city. It was seen for three days, showing a clear eagerness for the more famous seat it sought. Then it proceeded to the Roman ship and boarded it, staying where the tent of one of the ambassadors was, and there it rested. When they arrived at **Antium** <note>A coastal city in Italy, modern Anzio</note> by ship, the Serpent, which had remained on the vessel throughout the journey, glided down to the land and entered the Temple of Aesculapius that was nearby. It remained there for three days, being given food. Afterward, it returned to the ship and allowed itself to be carried to Rome. There, exiting onto the bank of the **Tiber**, it swam across to the **Island** <note>The Tiber Island, which remains a site of hospitals to this day</note> where a temple was dedicated to Aesculapius, and the plague ceased among the Romans. **Ovid** tells the same story in *Book 15* of the *Metamorphoses*. We have explained above who Aesculapius was and why a Serpent is attributed to him according to his primary origin. But what abuses later arose from ignorance...

...had adorned him with wonderful praises. It is likely that these stories were spread by rival poets after the death of Orpheus, since the earlier account of his demise is more consistent with history.

<margin>2. The Festivals of Ceres and Proserpina.</margin>
Another festival of the same institution and origin is celebrated among the Athenians in honor of **Ceres** <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture, equivalent to the Greek Demeter</note> and **Proserpina** <note>Ceres' daughter, the Greek Persephone, queen of the underworld</note>. In this festival, when matrons were initiated—specifically those who had resolved to maintain perpetual and incorruptible chastity and were thus adorned with crowns of vitex—it was not permitted to use wine. Since this rite, like others, was translated from the Greeks to the Romans, it was considered the great anniversary of Ceres, and it was a divine law that it should not be performed by those in mourning. Hence **Plautus** <note>A famous Roman playwright known for comedies</note> says in his play *Aulularia*: "You are about to celebrate a wedding for Ceres, because I see no wine brought in." <note>original: "Cereri nuptias facturi estis, quia nihil temeti allatum video." Plautus uses the word 'temetum,' an archaic Latin term for wine, to joke that a dry party is a 'wedding for Ceres' because wine was forbidden in her rites.</note>

<margin>Thesmophoria.</margin>
These solemnities were called the **Thesmophoria** by the Greeks, first instituted by **Triptolemus** in the town of **Eleusis** <note>The site of the famous Eleusinian Mysteries</note> as a gift for having received the art of sowing and the fruits of the earth. For while Ceres wandered throughout the world searching for her daughter Proserpina, who had been snatched away by Pluto to the underworld, she came to the town of Eleusis and to its prince of the same name. His wife, **Hyona**, who had already given birth to Triptolemus, was seeking a nurse; she accepted Ceres, who offered herself for the role.

This goddess, having nourished the boy with divine milk, would secretly hide him under the fire at night. And when he was nourished excellently through the night, the father, observing how this was done, cried out at the sight of it. For this reason, the angry Ceres struck Eleusis dead and gave Triptolemus a chariot drawn by dragons so that he might teach all mortals the sowing of crops, as **Callimachus** <note>A Greek poet and scholar at the Library of Alexandria</note> testifies in his *Hymn to Ceres*.

<margin>A Hieroglyphic sign. Note.</margin>
Who does not see, even at first glance, that these are the most secret **Alchemical** matters? For Triptolemus, nourished under the fire by his nurse Ceres (just as Achilles was by his mother Thetis), is our **philosophical offspring** <term>foetus philosophicus: a symbolic term for the Philosopher's Stone or the "Great Work" in its developing stages</term>, which is hidden under the fire for so long and is nourished by the fire as if by milk, until it can endure the full violence of the flame. And truly, even if no other sign were present to show that these fables were fashioned concerning the subject of Alchemy, this alone would suffice; for it is proper to the one and only true Alchemy, and fits no other science or art. For who has ever found it written, whether historically or allegorically, that men—and infants at that—were accustomed to be hidden under living coals?

Who has ever seen a salamander—an animal living in fire—or a true fire-fly <note>The original term "pyrausta" refers to a mythical insect supposed to live in fire.</note>, except in chemical works? Let the Palici brothers <note>Ancient Sicilian twin deities born from the earth.</note> emerge from the earth, Venus from the sea, and other monstrous offspring from the other elements; yet scarcely anything living can come forth from fire, except for the philosophical salamander and the Phoenix rising from the ashes left behind by the flames. Two things are unconquered by fire: gold and glass; all others eventually succumb to it. To these, a third may be added: namely, the Phoenix and its nest—the "seed" from which it is reborn—which is the ash restored to life from the dead. However, I think it would be superfluous to demonstrate with many examples that in Chemistry, the "infant" is, as it were, nourished and grows up by fire, since this concept occurs almost everywhere.

<margin>Only the philosophical offspring is nourished by fire.</margin>

Indeed, we shall be content here with quoting only one or two authors very briefly. **Arnold of Villanova** <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> in his *Rosary of the Philosophers*, Book 2, Chapter 25, says: *“When she has given birth, nourish the son until he can endure every fire.”* And **Raymond Lull** <note>A Majorcan philosopher and alchemist.</note> in the *Theory of the Testament*, Chapter 29: *“Son, therefore, impregnate the body from fire, and multiply its burning, and you shall have a strong tincture.”* <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a potent substance capable of transforming or "dyeing" base metals into gold.</note> And in the same place: *“Therefore, make your earth white, and nourish it, if you wish that the son of the father should come to your aid in times of need.”* Likewise in Chapter 57: *“The moisture of metals is fixed and permanent in fire: therefore, with such water, we fix the little birds flying in the air by the power of our Stone, which is created from their own proper substance.”* Chapter 41: *“And therefore, when our stone is created, make it be born from its mother's womb; do not put anything else in from now on; because it carries with it the power of its mother's womb, namely that sulfurous nature which congeals all quicksilver.”* <note>The "sulfurous nature" refers to the active, masculine principle in alchemy that stabilizes "mercury" or quicksilver.</note>

That this **Triptolemus**, cooked and ripened under fire, is our salamander, our fire, our earth and lime, our ash, and our seed which is cast into its natural earth, could be proved by six hundred testimonies. We shall place at least two or three here. **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath whose works were foundational to medieval alchemy.</note> says in his treatise, Chapter 5: *“One ought not to reap the seeds until the time of harvest has arrived.”* The Philosophers called this stone of ours a "salamander" because, just as the salamander is nourished and lives—that is, is perfected—by fire alone, so also is our stone. Regarding fire, **Lull** says in the *Practice of the Testament*, Chapter 22: *“Our sulfur has the power of sealing and forming something similar to itself, and everything that is sought, and of not retaining it in itself; and therefore we say that...”*

But let these propositions suffice. Herodotus writes that the *Thesmophoria* <note>An ancient Greek festival held in honor of Demeter (Ceres), goddess of agriculture.</note> took its origin not from the Greeks but from the Egyptians, namely brought by the daughters of Danaus <note>A mythical king who fled Egypt for Greece.</note> to the Pelasgian <note>The indigenous people of Greece before the arrival of the Hellenes.</note> women. Since it was not permitted by religion to reveal the secrets of that solemnity to anyone, the same author in *Euterpe* <note>The second book of Herodotus’s *Histories*.</note> uses these words: "And concerning the solemnity of Ceres, which the Greeks call *Thesmophoria*, may the omen be favorable and happy for me so that I may bring forth as much as is divinely permitted by religion." It was the daughters of Danaus who transferred this solemnity from Egypt and taught the Pelasgian women. Who Danaus was—namely, he who led colonies from Egypt into Greece and had knowledge of that most secret art—we have related in the first book; and therefore it is consistent with the truth that this celebration came to the Greeks with him.

<margin>Nothing was once held more secret than the Eleusinian rites.</margin>

That these matters were always held as the highest Mysteries among the Pagans, not to be scattered among the common people, is known both from histories and from the common proverb, by which it is said of a most secret thing that it is hidden "just like the Eleusinian rites" <note>The most famous of the secret religious rites of ancient Greece.</note>. Many think differently about this matter; we shall first present their opinion, and then our own. 
<margin>*Mysteries.*</margin>
**Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC) was a prolific Roman scholar and writer.</note> says that the *Mysteries* were enclosed by silence and by walls: by silence, so that it was not permitted to speak about them; by walls, so that their inspection was not open except to certain places and persons. As for the silence, as **Thomas Valois** <note>Thomas Waleys (c. 1287–1350), an English Dominican theologian known for his commentaries.</note> commented on Book 4, Chapter 31 of **Augustine’s** *The City of God*, 
<margin>*The triple cause for the concealment of the mysteries.*</margin>
it should be known that there seem to have been three causes why the demons and priests wanted the initiations <note>original: *theletas*, from the Greek *teletai*, meaning sacred rites or initiations into the mysteries.</note> and mysteries to be hidden:

One cause was that their errors could easily be proven wrong if it had been permitted to speak and dispute about them publicly.
<margin>*1st Cause.*</margin>

Another was that within those mysteries were contained the origins of the gods and the true status of those things being worshipped.
<margin>*2nd Cause.*</margin>
For example: what kind of being **Jupiter** was, and who he was, and how he first began to be worshipped; and so too with the other gods. If such things had been made known to the common people, they would have despised the gods, and thus all fear of the gods would have been removed. This would have greatly harmed the republic and the common social life of men. For this reason, as **Livy** says in Book 1 of *The Origin of the City*, **Numa Pompilius** <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing the city's religious laws and priesthoods.</note> believed it was extremely necessary to instill the fear of the gods into the people.

<margin>*3rd Cause.*</margin>
The third cause was because they performed certain purifications in secret and certain entirely abominable sacrifices which the people would have shuddered at had they come to their knowledge. For they very often sacrificed infants and pregnant women in secret, and they did many other horrific things in secret to appease the demons, as is evident in the case of **Emperor Julian** <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), the last pagan emperor of Rome, often accused by Christian historians of dark rituals.</note>. As **Socrates** <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century church historian.</note> relates in the *Tripartite History*, in the city of Carrhae—where that most wicked idolater had sacrificed secretly in a temple before going on a campaign for that war—a woman was found hanging by her hair, with her arms outstretched and her belly cut open. In her liver, he [Julian] looked for the victory he believed was owed to him. In his palace at Antioch, many chests were also found full of the heads of dead men. And **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the bishop and historian often called the "Father of Church History."</note> tells of the **Emperor Maxentius**, who sought out noble pregnant women for this purpose, cut them in half, and sought divinations <term>divinations (extis): the practice of seeking knowledge of the future through the inspection of animal (or here, human) entrails.</term> in the entrails of the infants. And therefore, says Valois, the priests took the greatest care so that their mysteries and initiations <note>original: *theletae*</note> would not be betrayed.

> Where, it was decreed (he says, concerning **Apis**, believed to be the King of the Argives), even regarding him, that whoever said he had been a man should pay the capital penalty. And since truly in all temples where Isis and Serapis were worshipped there was also an image which, with a finger pressed to its lips, seemed to admonish that silence be kept, the same **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar.</note> thinks this signifies that the fact they had been men was to be kept silent.

These are the words of **Augustine**, who in Chapter 3 of the same book reports that anyone among the Egyptians who said that **Isis**, the daughter of **Inachus**, had been a human, was made a defendant in a capital crime. And these reasons, which the aforementioned **Valois** <note>Thomas Waleys (c. 1287–1350), the commentator mentioned on the previous page.</note> brings forward, seem altogether probable to me, especially since a horrific idolatry had by then occupied all parts of the earth. However, our discussion concerns the primary origin of the concealment of the mysteries, especially the **Eleusinian** ones; <note>The Eleusinian Mysteries were initiations held annually for the cult of Demeter and Persephone in ancient Greece.</note> if we consider this from all circumstances, the first and second reasons previously narrated find a place here, but the third hardly does. For while it cannot be denied that such slaughters of men and inspections of their entrails—practiced by certain pagans through a most terrible abuse—were kept hidden under a secret, it is not reasonable to believe that they were committed in these sacred rites, which were held as most secret. **Saturn**, who was fabled through allegory to devour his own children, was perhaps appeased with this sacrifice by superstitious and idolatrous pagans, as was **Baal** and other such idols, or **Mars**, who was believed to delight in human blood; but concerning **Ceres**, **Dionysus**, or **Venus**, it is scarcely credible. For besides the fact that the sacred rites of **Ceres**, or the **Eleusinia**, were celebrated by chaste and immaculate persons (as we shall hear later) and not by others, it finally became known what was contained within them. This content is not of such a nature that it would be abhorrent either to human reason or to good morals, as we shall set forth below.

<margin>*The third reason for the concealment of the Eleusinian mysteries.*</margin>

We therefore believe, not without merit, that the first and second causes of concealment are found in the Eleusinian mysteries, but the third in no way. In place of that third reason, we add: that the third reason was for the purpose of involving and [keeping] under si...

### Book 4. Of the Egypto-Greeks.
A a 3

...[sil]ence keeping those sacred things, lest the craft by which they were all introduced should become known to the common people, as we have often warned above, led by evident arguments which we here pass over. And this triple cause was indicated by that image of **Harpocrates** <note>The Greek god of silence, adapted from the Egyptian child-god Horus.</note>, with fingers pressed to his mouth. The commentator on **Theocritus**, following the opinion of **Thelytus of Methymna** regarding this solemnity and its chosen participants, writes thus: *It was a law for the Athenians that every year, virgins and women of honest life should celebrate these **Thesmophoria** <note>A festival in honor of Demeter and her daughter Persephone.</note>, who on the day of the solemnity, carrying the legitimate and sacred books upon their heads like suppliants, would hasten toward **Eleusis**.* Access to these rites was not open except to the initiated, and the herald ordered the profane <note>The "profane" (prophani) were those outside the temple or uninitiated.</note> to stay away. And from here, **Virgil** took that little verse: *Keep far, oh keep far away, you profane ones!* <note>original: "Procul ô procul este prophani"</note>—**Servius** <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil.</note> is the authority for this. And they write that so much trouble was caused for **Alcibiades** <note>A prominent Athenian statesman and general.</note> because he, being uninitiated, was said to have been present at the rites of **Ceres** <note>The Roman name for Demeter, goddess of the harvest.</note>. Nor indeed was it permitted for anyone to be present there who was conscious of a crime committed, which the herald would proclaim aloud. The Emperor **Nero** did not even dare to be present because he was impious, while the prince **Antoninus** <note>Likely referring to the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus.</note> wished to be initiated to prove he was innocent.

<margin>The twofold Eleusinian rites.</margin>
In those later times, they say there were two Eleusinian rites at Athens: the "lesser," by which guests <note>Strangers or foreigners.</note> were received, and the "greater." Regarding the greater rites, there was an old law in that same place that no stranger should be admitted to them, as the commentator on **Aristophanes** mentions. For when many great foreign men came to Athens and sought to be initiated into those rites, they suffered refusal for no other reason than that the Athenians did not want those secrets of nature to become known to others. Therefore, they added certain "small" rites to them, as if superficial ones, into which the newcomers were initiated. Even the Prince **Antoninus** himself is believed to have been received into those small rites, not the great ones. For this, they pleaded the old law, [claiming] that even **Hercules** himself—though he was so great a hero—being a stranger, was not admitted; as if Hercules had once been at Athens or had sought those things. They called the "Great" rites those of **Ceres** and the "Small" those of **Proserpina** <note>The Roman name for Persephone, daughter of Demeter.</note> to distinguish them. From these facts, it appears clearly enough that in these rites no lusts or murders or anything else horrendous were performed, but there were most hidden causes why they were kept under silence. To many indeed, as I confess, among the Christians, a suspicion...

Since, indeed, human curiosity is so great that it attempts to inquire even into those things held most secret, the content of the **Eleusinian mysteries** <note>The most famous of the secret religious rites of ancient Greece, centered on the goddess Demeter and her daughter Persephone.</note> was finally investigated and recorded by a certain philosopher named **Numenius** <note>Numenius of Apamea, a 2nd-century philosopher who bridged Pythagorean and Platonic thought.</note>. When he had made public by interpretation the Eleusinian mysteries—that is, the sacred rites of the town of Eleusis, which were the rites of **Ceres** and **Proserpina**—he was afterwards sharply rebuked for this in a dream. *For the Eleusinian goddesses,* he says, *appeared to him in his sleep in the clothing of harlots, standing before an open brothel. And when he marveled, because this did not seem fitting for deities, and asked the cause, the angry goddesses responded to him that they had been violently dragged from the sanctuary of their modesty by him and prostituted to all who passed by.* 

Regarding this dream told within a dream, it is remarkable that **Socrates** is said to have argued in this manner, as **Juan Luis Vives** <note>A prominent Spanish Renaissance humanist and scholar.</note> recounts in his commentary on Book 7, Chapter 20 of **Augustine's** *The City of God*. He judges that "meretricious" <note>Meaning shameful or related to prostitution.</note> things were indeed contained within them. For if they were honorable and holy, they would never have been ashamed to be made public. *Socrates,* he says, *obliquely touches upon these and many other things, when he commands that the shameful and foul things committed by the gods be hidden in the most secret rites. And when he threatens that he will publish the hidden mysteries of **Isis** <note>The Egyptian goddess, often identified with Ceres by ancient syncretism.</note> (who is the same as Ceres), by which word he compels Isis herself to do what he commands, he declares clearly enough that those things are nefarious and shameful.* 

Truly, I would call this judgment too hasty or too clever; for nothing can be concluded from it against the Eleusinian rites. For if it is said that Numenius, in his dreams, prostituted the most chaste goddesses as harlots,

### Book 4 of the Hieroglyphics. 184

...very few discovered these secrets. We, who are most remote from them in both place and time, shall judge them from those things which we have truly learned as best we can; and "from the claw," as the saying goes, "we shall judge the lion" <note>original: "ex ungue leonem" — a classical proverb meaning one can judge the whole of a thing by a small part, or an artist by their style.</note>. That is to say, we judge the whole from the part, the signified from the sign, and the effect from its causes. 

These sacrifices were first celebrated at Eleusis; it was **Eumolpus** <note>A legendary Thracian king and bard who was said to have founded the Eleusinian Mysteries.</note>, the son of **Deiope** and **Triptolemus**, who first brought them to the Athenians—or as others say, it was a different Eumolpus, the fifth in descent from him. We recalled previously in Book 1 that the **Eumolpidae** <note>The hereditary clan of priests at Eleusis who held the office of "Hierophant" or "one who reveals holy things."</note> were descended from Egyptian priests; since they led colonies from Egypt into Greece and were simultaneously priests well-versed in Egyptian secrets, they are not undeservedly considered the authors of these sacred rites. 

To this, a sufficiently firm argument is added: all the priests who presided over those sacred rites were Eumolpidae and descended from a single ancestor. For thus **Acessidorus** <note>An ancient historian known for writing about the history of Eleusis.</note> says: *They relate that indigenous people first inhabited Eleusis, but then came the Thracians who brought aid to Eumolpus during the war that occurred with Erechtheus.* And **Androtion** <note>An Athenian orator and historian of the 4th century BCE.</note> in his second book *On Sacrifices* says: *For Eumolpus was a herald, from whom was born Eumolpus, from him Antiphemus, from him the poet Musaeus, and from him the Eumolpus who demonstrated the ritual of the sacred rites and performed the duties of the priesthood.* 

That it was indeed the custom for the Eumolpidae to be initiated into the rites of **Ceres** <note>The Roman name for Demeter, goddess of agriculture and the harvest.</note> and to serve as the priests of those ceremonies is attested by **Sophocles** in his play *Oedipus at Colonus* with these words:

<margin>SECRETS.</margin>

> of the ministering Eumolpidae

### Book 4 of the Egyptian-Greeks. 185

...ancient <note>The text begins mid-word from the previous page: "antiquus."</note> was the place called **Callichorus** <note>Meaning "The Well of Fair Dances," where Demeter was said to have rested during her search for her daughter.</note>. Truly, the common people of Eleusis, lest the story seem a mere fable and so that they themselves might be more certain of such a memorable deed of **Pluto** <note>Hades, the god of the underworld.</note>, said that it happened in their own land and dared to show stone monuments [as proof]. To these, however, many of the Poets—such as *Ovid in Book 4 of the Fasti* and others—are opposed, and say that it happened in Sicily while **Proserpina** <note>Persephone, daughter of Demeter.</note> was gathering flowers. 

But both the people of Eleusis and those of Sicily accepted it as history; we, however, recognize as a fable whatever has been chanted to the whole world concerning the abduction of **Proserpina**. We do so in such a way, however, that the fable demonstrates the matter as if it actually happened, but under a figure <note>That is, as an allegory.</note>. For **Pluto**, who abducted **Proserpina**, is explained by the mythologists as the earth, and **Proserpina** as the seed or the roots of the crops. And since the seed is hidden under the earth for nearly six months, she is said to be with **Pluto** for that much time, and for just as many months above the earth in the air with **Ceres** <note>Demeter, the goddess of agriculture.</note>. 

These things indeed fit the explanation, but are these secrets not very well known to everyone? Do these festivals and their concealment really require so many great things? We accept the explanation regarding the seed; but concerning our most secret Philosophy, which the rustics <note>The uneducated or common people.</note> do not know and only Philosophers understand, there are reasons for it to be hidden. Hence that institution of sacred rites; hence the priestly order within a single family; hence the golden key upon the tongue of the priests <note>A metaphor for the vow of silence (the *silentium*) regarding the mysteries.</note>. Nor would anyone be so insane as to believe that the people of Eleusis first received grain from **Ceres** and taught the rest how they ought to knead and eat bread, or that the **Thebans** received wine from **Dionysus**. No, no; bread and wine were in use by mortals long before those times, as is established from sacred literature <note>The Bible.</note> and also from the most ancient profane writings.

The **Rock** near Callichorus is shown as a Hieroglyphic, because a **Rock** always reveals some omen to us, if we pay attention. 
<margin>sign</margin>
Thus **Saturn** devoured a stone <note>Substituting it for his son Jupiter.</note>; thus **Cadmus**, **Jason**, and **Mercury**—the latter slew **Argus** with a stone, the former ones slaughtered the earth-born men with stones. 
<margin>proper to it</margin>
Thus **Pirithous**, sitting upon a stone, was left in the underworld—to say nothing of the stone of **Sisyphus**.

For it is not the way of the wise to speak foolishly, since the understanding of their words is most contrary to the sound of the letters; for he who accepts the sound of the words and does not have the inner understanding, it benefits him nothing, since to him is said that which is written: to read and not to understand is to neglect.*

### Book 4. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.

...to the immense sea, the benign giver of all goods and gifts, it must flow back; this is considered and prefigured through an image, as far as is humanly possible. Without Him, nothing happens; Therefore Hermes in Chapter 2 says: <note>original: "Fili mi, inquit, ante omnia moneo te Deum timere, in quo est nisus tuæ dispositionis"</note> *“My son,” he says, “before all things I warn you to fear God, in whom lies the strength of your endeavor.”* The same man confesses in Chapter 1 that he possesses this art and science through the inspiration of the whole living God, who deigned to reveal it to his servant. Then, the images of the Sun, Moon, and Mercury were each carried by individuals—not as gods (otherwise the Creator, who is the God of gods, would not be present) but as creatures.

<margin>The images of the planets denote the parts of the physical work.</margin>

Not as celestial planets, because among them Mercury is insensible in its operation compared to the others—Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, and Venus—and these would rather be joined with it then. Instead, they are viewed as terrestrial planets, or the homogeneous subjects of a single art. Ever since the most ancient times, it was an accepted practice among the Egyptians to use the planets or wandering stars of the heavens to foreshadow the virtues or parts of the **philosophical work** <note>The "philosophical work" or *opus philosophicum* is the alchemical process of transforming base matter into the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. That is, through known and visible lights, to represent those things that were and ought to be secrets; through designated signs, the things themselves. 

For just as in the **art of memory** <note>The *ars memorativa*, a classical and Renaissance system of using mental images to organize and recall vast amounts of information.</note>, a part is put for the whole, and vice versa—the container for the contained, the instrument for the work, the effect for the cause, the word for the sentiment, and the letter for the word (or the other way around), according to the will of the creative artist—so too the wisest inventors and possessors of the philosophical secret used their own known notes and signs, or **hieroglyphic images**, taken from familiar things. Unless the things that must represent the unknown were themselves known, both would remain unknown. Nothing, however, is more known to the sight than the sun and moon; therefore, they very frequently employed these two lights to illuminate their own obscure and hidden matters. To these, they join a third as a servant: **Mercury**.

<margin>Nothing else is to be understood by the names and signs of the planets.</margin>

Indeed, one must not think that the ancients, through the sign of the Sun, meant the known metal gold; or by the Moon, silver; by Mercury, <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "hydrargyrum"</note>; by Saturn, lead; by Jupiter, tin; or by Mars, common iron. For this would not be of great subtlety and would be of even less utility; since for them, toward the work...

### Hieroglyphics Book 4.

...that we might not lack the **Philosophical Stone**; but the consensus of all who truly Philosophize testifies that their metals are not common ones. They are one in kind, two in number, many in power and virtue; they are of the same essence and harmony, yet most diverse and discordant in their qualities; varying in color, but united in their final goal. Therefore, the image of the Sun (Sol) denotes the active force of our subject; the Moon (Luna), the passive; and Mercury (Mercurius), the receptacle of both.

<margin>
What the Sun and Moon are in the work.
</margin>

Thus the *Rosary of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Rosarius Phil." — a famous 14th-century alchemical treatise.</note> says: *“The Sun,”* he says, *“is the male, the Moon is the female, and Mercury is the sperm,”* and he calls those three “the water of those three,” adding: *“But so that generation and conception may occur, it is necessary that the male be joined to the female, and beyond this, the seed is required.”* And Lull <note>original: "Lullius Theor: test." referring to Ramon Llull's "Theorica Testamenti."</note> in chapter 47 says: *“Cook your work equally with residence, constancy, and existence, and compose it according to the composition of those things from which it wishes to be composed: namely, our Sun, Moon, and Mercury.”*

The *Rosary* also quotes from the *Light of Lights* <note>original: "ex lumine luminum"</note>: *“And know that these are the same things that whiten and redden <note>These refer to the "Albedo" (whitening) and "Rubedo" (reddening) stages of the alchemical process.</note> inside and out, namely the Sun, Moon, and Mercury.”* These three, once dissolved and fermented, he calls **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, saying: *“Quicksilver has within itself body, spirit, and soul.”* And a little before this: *“Both medicines <note>The White Elixir and the Red Elixir.</note> are begun with the Sun and Moon; but for the red, the ferment is made with the Sun; for the white, with the Moon. 'Sun' is understood in two ways: in one way as the water of the Sun, and in the other as the body of the Sun. For the water of the Sun,”* he says, *“is volatile and its body is fixed, and the reverse is true of the Moon.”*

Hermes reduces these to two when he says: *“Its father is the Sun, its mother is the Moon.”* <note>A famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus.</note> Likewise, when he says, “that which is above is as that which is below,” Hortulanus <note>A 14th-century commentator on the Emerald Tablet.</note> explains it thus: *“Here, by ‘the above’ is meant the more noble, and by ‘the below’ the less noble, so that one thing may be made from those three—or from the Sun and Moon one thing may be made whose parts are equal—and this union is called the **sublimation of the Philosophers**.”* It is also called **exaltation** or **dignification**, because the Moon and Mercury are “dignified.” For when the union is completed, the Moon is of as much dignity as the Sun and Mercury.

They also called Mercury the **Dragon**, as in the same *Rosary*: *“And I further notify you that the Dragon does not die unless it be killed with its brother and sister, and not by one alone, but by two together. The brother is the Sun, the sister is the Moon.”* And from this it is clear, since this form of speaking is common...

<margin>
*The Adonia celebrated among the Syrians.*

but also in Phoenicia and Egypt, from whence these things originally took their beginning: The wailing and lamentation, which stirred the common folk with great dejection of spirit and sadness on account of the believed death of Adonis, is clearly seen to agree in cause and principle with the mourning and wailing of Ceres seeking Proserpina, or of the Egyptians deploring the dead Apis <note>The sacred Apis bull of Egypt, which was mourned upon its death until a new one with specific markings was found.</note> and desiring a new one: For why would these peoples mourn like madmen and afflict themselves, unless they had some foundation in the truth of the matter? We know, however, that Adonis was never a man, nor Venus his lover a goddess, nor was he himself killed at the instigation of Mars; much less that, when dead, he was or is for six months in the embrace of Proserpina in the underworld and six months with Venus <note>This refers to the seasonal myth of Adonis, where his time is divided between the goddess of the Earth/Love and the goddess of the Underworld.</note>: We say the same regarding the abduction of Proserpina, who is feigned to remain by turns for the same periods of time with Pluto and her mother Ceres: But why did the Egyptians mourn a beast <note>Referring to the Apis bull.</note> that they themselves had killed? There was no reason, except that they might hand down their sacred secrets to posterity to be propagated with the greatest care and vigilance; and since the priests, knowing the cause of the matter, appeared sadder at the death of Apis—being anxious, of course, for the search for a new one—the common people, as is wont to happen, turned that sadness into wailing, and that diligence into madness; the same appears to have happened regarding the loss of Proserpina and the death of Adonis, when understood allegorically: Did Ceres lose a daughter Proserpina, whom she never had? Does she grieve for one snatched by Pluto, who never existed, just as she herself did not?

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Adonia (festivals of Adonis) and transitions from a literal or historical interpretation of mythology to a symbolic, alchemical one. ### Book 4. Of Hieroglyphics.

Let us grant that Ceres, Proserpina, and Pluto existed, and that the one was abducted by the other, and the mother was sorrowful; what does this matter to living and rational men? Let us grant that there were Adonis, Venus, and Mars, and that Adonis was taken away by the trickery of Mars, and held in delight by Venus both while alive and dead; this could provide no cause for either grief or joy to men, unless they wished to imagine it for themselves. But we confess that human minds, prone to superstition and blinded by the mists of the devil, fall very easily into most pernicious and detestable errors, unless that eternal Sun, the God of His Word—which is truth itself—graciously illuminates them with His rays. Therefore, it is not to be wondered at that the festivals of Adonis <note>original: "Adonia"</note> were performed with such great mourning throughout Syria, Phoenicia, and Egypt without an apparent cause. However, since Adonis, the Sun, Osiris, Pluto, and even Jupiter himself are held to be one and the same subject (as has been demonstrated thus far), and are commonly accepted as the great light of the world, once one of them is known, the significance of those remaining names becomes clear—subjects which we have treated copiously in various places. 

<margin>Who Adonis is.</margin>
We say, therefore, that Adonis is the *Philosophic Sun* <term>Solem Philosophicum: In alchemy, this refers not to the literal sun in the sky, but to the perfected "gold" or the active spiritual principle within the chemical matter.</term>, truly loved by Venus <note>Venus often represents the "copper" or the transformative, receptive principle in alchemical reactions.</note>, and entangled by her alluring beauty, he is killed by a furious boar possessing the force of Mars <note>Mars represents iron or a violent, corrosive force that breaks down the initial matter.</note>. Once dead, he is placed among lettuce plants—which are cold and humid—and is held for six months with Dis <note>Dis is another name for Pluto, the god of the Underworld.</note> or his wife Proserpina, and for just as many months with Venus. There he acquires blackness <note>The *nigredo* or "black stage," representing the decay and purification of the matter.</note>, which is the color proper to Dis; here he acquires redness <note>The *rubedo* or "red stage," the final perfection of the alchemical work.</note>, because Venus herself is Rosy; and thus he makes white roses purple with his blood. Certain poets sing gracefully of this tinting by Venus, among whom Giovanni Gioviano Pontano <note>An Italian humanist and poet (1429–1503) known for his astronomical and mythological poetry.</note> should especially be consulted in the appropriate passage. Orpheus, as we have also suggested elsewhere, always looks toward the common meaning in his hymns, accommodating them to the understanding of the common people; therefore, he seems to interpret Adonis as the Sun, while describing him thus:

<margin>That Adonis is allegorically the Sun, not of the sky, but the Hermaphrodite of the physical work.</margin>

> *You who bring nourishment to all, whose wisdom is*
> *Greatest, you who rejoice in various names, O Adonis,*
> *The author of sprouts, likewise both boy and girl,*
> *Extinguished and then shining again as the hours glide by.*
