<page-num>194</page-num>
<header>Book 4. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.</header>

In these verses, he affirms that many names are attributed to Adonis, as we reviewed before. He is the one who provides nourishment to all things—that is, to *Philosophical* things <note>The author uses "philosophical" here in the alchemical sense, referring to the hidden properties of matter.</note>—and causes all the colors to sprout in the Great Work. He is the one who is extinguished by blackness <note>original: "nigredine." In alchemy, this is the "nigredo" or black stage, representing the initial decomposition of the matter.</note> and shines again with the passage of time; he is equally male and female, and forever young. Thus far, it has been demonstrated that Jupiter, Osiris, Dionysus, Apollo, and the Sun are all one and the same. All these attributes belong solely to the **Philosophic Sun**, not the celestial one. For who but a madman would attribute a hermaphroditic sex <note>original: "sexum hermaphrodyticū." A reference to the Alchemical Rebis, a figure representing the union of opposites, often depicted as a single body with two heads.</note> to the common sun, or say that it is extinguished, since in its own respect it remains always the same, and is never extinguished as far as we are concerned? Who would boast of the sun's "prudence" unless they themselves were imprudent? 

Let us grant, however, that the Greeks ascribed divinity to the sun, as is clear from the Athenians, who gave poison to **Anaxagoras** <note>A 5th-century BCE philosopher who was exiled (or, as the author suggests, nearly executed) for claiming the sun was a red-hot stone rather than a god.</note> for asserting that the sun was a burning stone and not a god, just as they did to **Socrates** for his views against their gods. Yet this was done more out of brutal passion and irrational persuasion than from the tradition of Orpheus or the Egyptians. Indeed, it is written that elephants in Africa greet the rising Sun and adore it as if with a kind of devotion, and wild people (or any savage peoples without any doctrine) have always worshipped the celestial lights, the Sun and Moon, as gods. There would have been no need for Orphic instruction or the importation of Egyptian practices to teach that.

Furthermore, our discourse here concerns the primary causes and true use of these solemnities, not the later additions and abuses. In this way, we concede that the Sun was worshipped as a God and sacrifices were made to it by the common people, but by no means by the wise. Rather, the wise always denoted something hidden—not the Sun of the sky exposed to everyone's eyes (which is the best of creatures, but not God).

And this is because we find the true origin of these games—regarding the authors who first organized them by their own expense, authority, and judgment, as well as the specific purposes to which they were dedicated—to be shrouded in poetic fables and **chemical allegories** <note>The author implies that the myths contain hidden alchemical or "chymical" secrets regarding the transformation of matter.</note>. Regarding the first point, it is well established that if an Emperor, King, or Prince initiates a solemnity of this kind, his memory is never erased as long as the tradition endures, and it is celebrated thereafter in literature. Yet now, it does not come to mind which king or prince established those contests, or who possessed such authority that they would have wanted, or been able, to summon other nations—both near and far—to a single location.

<margin>
The Greek festivals seem to have been established by private individuals.
</margin>
It is therefore credible that these games were begun by private persons; specifically, by those who thought more of benefiting the common state than looking out for their own personal profit. And so that these festivals might be held in greater esteem, the gods were presented as the very first victors in them. This becomes more clearly apparent when considering each one individually. Furthermore, it is a matter worthy of wonder that in all of pagan antiquity, no true, certain, and definitive marker of time—which chronologists call an **Epoch** or an **Era**—existed before the start of the **Olympiads** <note>The four-year periods associated with the Olympic Games, the first of which was traditionally dated to 776 BC.</note>. Because of this, almost all the deeds of the ancient kings (of whom it is clear there were many even before the Olympiads began) are rendered uncertain and doubtful.

The Heroic Age is intellectual.
</margin>

It began after the fifteenth day of the Moon had passed—that is, at the very full moon—after the customary solemn sacrifices had been performed. It was celebrated over five days with as many types of games: namely, **running**, **wrestling**, the **discus**, **jumping**, and **boxing**. In these, crowns of wild olive were offered as prizes to the victors, and great honor was shown to them; gifts were given by fellow citizens, and many immunities and privileges were granted by the magistrate. These contests were called **Olympic** because Mount Olympus was near the place where they occurred, namely in the region of the **Eleans**, not far from the city of **Pisa** and the river **Alpheus**, according to **Strabo**, Book 8.

### Book 4 of Hieroglyphics

Strabo writes that the Olympic contests began after the era of the Trojan War, using the argument that Homer made no mention of the Olympics, even though he recorded several **funeral games** <note>Games held to honor the deceased, such as those for Patroclus in the Iliad.</note>. This reasoning convincingly suggests that Homer lived before the start of the Olympiads and, consequently, could not have mentioned these games. Indeed, Homer himself does not clearly express the time in which he lived, which kings were reigning in Greece, Egypt, or other places, or precisely how much time had passed since the fall of Troy, or which kings ruled each kingdom when that event occurred; these matters will be discussed later. Therefore, Strabo wrote truly that the Olympiads began after the Trojan era, since those Trojan times are included in the **Heroic Age** and were pushed back long before the start of the Olympiads.

Regarding the first authors of the games, it is surprising that no certain memory exists of such a celebrated event. However, it should be believed, 
<margin>First Opinion.</margin> as with many other things, that these began from small beginnings after great deeds were accomplished. 
Others say that five **Idaean Dactyls** <note>Mythical male figures associated with Mount Ida in Crete, often credited with discovering metalworking and the rhythmic arts.</note>, who came from Mount Ida in Crete to Elis, first proposed a running contest, 
<margin>2nd Opinion.</margin> and that one of them, called **Hercules** <note>This is the "Idaean Hercules," a distinct figure from the famous son of Alcmene mentioned later.</note>, emerged as the principal founder. 
Others think that **Jupiter** himself established these contests after the **Titans** were defeated, in which 
<margin>3rd Opinion.</margin> **Apollo** outran **Mercury** in a race and **Mars** won at boxing. 
<margin>4th Opinion.</margin> Others wish for **Iphitus** to have first established them, as **Eusebius** and **Pausanias** (in Book 5) testify. 

Some, including **Pindar** and **Isacius**, have left written accounts that **Hercules**, the son of Alcmene (not the Idaean Dactyl), began the Olympics in honor of Jupiter. For they report that after he had defeated **Augias**, the King of Elis—who was said to be the son of the **Sun** and **Iphiboea**—because he had not received the promised reward for cleaning the dung of the cattle <note>Refers to the famous Labor of cleaning the Augean stables.</note>, Hercules established the contest for **Olympian Jupiter** using the spoils and plunder from Elis, and named it the "Olympic" game. From this, they believe that Hercules himself measured the Olympic **stadium** <note>A unit of length approximately 180-200 meters; also the place where the race was held.</note> with his own feet, making it 600 feet long. # Book 4 of the Hieroglyphs

... <note>original: "tus"</note> always hidden under fables, something of **Chemical Truth** <term>Veritas Chymica: The author suggests that ancient myths are allegories for alchemical processes or natural philosophy.</term> lies concealed, bearing witness to their authors. The same principle finds its place when speaking of the **Pythian Games**. It is established by historians and poets alike that these were next after the Olympic Games in both antiquity and fame. 

<margin>
2.

They are said to have been instituted in honor of **Apollo**, because he pierced the **Python** at Delphi with arrows; the creature afterwards lay there unburied and rotted away, which is where the name is said to come from <note>The name Python was often etymologically linked to the Greek word *pythein*, meaning "to rot."</note>. Some among the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicis"</note> take the Python to be a bandit, others a huge dragon. Since the Pagans believed and presupposed that the god Apollo lived on earth and was very powerful with weapons and arrows (as he is depicted), and they neither could nor dared to deny this, it nevertheless seemed irrational to them that so great a god should achieve such honors merely for killing a serpent. Because they did not understand what kind of serpent it was, or what kind of Apollo, they explained it as best they could—namely, that he was a famous bandit or a dragon. 

But we Christians, who do not recognize such an Apollo, shall we be content with that answer? Not at all. Therefore, let us not explain these things so thoughtlessly as to say Apollo was merely a man who killed a bandit or a dragon. For what would be new in this—a man piercing a serpent with arrows? Would this be worthy of such a great memorial by the poets? Or the celebration of such great games? Let us not believe it, I pray. For if those games had begun from such a lowly origin, the first authors would have been of the most abject mind and judgment. I speak of the beginning of the celebration, not its later success. 

The poets imagine that the **Python** was formerly called **Typhon** (by a transposition of letters <note>An anagram: P-y-t-h-o-n and T-y-p-h-o-n.</note>). He was a serpent not far from the **Cephisus** river, which flows at the roots of **Mount Parnassus**. As **Dionysius** <term>Dionysius Periegetes, a dual-language author of a world description (Description of the Habitable World).</term> also says in his little book on the layout of the world, he was born from the earth when **Juno** struck the ground in a struggle (we have already mentioned before how many numerous offspring he fathered), and Apollo killed him. When he had been wasted away by rot, he was called "Python." 

These games were celebrated at the beginning of spring by all the islands of the **Cyclades** <term>A group of Greek islands in the Aegean Sea.</term>, as the same Dionysius relates. Some refer the authorship to **Diomedes** returning from **Troy**, when he had escaped the storm that drove the Greeks from **Ilion**...

### Book 4. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.
#### 103

It is said that for those returning from Troy, a temple of **Apollo the Kindler** <note>original: "Apollinis Incensoris"</note> was dedicated among the people of Troezen, and the Pythian games were instituted in his honor. In these games, it was the most ancient custom that the most beautiful of all the hymns brought forward would be sung in honor of Apollo. Later, however, singing to the **kithara** <term>cithara: a professional version of the lyre</term> was established, as well as competitions for flute players and pipe players. Other variations followed thereafter, which we have omitted here. Prizes were eventually taken away and only a crown of laurel, which was held sacred to Apollo, was proposed. These spectacles in the Pythian games were nearly the same as those in the Olympic games, with the exception of the four-horse chariot races. Some say the prize for that game was a palm branch which the victors carried in their hands wherever they went; others say it was the winter oak, before the laurel had been discovered. Others say that certain apples consecrated to the God were usually given to the victors, as **Ister** <note>A 3rd-century BC Greek historian</note> wrote in his book *On Crowns*. At first, the Pythian games were held every nine years, and later every five, because that many nymphs called the **Parnassides** were said to have offered gifts to Apollo when he slaughtered the beast. In the first **Pythiad** <term>Pythiad: the four-year interval between Pythian Games</term>, in which the gods themselves competed, they say that **Castor** won in the foot-race, **Pollux** in boxing, **Calais** in the sprint, **Zetes** in the race in armor, **Peleus** in the discus, **Telamon** in wrestling, and **Hercules** in the **pancratium** <term>pancratium: an ancient Greek martial art combining boxing and wrestling</term>; and they say these victors were crowned with a branch of laurel. **Paeans** <note>hymns of praise or triumph</note> were named after these hymns, which were composed and sung in praise of Apollo. Moreover, their rhythm was usually that which is preserved by **Sophocles** in this song, in *Oedipus the King*:

-> O Healer of Delos, Paean! <-
<note>original Greek: "Ἰήϊε Δάλιε παιάν"</note>

That is, "Ieie Delie Paean." From this, Apollo began to be called **Ieius**, just as Bacchus is called **Eueius**; <gloss>from the shouting of 'Evoe'</gloss> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ εὐάζεσθαι"</note>, that is, from healing; and **Paean** <gloss>from striking</gloss> <note>original: "ἐπὶ τῷ παίειν"</note> from the act of hitting. ### Book 4 of the Hieroglyphics
#### 204
<meta>catchword: Dragon</meta>

As Tibullus says in the second book of his *Elegies*:

> But come, shining and beautiful, now put on your 
> Purple garment, now bind your long hair well: 
> Just as they remember you, when King Saturn was driven away, 
> Singing the praises of victorious Jove.
<note>original: "Sed nitidus pulcherq; veni... Victoris laudes tunc cecinisse Iovis." Tibullus was a Roman poet; here the author uses his description of a radiant Apollo to transition into a philosophical discussion.</note>

But we, setting aside the trifles of the heathens <note>original: "Ethnicorum nugamentis"</note>, know that such an Apollo never existed in the nature of things. Instead, we know that Orpheus and the poets who followed him understood our **Hieroglyphic Apollo**—previously described well enough under the "Golden Genealogy of the Gods"—to be neither the Sun of the Heavens, as others think, nor a man of the earth. Our hero, walking forth most strong with arrows and weapons, kills **Typhon**, a most monstrous serpent. Since he was explained above, he is not repeated here. Regarding the **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the alchemical stage of decay or "blackening," necessary before purification</term> of this Typhon, from which the names **Python** and **Pythia** are derived, our Count Bernhard <note>Bernhard Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist</note> says, quoting Morienus: *Unless it putrefies and turns black, it will not be dissolved; and unless it is dissolved, it cannot be penetrated by its own water, from which there is no conjunction, no mixing, and consequently no union at all.*

And the *Rosary of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Rosarium Philosophorum," a famous 16th-century alchemical series of illustrations and texts</note>, citing the same Morienus, says: *This earth putrefies and is cleansed with its water; when it has been cleansed, the whole mastery shall be directed by the help of God.* **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> also says: ***Azoth*** <term>Azoth: the universal solvent or "mercury of the philosophers"</term> *and fire wash **Laton** <term>Laton: an impure metal (often associated with brass or lead) that must be whitened</term> and take away the blackness from it.* To this, others add that by "fire," the "fire of putrefaction" is understood.

The *Rosary of the Philosophers* continues: *The **Dragon** does not die except with his brother and his sister, that is, the **Sun** and the **Moon**, which is the extracted sulfur having in itself the nature of moisture and coldness by reason of the Moon. With them the Dragon dies, that is, the **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> extracted from those same bodies from the beginning. This is the **Permanent Water** of the Philosophers, which is made after putrefaction and after the separation of the elements, and that water is called by another name, **Foul Water**.*

These things can sufficiently clarify who Apollo is—namely, our Sun—and who the Dragon, serpent, or Python is—namely, that foul water which putrefies. **Lullius** <note>Raymond Lull, a 13th-century polymath and reputed alchemist</note> testifies to this most clearly in *Theory of the Testament*, Chapter 10: *And for this reason,* he says, *it is necessary to say allegorically, that the great...*

### Book 4. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.
#### 205
Dd 3
<meta>catchword: Who</meta>

The **Dragon** is composed of the four **Elements**—not in a literal sense <note>original: "non intellectu literali"</note>, as if it were simply earth, air, water, or fire, but rather it is a single nature that contains within itself the nature and properties of all four. This **Dragon** is said to have been slaughtered at the roots of Mount **Parnassus**, because our **Apollo** emerged from Parnassus and dwells upon its peak with his sisters, the **Muses**; thus, he dispatched the serpent with his arrows at its base. Truly, this beast was worthy of being slain by such a noble hunter, especially since it produces so many "triple-formed" offspring—which we listed above—that could easily strike down an inexperienced person like a condemned criminal.

**Ovid** relates that the earth, due to the putrid moisture following the flood of **Deucalion**, produced this **Python**; and this is not without reason. For after the "stony bones" of the Great Mother <note>In mythology, Deucalion and Pyrrha repopulated the earth by throwing stones—the "bones" of Mother Earth—behind them.</note> were cast by the descendants of Deucalion and **Pyrrha**, and the Sun warmed the earth with its rays, this putrid animal **Typhon** arose.

Regarding what is said of **Diomedes** returning from Troy, it has the flavor of history <note>original: "hystoriam sapit"</note>, unless a fable lies beneath it; more on him below. If the **Pythian games** were supposed to have been instituted by Diomedes, they would be far older than the Olympics; indeed, the Egyptians place **Osiris, Isis, Apollo, Castor, Pollux, Calais, Zetes, Peleus, Telamon,** and **Hercules** much earlier—as gods and descendants of gods—long before the six thousand years since the Creator fashioned this world, if the gods will it!

It also appears from the hymns that this is a poetic introduction, proceeding from men of letters rather than men of arms. For a musical god was honored with musical tributes by the poets who loved him. Hence the **laurel** remains, even to this day, the reward and prize for those who sound forth hymns. Regarding the **apples** proposed as a prize <note>original: "pro bravio"</note>, it is likely they were brought from the **Gardens of the Hesperides**; otherwise, it would have been ridiculous to offer mere apples—usually given to children—to such great heroes.

It is most true that the nine **Parnassian nymphs** (that is, the **Muses**) offered gifts to Apollo once he had slaughtered the beast. For it is taught that a tenth part of earth remains at the bottom with nine parts of water, according to the number of the "Nine Eagles" found in the figure of the **Senior** <note>This refers to Senior Zadith, an influential 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose "Table" depicts birds representing chemical proportions.</note>. These nine Nymphs—who also seem to represent "lymphs" or waters <note>The author is making a linguistic connection between "Nymphae" and "lymphae," the Latin word for clear water.</note>—offer gifts to Apollo, but not until he has slain the **Python**.

### Hieroglyphics, Book 4.

Anyone who explains these matters differently than the nature of the thing itself allows, understands nothing of the hidden writings <note>original: "abditis literis"</note>; indeed, they barely understand the first three letters, even if they are otherwise learned in every respect. Regarding the first victors, it has been said elsewhere and will be mentioned in what follows. 

Why **Apollo** is called *Ieius* <note>original: "Ieius," from the Greek *Iēios*, an epithet for Apollo as a healer or "shouter."</note> is derived from etymology, because he is a healer; and why the **Paean** <note>A hymn of praise or victory, specifically associated with healing or warding off evil.</note> is sacred to him is because he is a soldier; namely, a warrior equipped with medicine, by which he conquers diseases. For **Philosophical Medicine** <term>Philosophical Medicine: A term for the Philosopher's Stone, viewed here as a universal cure for both metals and the human body.</term> is the conqueror of all human diseases that can be healed in any way. 

The reason added for why **Apollo** is decorated with hymns is probable to those who possess knowledge: because he sang the praises of **Jove** after **Saturn** was driven out. For unless **Saturn** were cast down from his kingdom into **Tartarus**—that is, the **first blackness** <note>original: "prima nigredo." In alchemy, the *nigredo* is the initial stage of decomposition and purification, often symbolized by the death or overthrow of an old king.</note>—**Jove** would have no power or praise. Therefore, **Saturn** was justly deposed, and even disemboweled <note>original: "exenteratus"</note> by his son **Jove**, because this was fitting in the **Philosophical Art** <note>Alchemy.</note>, though not in Politics. In the former, there is no crime of impiety, but rather a reward of knowledge; in the latter, it would be a detestable and horrendous parricide.

The **purple robes** which **Apollo** puts on are what we most admire: because it is necessary to be clothed in them if a **Paean** is to follow. But we do not sing the **Paean** to **Apollo**—who exists nowhere except among the philosophers—but to the giver of Apollo; (upon whose birth that pagan Apollo, the spirit of darkness, became mute); that is, to **Christ**, the victor over all false gods and the greatest conqueror.

They were celebrated, however, on the **Isthmus of the Peloponnese**, at the very famous temple of **Neptune** located there, every five years. > *These belong to Jove, Phoebus, Palaemon, and Archemorus;* <note>original: "Iovis, Phœbi, Palæmonis, Archemoriq;" Jove (Jupiter) presided over the Olympics; Phoebus (Apollo) over the Pythian; Palaemon (Melicerta) over the Isthmian; and Archemorus over the Nemean games.</note>

Now, **Melicerta** and **Learchus** were the sons of **Athamas**, King of the Thebans, and **Ino**. **Athamas**, driven by madness, killed **Learchus**, whom his mother then threw into a cauldron of boiling water. She herself, also losing her mind and fearing the wrath of **Athamas**, leaped into the sea from the rock called Moluris with **Melicerta**. **Ino** became one of the **Nereids** <note>Sea nymphs in Greek mythology.</note> and was called **Leucothea**; but **Melicerta** became the god **Palaemon**. The body of **Melicerta** was carried by a dolphin to the Isthmus, where **Sisyphus**, the King of Corinth, saw it. From this, the **Isthmian games** began to be celebrated by **Sisyphus** in honor of **Melicerta** by the command of the **Nereids**.

Others bring forward other causes, but these are sufficient for us. Since these stories are similarly drawn from the secrets of **Chymia** <term>Chymia: An early term for alchemy, focusing on the chemical transformation of matter.</term>, we shall not doubt that the authors of these games were quite knowledgeable of this **Philosophy**. For the **Etymology**—if not the very context of the fable—sufficiently teaches who the characters of **Melicerta** and **Leucothea** (son and mother) truly are. We need not even point out the boiling of **Learchus** in the cauldron performed by the mother's design; in this same way **Procne** cooked **Itys**, **Tantalus** cooked **Pelops**, and **Isis** cooked **Osiris**. The mother always cooks the son, and all these things are drawn from the secrets of **Egyptian Philosophy** and are most fitting for the **Hermetic** mastery <note>In alchemy, "cooking the son" is a common metaphor for the heating and transformation of the "mercurial" substance in the vessel.</note>. Since we have spoken more broadly of these matters elsewhere, we hasten to the **Nemean** games:

Others bring forward various other very different opinions about the institution of these games. We, putting aside the rest, embrace the views of those who preferred that they were instituted by **Hercules**, because he killed the **Nemean lion** there. This contest was a funeral tribute...

### Book Five.

# ON HERCULES’S
## Labors.

<image-desc>A large ornate woodcut initial 'F' at the beginning of the text, featuring the letter entwined with intricate scrolling vine and leaf patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

The fame regarding the virtue, strength, and immense labors of Hercules has spread so greatly throughout the whole world that there is not a single corner in the four quarters or parts of the earth where he is not known, or where his name is not on everyone's lips and held in honor. Whence, when a certain man in an assembly of most distinguished men took it upon himself to sing the praises of Hercules in verse, another silenced him with this Laconian <note>Laconian refers to Sparta; "Laconian wit" was famous in the ancient world for being brief, pithy, and blunt.</note> saying: *Who is ignorant of the praises of Hercules?* Therefore, we consider it inopportune and almost absurd—indeed, impossible—to take it upon ourselves to demonstrate that Hercules (who has been received and recognized for so many centuries as a most excellent Hero) either did not exist at all, or at least existed only in the minds of Poets and Philosophers as an "idea" of a most industrious tamer of monsters and tyrants. *For our part, we allow that he remains, whoever Hercules may have been, whether he is called Egyptian, or Idaean <note>Refers to Mount Ida, either in Crete or Turkey, associated with early myths of "Dactyls" or regional Hercules figures.</note>, or Germanic <note>original: "Alemannicus." This refers to the theory that different nations had their own "Hercules" figures who performed similar civilizing feats.</note>, or of another nation; for we know that every age and every region of the world produces its own Herculean figures, most industrious both in war <note>original: "Marte" (Mars, the god of war).</note> and in skill <note>original: "arte."</note>, so that it is not [necessary]* <note>The text ends mid-sentence. Based on the catchword "pus," the complete word is likely "opus," meaning "so that there is no need" or "so that it is not a [new] work."</note>

...it would be [superfluous] to summon from the underworld other invented or fictitious characters who are utterly remote. Truly, we could easily be convinced that this very Hero, to whom so many and such great labors were said to have been commanded, hardly ever existed. This is shown not indeed by historical monuments—since there are almost none, except for the allegorical tales of the Poets—but from a consideration of the subject himself and the labors he is said to have endured. For these labors are such that some do not suit a man of such great soul because of their triviality and baseness, while others far exceed human strength and all reason. In every way, these stories align better with the aforementioned gods and goddesses of the "golden genealogy" than any writers ever could, painting Hercules in his true and living colors.

<margin>*Painting is silent poetry; poetry is a speaking picture.*</margin>
For just as highly skilled paintings are called a kind of *silent poetry*, so the poetic faculty itself may not undeservedly be judged a *speaking picture*. From this source—namely, the fictions of the most ancient Poets—we have drawn whatever we know about Hercules in these recent centuries. Let the historians who lived after the time of Hercules write what they wish; hardly any of them reached the age of Homer, much less that of Orpheus, the leader of the Poets <note>original: "Poëtarum Coryphæi," referring to Orpheus as the head or conductor of the poetic tradition.</note>. These poets themselves were found to be by no means contemporaries of Hercules, such that they could have composed a history of his deeds without the suspicion of fiction.

<margin>*The works of Orpheus.*</margin>
It is most certain that Orpheus was the first of all to transfer fictions and allegories concerning gods and heroes from Egypt to Greece. Among other things, he composed works—which he himself lists at the beginning of the *Argonautica* <note>The *Argonautica* is an epic poem about Jason and the Argonauts' quest for the Golden Fleece; the version attributed to Orpheus is known as the *Orphic Argonautica*.</note>—concerning the labors of Hercules. He did the same regarding the giants fighting against Jove <note>The Roman name for Zeus.</note>, the abduction and mourning of Proserpina <note>Persephone, daughter of Demeter, taken to the underworld.</note>, the wanderings of Ceres <note>Demeter, the goddess of agriculture, searching for her daughter.</note>, the mourning of the Egyptians for the sake of Osiris, the sacrifices of Venus <note>Aphrodite</note> and Minerva <note>Athena</note>, and other such things. These were thereafter spread to the Greeks as the lineages of gods and heroes.

<margin>*Before Orpheus, hardly any Greek writer exists.*</margin>
If, therefore, Orpheus is the first author of these things, and no Greek writer exists before him (unless perhaps a fictitious one), much less writers of other nations (I always except the Israelites <note>Renaissance scholars often held that Hebrew scripture was the only "true" history of the ancient world, while all other ancient traditions were poetic fabrications or corrupted versions of Biblical events.</note>), then what nonsense is spoken by those who prattle on about the Heroic Age—which divine and heroic personas lived then, what they achieved, or what [fanda] <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword, which suggests the next word will be "fanda" (things to be spoken).</note>

<meta>This page continues the critique of mythical chronologies begun on page 210, specifically targeting those who invent ancient histories and impossibly long timelines to glorify their own nations.</meta>

# Book 5. The Egyptian-Greeks.

...performed things speakable or unspeakable, how much time they lived before our age, and similar matters; let those perverse judges of things they do not understand be silent, or let them produce for us writers who are truly older than Orpheus. Nor is it enough to bring forward someone who is much younger than Orpheus and Homer, yet extends his fictions—or rather his chronologies and the deeds of invented persons—far beyond Orpheus. There is no doubt that many such people were found among the Greeks in those times, and not only among the Greeks, but among others as well. I would not wish to say this as if I called into question all the most ancient records of the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum," referring to non-Christian/non-Jewish ancient peoples.</note>, but rather so that the errors of certain writers might be recognized. These men, sitting at home, fashioned great genealogies of kings descended from gods and recorded their deeds looking back over a thousand years, simply to prove that the origin of their own city or nation came from the gods.

<margin>*Statue of Berosus*</margin>
We know that Berosus <note>Berosus was a Babylonian writer and priest of the 3rd century BCE who wrote a history of Babylonia in Greek.</note> is quite ancient among the Pagans, and similarly we know that many others make mention <margin>*with a golden tongue*</margin> of Abraham, the father of the Israelites. Yet, as Pliny testifies in Book 7, Chapter 37 <margin>*witnessed by Pliny, Book 7, Chapter 37.*</margin>, they received many things through tradition from the Patriarchs, the Chaldeans, or the Jews. However, what they hold concerning those gods and heroes they have drawn from their own writers—rarely from eyewitnesses, but most often from themselves, spinning them out like spiders.

In this regard, the Egyptians snatched the prize from all others, and they left behind an example of <margin>*The vain glory of the Egyptians regarding their antiquity.*</margin> vain-glory in competing over their antiquity. Some of their more recent writers shamelessly assert that gods and heroes reigned in Egypt for eighteen thousand years. Nor is that enough: there are those who attribute a hundred thousand years to Egypt, because it possessed the knowledge of astronomy and geometry. Who could hold back their laughter at this? Who does not have the "nose of a rhinoceros" <note>A Latin idiom for being skeptical or mocking; essentially "turning up one's nose" at an absurdity.</note>? What boy would not mock these old men, raving in their dotage?

But it is not our place to provide an answer to such obvious lies, since these people, like *polypuses* <note>The "polypus" (octopus) was believed in antiquity to eat its own limbs when starving; here it serves as a metaphor for self-defeating or self-consuming arguments.</note> in their hunger, devour their own feet. If *Horus* <margin>*Horus is called the Sun and the Sky.*</margin> is the last of the gods who reigned over the Egyptians, since his father is *Osiris*, and his father *Saturn*, and his father *Caelus* <note>Caelus is the Roman personification of the sky, equivalent to the Greek Uranus.</note>, who will be his father? No one, as *Boccaccio* <note>Giovanni Boccaccio, the 14th-century author of the "Genealogia Deorum Gentilium," a major source for Renaissance mythographers.</note> testifies...

# Book 5 of Hieroglyphics.

<margin>
Mercator <note>Gerardus Mercator (1512–1594), the famous cartographer, who also wrote on chronology.</note> counts the Year of the World as 3,494 up to Alexander.
</margin>

Caelus <note>original: "Cælus," the Roman personification of the sky, equivalent to the Greek Uranus.</note> is without a father: the whole series of gods, according to the Egyptians, consists of Caelus, Saturn, Osiris, Horus, and these are the Gods who reigned for so many thousands of years. After these, it is told that men reigned as kings to the number of 475 up to the time of Alexander. If ten years were attributed to each of these, it would make 4,750 years during which men reigned in Egypt; and yet, from the creation of the world to Alexander, only 3,629 years are counted; from the flood 1,973; and from the first reign of Nimrod <note>A biblical figure described as a mighty hunter and the first king on earth.</note> 1,842 to that same Alexander. In this small span of time—not yet two thousand years—how could 475 Egyptian kings have reigned, unless we attribute only four years to each? If indeed they count four months for a whole year, as they are commonly said to do, the sum of years will be far smaller than the former, but the number of kings will not correspond. But if they calculate a month for a lunar year, we might concede that they had kings over a space of 20,000 years until Alexander’s time. We are not greatly concerned about the number; just as the deeds of Hercules are told as monstrous, so too is his birth narrated as incredible; about which Orpheus writes in the *Argonautica* <note>An epic poem about the voyage of Jason and the Argonauts, traditionally attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus.</note> in this manner:

> *Here first the strength of Hercules is seen by me: once*
> *Alcmena bore him, joined with heavenly Jove,*
> *When Phoebus lay hidden for three long nights in a row,*
> *Continuous, and the sun lacked day, the suns lacked light.*
> <note>original: "Hic prius Herculeum robur mihi cernitur: olim / Hunc Alcmena Iovi peperit coniuncta superno, / Cum latuit Phœbus longas tres ordine noctes / Continuas, caruitq́ue die sol, lumine Soles."</note>

# Book 5. Egyptian-Greeks.

[They] fashioned [the first] <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely referring to Hercules or a similar hero discussed on the previous page.</note> as born not from a man but from a god, and that not just in a common way, but after such an interval of time in which a thousand others could have been propagated. In the same way, they imagined **Pallas** <note>Also known as Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note> born from the **Brain of Jove** <note>Jupiter/Zeus.</note>, a preternatural birth, suggesting by this her supreme wisdom and the subtlety of her intellect. Therefore, since **Hercules** ought to represent and denote strength and constancy, he is imagined as sired by the strongest, namely Jove, and over a longer period of gestation. For the poets, or the first Egyptian authors, do not care for the common logic of nature or morals in their fictions, so long as they conveniently express what they intend. Hence so many adulteries, forms of lust, and monsters of vice committed even by the gods they invented are sung by them even with praise and celebrated with hymns throughout the towns; it is as if they were saying and confessing that those about whom they imagine so many and such great things are not truly gods, but were men (as some of the priests confessed), or are considered gods manufactured by human hands, about which we recognize **Hermes** debating in the *Asclepius* Dialogue <note>A famous Hermetic text where Hermes Trismegistus discusses "god-making," or the animation of statues by indwelling spirits.</note>. Then Hercules was born at Thebes, to Jove as father and Alcmena as mother, as was said. He had a brother, **Iphicles**, younger by one night, the son of Amphitryon, a man of wondrous speed and light-footedness. But so that the cause of so many labors to be endured by him alone might be clear, they imagined these were imposed on him by a certain fate in this manner: When Hercules was in his ninth month in the womb, and **Eurystheus** (son of Sthenelus, king of Mycenae, and Archippe) was in his seventh, Jove said that of these two, the one who was brought forth into the light first would rule the other. Hence **Juno** <note>Hera, the queen of the gods and Jove’s wife, who was famously jealous of his affairs.</note> brought forth the seven-month-born Eurystheus, while Hercules was born later on the first day of the tenth month. Juno, moreover, held Hercules in hatred in every way as the son of a concubine, even when he was newly born.

# Hieroglyphics, Book 5.

<margin>*The constellations of astronomy are derived from fictions or from their gods.*</margin>
...fled the breast of Juno more violently; some attribute this to **Mercury**, as we mentioned above. For the poets wished even the heavens to be a participant in the traces of Hercules. Hence, they imagine not only that the **Milky Way** <note>original: "viam lacteam"</note> was made by him, but they also derive almost all the stars or constellations from these "golden gods" and heroes, and from their works or deeds. This is evident in those twelve signs of the zodiac and many others. Regarding these, one might consult **Ovid** in his pagan *Fasti* <note>A poetic Roman calendar explaining the origins of festivals and constellations</note>, and the other, **Novidius** <note>Andreas Novidius, a 16th-century author who wrote a Christianized version of Ovid’s work</note>, the Christian, as well as many others.

On the night following his first day of birth, Juno is said to have sent two most ferocious snakes against Hercules. He squeezed them to death with his hands, displaying the force of his strength on the very threshold of life. Later, when he had grown up, although he had the most noble seeds of his nature imprinted within him, he was nonetheless unable to bring any of them into action without the discipline and exercise of teachers. Thus, for each of the arts he had to learn, he obtained an individual preceptor. 

He learned the art of the javelin from **Teutarus** the Scythian shepherd, or as others would have it, from **Rhadamanthus**. According to others, he learned from **Thestiades** or **Eurytus**. He received his education in letters from **Linus**, the son of Apollo, upon whom he inflicted death—as a "tuition fee" <note>original: "pro didactro"</note>—when he was beaten by him. He learned music from **Eumolpus**, and wrestling and other athletic games from **Harpalycus**, the son of Mercury and Phanope. From **Autolycus**, he learned to drive chariots, and from **Amphitryon** himself, the skill of riding. He learned to fight in armor from **Castor**, while in matters of astronomy, he had that most wise and excellent man, **Chiron** <note>The centaur famous for mentoring many Greek heroes</note>, as his master. 

<margin>*The eight masters of Hercules.*</margin>
These eight individuals each contributed their effort to the education of a single Hercules. For just as many nights were required for his conception <note>Referring to the myth that Jupiter made the night three times longer to sire Hercules</note>, so many teachers were required for his instruction. From the former, it was provided that he should exist and live, but from the latter, that he should live *well*. 

But what sort of person would Hercules eventually be? One might ask whether he was merely a fable wandering through the mouths of men, or whether such a hero was ever truly born outside of allegory? <margin>*What the supreme god of the pagans was considered to be.*</margin> The pagans <note>original: "Ethnicis"</note> were easily persuaded that Hercules was such a great man, or rather a demigod. They were a people who believed that the god **Jove**, son of Saturn, had lived on earth and committed all kinds of adultery, debauchery, homicide, and other things of this sort...

### Book 5. Egyptian-Greeks.

...had committed, that he had lain with the daughters of many kings and gods and sired children by them. Among these children was **Hercules**, upon whom they believed **Jupiter** had bestowed all the vigor and might of his own body. Since Jupiter is presupposed to be the most powerful of the gods and almost omnipotent, they did not consider it a difficult or impossible task for him to produce and present to the world a son who was the tamer of so many monsters and the achiever of otherwise incredible things. Therefore, they accepted all the deeds of Hercules as facts rather than fictions. How this opinion entered the minds of the common people can be gathered in part from the circumstances mentioned previously:

<margin>Francis Junius <note>A 16th-century Huguenot scholar and linguist</note> in the preface to his *Hebrew Grammar*.</margin>
There is no doubt that the name **Jove** <note>original: "Iovis"</note> remained among the pagans as a derivation from **Jehovah**. And since Jehovah is the Almighty, who was destined to send his own son into the world to destroy the monstrous works of the Devil—that is, **Cerberus**, the **Underworld**, and other related things—this may have provided the basis for the fiction concerning the strength and invincible fortitude of Hercules, the son of Jove. This was known among the more learned pagans through "shadows," or even, as it is said, from the explicit prophecies of the **Sibyls** <note>Ancient prophetesses believed by early Christians to have foretold the coming of Christ to the pagans</note>. This also seems to be the point of the fiction that the same Hercules spent three days and nights in the belly of a whale <note>original: "ventre ceti"</note>, just as we read in the Holy Scriptures concerning **Jonah**, who was an image of **Christ**—who was likewise to remain for the same amount of time in the heart of the earth and afterwards rise again. Furthermore, since Hercules is said by others to have lived during the time of **Samson**, it is possible that many things were attributed to Hercules because of him. Samson, a hero of immense strength, was undoubtedly a figure and *type* <note>In theology, a "type" is a historical person or event in the Old Testament seen as a precursor to Christ</note> of Christ, who would triumph over the devil and all his enemies. Such things, I say, sought from true Israelite history, perhaps provided the occasion...

<margin>Many things added to the labors of Hercules.</margin>
...for many things to be added to the labors of Hercules, so that the Egyptians themselves or other pagans might appear to possess so great a Hero. For since Hermes makes mention of Hercules—specifically that he, along with **Prometheus** and **Mercury**, was appointed by **Isis** as a prefect of Egypt—

->### Book 5 of Hieroglyphics<-

...having been established by **Osiris**, it seems the name of **Hercules** is of the most ancient memory. And if he is recognized by his associations or parallels—or as it is said, "he is known by his companion who is not recognized by himself"—or from the effects of his causes, the disciple from his masters, or the producer from his deeds, then we do not doubt that the allegory of **Hercules** was fashioned from so many and such great labors to graphically depict the persona of the **Artificer** <note>In alchemical texts, the "Artificer" or "Artist" refers to the chemist or philosopher performing the work</note> who wishes to investigate and perfect the most secret mystery of the **Egyptians**. For if we were to grant these labors historical "faith," we would be not only more insane than the Pagans, but we would also be deprived of our own sacred faith. Although this may appear obscure at first glance, I shall—God willing—make it shine most clearly once all the clouds of doubt have been discussed and removed, first in general, and then specifically under each individual labor.

<margin>The parents of Hercules.</margin>
If we consider the parents of **Hercules**, his father is the foremost of the **Golden genealogy**. To that same end, therefore, both the father and the son are referred. It is established from the third book who **Jove** <note>Jupiter</note> is, and of which sons he is the father. Those things demonstrated there are so firm that they cannot be shaken in any way, even by one who would rather be a Pagan than a Christian, provided he does not turn fiction into history; thus, they should not be repeated in this place. **Hercules**, therefore, as a son, is such as his father, but in a different respect: the father designates the **internal agent** of the Art—namely the primary subject—while the son designates the **external agent**, which is the **Artificer** himself. And indeed, he does not represent the whole Artificer, but rather the operation of his hands, and his invincible constancy and strength in investigating and perfecting that which is required. 

For besides this, there is considered in the Artificer a subtle, natural, and non-sophistic <note>Meaning "not false" or "not deceptive," referring to true natural philosophy versus fraudulent "puffing"</note> wit and wisdom; these are foreshadowed by **Minerva** or **Pallas**, as has been said often: previously under **Jason**, and later under **Ulysses**. For these three seem to depict the **Philosophical Artificer**: namely, **Jason** shows what must be investigated, how it must be treated, and by what art it must be conquered; **Hercules** shows with what constancy of mind and body that same thing should be sought, labored upon, and perfected. Lest anyone think this is my opinion alone, **Aurelius Augurellus** <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (1441–1524), an Italian humanist who wrote "Chrysopoeia," a famous poem about making gold</note> writes thus in Book 2 of his *Chrysopoeia* <note>The term for "gold-making"</note>: *where [you strike] the riches with the ivory comb...*

# Book 5. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.

Hercules is established as a contemporary <note>original: "coætaneus"</note> [of Osiris], and was left by him as the Governor of Egypt to restrain the flooding of the Nile. He had Busiris, Antaeus, Prometheus, and Mercury as colleagues, appointed to specific duties, as we taught in the first book. Of these, he is imagined to have killed the first two <note>Busiris and Antaeus were legendary tyrants killed by Hercules in Greek myth; here, the author interprets them as historical figures in an Egyptian context</note> on account of their tyranny. This Hercules lived in the time of Saturn, Osiris, Jupiter, and the other gods—indeed, even during the time of the Argonautic expedition and the Trojan War. If one were to calculate the dates, his life would perhaps extend across several millennia, according to Egyptian tradition. But just as his companions from the Argo and Troy are regarded, and likewise Mercury and Prometheus, so too is he. We have already discussed all and each of these figures under their respective tribes. The masters also depict Hercules as a disciple and place him before the eyes of the ignorant.

<margin>
Gellius, Book 5, Chapter 10.
</margin>
From this, as is held in the writings of **Gellius** <note>Aulus Gellius (c. 125 – 180 AD) was a Roman author known for his "Attic Nights," a collection of notes on grammar, philosophy, and history</note>, a judgment could easily be made concerning **Euathlus** and **Protagoras** <note>This refers to a famous legal paradox where the teacher Protagoras sued his student Euathlus for tuition fees</note>, which gave rise to the proverb: *A bad crow, a bad egg.* <note>original: "Mali corvi malum ovum." This proverb suggests that a bad teacher produces a bad student, or that evil nature is inherited.</note>

<margin>
The arts in which Hercules was educated.
</margin>
These, moreover, are the arts in which he is recorded to have been learned: javelin-throwing, poetry, music, wrestling, chariot-driving, horsemanship, training in weaponry, and astronomy. These were his teachers: Rhadamanthus, Linus, Eumolpus, Harpalycus, Autolycus, Amphitryon, Castor, and Chiron. Having been instructed in these arts by these teachers, Hercules accomplished so many and such great, illustrious deeds. Thus he emerged as a hero renowned both for **war** and **skill** <note>original: "Marte & arte," a wordplay on Mars (god of war) and Art (learned skill/craft)</note>, with virtue as his guide and labor as his companion. But let others judge these matters from what was previously related; now we approach the Herculean Labors, the most prominent of which we shall taste, even beyond those famous twelve. Juno is thus imagined as being most hostile to Hercules, imposing these labors upon him through Eurystheus so that he might purge the whole world of horrific monsters.

<margin>
1. The Nemean or Cithaeronian Lion.
</margin>

Hence **Anaxagoras** <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500 – 428 BC) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who famously suggested the sun and moon were physical bodies</note> asserts that this lion fell from the sphere of the moon down to the earth. It was utterly invulnerable, and neither by arrows...

...it could be finished; Some say that **Iris**, the messenger of **Juno**, clutching that lion in her lap, carried it down to Mount **Opheltas**. Having stripped off the skin, he wore it as a covering for his body from then on. ### Book 5. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.

This is a **metaphor**; just as the strong Lion, the king of animals, becomes weakened by his own frail flesh—for every fourth day he naturally suffers from a quartan fever <note>original: "quartanam"; a recurring fever associated with melancholy and the planet Saturn in ancient medicine</note>—so the Lion of our Nature, through its own lunar-tempered flesh, becomes weakened and eclipsed. From these things, it is clear enough what the **Lion** represents in the **Art** <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy or the "Great Work"</note>, and that it is frequently used to represent its primary subject. The author cited last also says that the Lion is the **Sun**, which has a lunar nature joined to it; hence it is clear why this lion is said to have "fallen from the **Moon**." For in truth, the Lion—or the Sun of the Art—falls from the Moon.

But regarding what is said of the <term>spittle of the Moon</term> <note>original: "sputo Lunæ"; in alchemical literature, this refers to a white, mercurial liquid or "foam" that appears during the process, sometimes identified with silver or a specific mineral dew</note>, it might perhaps be considered a strange thing from which that Lion was generated; however, if our own authors are consulted, it will be clearly established that they very often make mention of the **spittle of the Moon**. Thus says the author of the *Aurora* <note>Referring to the *Aurora Consurgens*, a famous 15th-century alchemical manuscript attributed to Thomas Aquinas</note>, chapter 12:

> Some of the philosophers, he says, have placed the entire secret in it, and they have called it by various names because of the excellence of its nature, as is written in the book *The Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum"; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>, because some called it after its location, such as "gum" or "spittle of the Moon," and some after its color, such as "blood."

Where it should be noted that the author says it is called the **spittle of the Moon** because of its location; by which he seems to refer to the **Lion** generated from foam in the "place" of the Moon; for "spittle" is said and held to mean "foam." If we consult the *Assembly* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*</note>, the spittle of the Moon will be found in many places; for **Astratus** says:

> He who wishes to attain the truth, let him take the moisture of the **Sun** and the spittle of the **Moon**.

Likewise, **Pythagoras** says:

> You must understand, O Assembly, that **Sulfur**, and **lime**, and **alum**—which comes from apples—and <term>Kohl</term> <note>original: "Kuhul"; a reference to stibnite or powdered antimony, often used as a starting material in the Work</note>, and the spittle of the Moon and combustible spittle: all of those things are, of course, nothing other than sulfur-water and burning water.

And **Anastratus** says:

> Beyond these things, I say that nothing is more precious than the red sand of the sea, and it is the spittle of the Moon which is joined to the light of the Sun and congealed.

**Belus** also says:

> Some have named the same water the "spittle of the Moon," and others the "heart of the Sun."

From these examples, it is clear enough what sort of thing the **Lion** is, and what sort of thing the **Moon** is, from whose foam or spittle the lion is said to be generated. Likewise, what the **Herculean labor** is in slaying this beast—namely, a **Philosophical** labor. For he did not kill it from a distance with arrows, but at close quarters with a club, which he afterwards consecrated to **Mercury**, and with his bare hand...

<margin>
The Lernean Hydra.

This creature had been reared to an immense size under a plane tree at the spring of **Amymone** <note>In Greek mythology, a spring created by Poseidon near the city of Argos</note>. It had seven heads according to some, nine according to others, or even fifty; if one of these was struck down <note>original: "caedebatur" — the OCR "ædebatur" is a transcription error for the decapitation of the heads</note>, the previous number was immediately doubled, unless the remaining stump of the neck was instantly seared with fire. They say the Hydra’s venom was pestilential to humans, infecting both the waters and the air, and that it devastated the lowlands with its violent attacks. As Hercules approached it with lit torches, aided by his charioteer **Iolaus**, a **Crab** sent by **Juno** <note>The Roman name for Hera, who famously hated Hercules and sought to hinder his labors</note> came to the Hydra's aid, but it was eventually crushed by him. It is established from these myths that the Crab and the Hydra were translated into the Heavens by Juno.

<margin>
Astrology appears to have originated from Egyptian and Greek myths.
</margin>

Here it should be noted that **Astrologers** assign many traits to the sign of the **Crab**—which is unequal to the celestial sign in both its position and size (being outside its proper place and far too small)—derived from the nature of the backward-moving shellfish. And they do the same for the **Lion**, the **Bull**, the **Ram**, the **Virgin**, the **Twins**, and all the other constellations, as well as for the individual **Planets**, according to their own judgment. Yet they ought to consider whether God imposed that nature and name upon those stars, or whether men did so by their own choice; and if men did so, for what reason? Was it because it suited the nature of those stars, or for some other reason? In this way, they would discover that all those names originated from myths.

<margin>
Upon what the construction of the celestial figures depends.
</margin>

These myths were fashioned from earthly things, not heavenly ones; nor do they signify anything concerning the stars of the firmament or the Planets of the higher World. Instead, they were devised and introduced to represent other hidden matters <note>The author is likely alluding to alchemical processes, where celestial names represent chemical substances or reactions</note>. **Geometry** can also divide the Sky into twelve equal celestial signs according to the poles of the **Zodiac**, or into as many houses according to the equator and the poles of the World, or according to the horizon and the Zenith; but what can these divisions bestow upon the stars in terms of their powers?

### Book 5 of the Hieroglyphics

...in my opinion, whatever proof is sought from experience is worthless, for there is none. I wished to advise these things so that the abuse of **Astrology** <note>The author distinguishes between "Astrology" as a superstitious pagan practice and "Astronomy" as a legitimate science</note>, which was derived from the Pagans together with so many superstitions, might be avoided, and the true and legitimate use of **Astronomy** might be approved. For the ancient Pagans, who truly believed that the **Hydra**, as well as the **Crab**, had been carried into the stars by **Juno**, and that all other animals likewise migrated into the starry nature of the gods, attributed to those constellations—almost by their own right—the force and power of those animals.

<margin>
The reason why certain powers are ascribed to certain stars among the Pagans is clear from these allegories.
</margin>

For if **Achelous** <note>A river god who wrestled Hercules; he took the form of a bull during the fight</note> was a **Bull**, and was afterwards translated into Heaven and arranged into certain stars, they believed he would possess something of the bull-like virtue; and so it was for the rest. This was the foundation of the astrological doctrine propagated to us from the Pagans, which, if it cannot be noticed from these examples, could easily be demonstrated in an entire book if necessary. 

But to return to the matter at hand: the very name indicates that the **Hydra** is a water-serpent, or one living in water. Yet it has many heads, and when one was cut off, the number of the previous ones increased; the only remedy was cauterization with fire. If **Hercules** had been such a man as he is imagined in fables, it would nevertheless be apparent that this story is an **Allegory**. Why say more? Our **Serpent** in the <term>Art</term> <note>Referring to the "Great Art" of Alchemy</note> grows together from water. The books of our authors are full of this description. 

**Basilius Valentinus** <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, supposedly a Benedictine monk</note>, in his work *On Occult Philosophy*, chapter 1, relates among other allegories how **Mercury** was born: he tells of a serpent or hydra, called **Orcades**, cast out from the waters, from whose jaws an igneous vapor and smoke breathed out; the further details he adds need not be brought up here. Furthermore, there are infinite passages attesting to our Hydra which we shall pass over, but we will provide at least one single testimony from **Lullius** <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century philosopher whose name was attached to many later alchemical texts</note> that is proper and relevant to this subject, who in *The Theory of the Testament*, chapter 3, says:

And by another name it is called **Vrisius**, shining and white, red in secret, but black and green in public; it has the color of a poisonous lizard, immediately ge-" <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "neratus" (generated)</note>

as is commonly said, but Hercules alone is bound by incredible labor: Thus he had already undertaken a nocturnal labor of this kind to be finished in a single night, which he could not have refused for many; indeed, he had undergone the tiring out of the doe by running, and the tearing apart of the lion with his hands, whom to have laid low with spears or arrows would have been a matter of greater skill than labor. They tell stories that these cattle belonged to Augeas, the son of the Sun <note>original: "Solis filij"; in alchemy, the Sun often represents gold or the active sulfurous principle.</note>, which he undoubtedly received from his inheritance; for it is recorded in memory that the Sun had many cattle and sheep in his own pastures. But what is understood by the cattle we have stated under the explanation of *Apis* <note>The sacred bull of Egypt, here linked to alchemical matter.</note> and elsewhere—namely, the <term>Philosophical Matter</term> <note>The "materia Philosophica" is the raw substance alchemists seek to transform into the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, which, since it is found in dung—that is, it is vile in appearance and surrounded by many superfluities from which it must be purged by the Philosopher—it is not inelegantly handed down that this stable-work was imposed on Hercules. For it must not be thought that this is done without labor and stench. Concerning its vileness and its 

<margin>Stercutius <note>The Roman god of manure and fertilization, here used to represent the "lowly" origin of the work.</note></margin>

discovery among the duties of Stercutius or in the dunghill, all authors agree, a few of whom we shall cite. *Morienus* <note>A legendary alchemist said to have taught the prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> *says: "The Sages have arranged and said: if you find this which you seek in a dunghill, take it; but if you do not find it in a dunghill, take your hand away from your purse: for every thing which is bought at a high price is found to be false and useless in this kind of art." So Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose works were central to medieval alchemy.</note> in discourse 1, chapter 2 concerning the soul: "We find written in the book of Aristotle which he made concerning stones, where he says: Two stones lie in the dung, one stinking and the other sweet-smelling, held in low esteem in the eyes of the people; if the people knew their worth, they would hold them honorably, but because they do not know their worth, they despise them and leave them upon the dung in stinking places, and whoever joins them together, therein lies the mastery." And Gratianus: "Even if you find that which pleases or profits you in the dung, take it nonetheless." And Merculinus in the Rosary <note>referring to the "Rosarium Philosophorum," a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note>: "There is a hidden stone, buried in the deepest spring, vile and cast out, covered by filth or dung." That it is vile, of little price, and not rare; Arnold <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says in the New Light, chapter 1: "It is sold openly at the lowest price." And Count Bernhard <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), an Italian alchemist.</note>: "It is turned before the eyes of the whole world,"*

# Book 5. of the Egyptian-Greeks.

229

Anyone can see that these stories are most trifling, even foolishness and childish trifles; for why would such a great Hero be said to drive away birds with the rattle of Archytas <note>original: "crepitaculo Archytæ"; Archytas was a Greek philosopher and mathematician credited with inventing a child's rattle.</note> when they could not be driven away by arrows? This would be considered contrary to nature, and that contrary to reason. If, however, one applies this to the philosophical work—where it uniquely points—it is the most beautiful and evident of all the Labors. Indeed, I dare to assert that among almost all recent authors, there is scarcely a more secret or distinguished example of the foundation of the Art than this very one, which has remained misunderstood through so many ages of the world and has been handed down to us. I call to witness those who are not imaginary (mere "sailors from a painting," or those "swimming on bark," or those writing after only saluting a single book through a lattice), but those who truly recognize that type of Rattle <note>original: "Crotali"; a percussion instrument or clapper.</note> forged by Vulcan, as well as the Stymphalian birds. Concerning these birds, many philosophers have made mention, now calling them "volatile parts" that easily flee, now "flying birds"; just as they speak of the Rattle or the philosophical brass <note>original: "ære philosophico"</note> which is fixed and fixes them. The author of the *Consilium*, Constans, says in the *Assembly*: <note>original: "in turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, an influential early alchemical text.</note>

> Care for nothing else except how there are two quicksilvers <note>original: "argenta viua"</note>, namely the fixed one in the brass, and the volatile one fleeing in the Mercury;

And Invidus says,

> because this sulfur, that is, the quicksilver, is accustomed to flee and is sublimated like vapor: for it must be held back and its flight restrained by another quicksilver of its own kind, that is, of brass; for if it is not mixed with the white or red sulfur of its own kind—that is, gold or silver—it will without doubt flee:

Thus he says; and a little later:

> And Eximidius says: I tell you truly there is no tincture of Venus except in our brass:

And regarding the figure of Senior: <note>Referring to Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail), a 10th-century alchemist.</note>

Lull <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note> says it best in his *Theory of the Testament*, chapter 57:

...are said to be scattered when they no longer appear flying. Some add—among whom is Timagetas—that these birds had iron wings and claws, just as the Harpies had golden ones. This is a thing to be wondered at, and it clearly declares the nature of the birds: namely, that they are metallic, although this refers more to their force and violence than to their physical substance.

<margin>
9.
The raging Bull of Crete captured.
</margin>
Next, Hercules traveled to Crete by the command of Eurystheus, for a most furious bull was wandering there. It had been sent into the fields by the wrath of Neptune, breathing fire from its nostrils, killing anyone it met, and laying everything waste. Hercules soon captured it and brought it back to the king. What is signified by bulls has already been repeated often; and although this one scatters fire from its nostrils, it is of the same class as those bulls tamed by Jason and many others <note>In alchemical symbolism, the bull often represents a volatile, "earthy" principle or a crude metal that must be tamed or fixed through heat.</note>.

<margin>
10.
The horses of Diomedes slaughtered along with him.

Soon he was sent to tame the horses of Diomedes. Now Diomedes was a King of Thrace, the son of Cyrene and Mars, who possessed most ferocious horses to which he exposed captured guests to be torn apart. Hercules, having captured him, cruelly exposed him to be torn to pieces by his own horses, by the law of retaliation <note>original: "talionis lege"; the principle of "an eye for an eye," where the punishment fits the crime.</note>, and afterwards slaughtered the horses themselves. It is strange that Hercules attempted anything against Mars and his son, since he seems entirely dedicated to Mars on account of his vigor and bravery. But it should be noted that he received some help and aid from Pallas <note>Athena/Minerva, goddess of wisdom</note>, Vulcan, and even Mercury, but nothing from Mars. For he was instructed in many arts by the son of Mercury, frequently advised by Pallas, and obtained his tools from Vulcan—to say nothing of Linus, son of Apollo, or Chiron, son of Saturn <note>referring to Chiron the Centaur, who tutored many Greek heroes</note>. Therefore, after the end of his labors, he dedicated and consecrated an altar not to Mars, but to Pallas, and his club to Mercury.

It is most certain that the same philosophical subject <note>In alchemy, the "philosophical subject" or "First Matter" is the base material used to begin the Great Work.</note> is denoted by the horses. Since that substance bears almost all the names in the world, why should it not also be called "our horse"? Thus Rhasis <note>original: "Rhases"; Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, an influential Persian polymath and alchemist.</note> says in his letter: *The covering of the horse is our white cloak, and our horse is the strong lion covered beneath the cloak.* Because Diomedes is the son of Mars and the grandson of Jupiter, he seems to participate in the "golden genealogy"; and therefore, on account of his grandmother Juno, he is depicted as hostile to Hercules. His horses are said to [devour] guests or unknown strangers...

Book 5. Egyptian-Greeks. 233

H h

...if we believe the writers, not in those things which are said to have occurred in that Heroic Age, long before the world was founded by our Creator: Therefore, we accept them as things never actually done, but very often spoken and fashioned and always believed. The most ancient Egyptians, very remote from these places, fashioned these things and inserted them into their writings, from which the Greeks, and from them others, borrowed. Previously we told how these places, situated toward the West and the Sunset <note>original: "Hesperum," referring to Hesperus, the evening star, symbolizing the West.</note>, were celebrated for their metal mines, and therefore were first sought out and occupied by the Phoenicians, a maritime people. This gave rise to the allegory fashioned about the cattle to be led away from Iberia <note>Ancient Spain.</note>. Let us contemplate these cattle more deeply: who their possessor or lord is, and of what color and excellence they are, and we shall easily recognize them:

<margin>
Who Geryon was.
</margin>
That three-bodied Geryon, son of Chrysaor, possessed these cattle. Some imagine he was a king of Iberia or Spain, and thus called "three-bodied" because there were three brothers united and in harmony in their kingdoms. I confess these things are said, but they can in no way be proven. So the heathens <note>Non-Christian authors or those following Greco-Roman religion.</note> explained it—those who had never seen a three-bodied person in the natural world—lest the deeds of Hercules seem like mere fables. But why is Geryon the son of Chrysaor, who himself was born from the blood of Medusa? Why did he have a two-headed dog and a seven-headed dragon? Why were the cattle purple <note>original: "punicei," a reddish-purple color often associated with the "Red Work" in alchemy.</note>? All these things, beyond what was said before, point to an allegory. And lest I linger here too long, Geryon is that one, as we also mentioned here and there before, about whom the Author of the *Marriage of Hermes* <note>Likely referring to a text from the Hermetic or alchemical tradition regarding the union of substances.</note> says: *I saw three faces, that is, spirits, born from one father—that is, from one lineage—because their kind is one: of which one is in fire, the second in air, and the third in water.* <note>original: "Tres facies, id est spiritus vidi, ex uno patre natas..."</note> This is because Hamuel, the commentator on Senior <note>Senior Zadith, also known as Ibn Umayl, a famous 10th-century Arabian alchemist whose work "The Silvery Water and the Earthly Star" was highly influential.</note>, says: *The water of life is triple, because it is one thing in which they exist: namely, air, fire, and water, in which the soul has arisen, which they call gold, and they call it divine water; which faces, indeed, their father joined—the father, that is, the one genus, because they are of the same nature.* <note>original: "Est aqua vita triplex..."</note> Thus he says. The same is found in the verses of a certain philosopher, who says of those three faces so united: *But by the grace of God they always remain together and triumph in a magnificent kingdom.*

### Book 5 of the Hieroglyphics ###

The Father sits together with the Son on one seat, and the face of an elderly master appears in the middle, visible in a blood-colored cloak: From these final words, one may also judge concerning the crimson or purple color, and the most intense red and Tyrian hue <note>Tyrian purple was the most expensive and vibrant dye of antiquity, often associated with royalty and, in alchemy, the final "Red" stage or Rubedo.</note> of Geryon's cattle. For this color suits those cattle when they are of a mature age. A dog and a dragon, the offspring of Typhon and Echidna, are assigned as their guardians; of whom enough was said before. If anyone says that Hercules truly drove away those cattle of such a color, let him please himself, but not me; For

<margin>
A king despoiled of his cattle and life by Hercules.
</margin>
if Hercules had existed in the nature of things, and were such a great hero, would he have stood as a cattle-thief? Would he have wished or been able to slaughter a king and his people for that reason? Would he have driven cattle through such a vast space of locations across the greatest part of the earth? Should we believe they were purple at that time and have since ceased to be? These are considered the trifles of trifles if the history is examined; but if the allegory is considered, a serious sequence of things presents itself. Should we also believe, as the same pagan writers add, that Hercules then separated Libya from Europe and gave the Mediterranean Sea an entrance? <note>This refers to the creation of the Strait of Gibraltar.</note> If we were all lying in cradles, we might be persuaded by them, as if by old women prattling—the writers and poets of ancient paganism. ...also making an attack on the cattle, he put them to flight. To this fable, Natalis <note>Natalis Comes (Noël Conti), a 16th-century mythographer whose "Mythologiae" was a standard reference for interpreting ancient stories.</note> soon adds an interpretation of this kind: *“I would certainly believe,” he says, “that this matter signifies nothing other than a certain dogma of physicians—namely, that opposites are to be cured by opposites. For since Hercules represents the Sun, the cold earth, when touched, restores those things which were scorched by excessive heat, and for this reason it recalls Antaeus himself to life. For thus we are taught that cooling medicines are to be applied to hot illnesses, yet not so violently that an abscess <term>apostema<gloss>a localized collection of pus or a morbid swelling</gloss></term> is formed because of <term>antiperistasis<gloss>the reaction of a quality, such as heat, when it is surrounded by its opposite, like cold, which can cause the internal quality to intensify</gloss></term>.” So says Natalis.* We consider these interpretations to be true in themselves and very well known even to those only slightly trained in the school of physicians. However, we do not believe such dogmas are the kind that ought to be hidden under the shadows of allegories, both because they are obvious to common people without fables, and because they are not found to be of great subtlety (for even to donkeys and sheep, the most stupid of brutes, excessive heat...
