<header>Book 5. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.</header>

...they strive by natural instinct to avoid heat and cold, as well as humidity and dryness—as those who are skilled do—and to remedy the excess of one by the opposition of the other. Yet, if these truths were not clear without the use of stories, they would be even less understood through them. Thus, they appear more foolish than fools who believe and broadcast that these myths were fashioned to represent such matters. For who would identify Hercules as the Sun of the heavens, when he aimed his bow at the very Sun of the heavens, as we mentioned before? <note>The author refers to the myth where Hercules, frustrated by the heat of the sun while crossing the desert, threatened Helios with his bow; Helios, impressed by his boldness, lent him a golden goblet to travel in.</note> It would be better to admit that one does not perceive the secrets hidden beneath these myths than to scavenge for interpretations that fit neither the subject being explained nor the source they are drawn from.

Anything that is spoken, written, imagined, or painted can be forced into a general category—whether of Moral Philosophy <term>Ethics</term>, Natural Philosophy <term>Physics</term>, or legendary history. Doing this does not require great skill, but merely a good memory. However, to restore hidden things <term>arcana</term> to their own true nature, to truth and consistency—that is the mark of a brilliant mind and a lover of truth. A single thing corresponds to a single truth, and a single truth is proclaimed about one and the same thing, and not about others, strictly speaking.

<margin>
Very different attributes assigned to Hercules in the explanation.
</margin>

How then can Hercules be the Sun of the heavens in one moment, and a hero of the earth, or a King of Egypt, or anyone else in the next? How can he represent "opposition" in Natural Philosophy <note>In the 17th century, "Physics" referred to the study of the natural world and the properties of matter, often linked to alchemy.</note>, then a moral lesson in Ethics, and shortly after signify a historical person? How can he be the son of Jupiter, the governor of Egypt, the subduer of monsters, and a paragon of virtue, while also being the perpetrator of so many vices, adulteries, thefts, robberies, and murders? All these things cannot belong to a single truth; they are utterly contradictory—unless one wishes to say and believe everything about everyone, both true and false at once.

Whatever is said here regarding Hercules must also be understood regarding Jason, the entire genealogy of the gods and goddesses, and all the allegories and myths explained thus far. We know—and have proved by repeating it almost to the point of exhaustion—that there is one, and I say *one*, thing held in secret from the most ancient times until today. All those myths and allegories were fashioned about this one thing and brought into the "midst of the world"—that is, into the writings of both the Pagans <term>Ethnicorum</term> and the Christians. With that one thing, not only do all the stories of Hercules agree marvelously, but also most of the others...

### Book 5 of the Hieroglyphics

<margin>
Chemistry is the mother of the sciences.
</margin>
...so many things, so that it is not necessary to explain these subjects in such an intricate and foreign way—applying them now to the doctrine of morals, now to common Physics, and a little later to some other science. Let those men, therefore, be silent and pay their dues to the Egyptian Harpocrates <note>Harpocrates was the Greek interpretation of the Egyptian god Horus the Child, typically depicted with a finger to his lips as a symbol of silence and secrecy.</note> who take it upon themselves to explain things of which they do not grasp even a shadow. They do not blush to teach others what they themselves never learned. Meanwhile, like ungrateful mules, they kick and rail against the mother of all sciences—the most ancient and genuine art after the most holy doctrine of God—by attacking her with insults. They are unwilling to acknowledge her even among the common sciences; I speak of Chemistry <term>Chymia</term>, the parent of Medicine (which is most useful to the human race) and the Queen of the rest of the arts. What if those self-appointed and foul censors of God’s gifts were deceived by their own judgment? They would extort what they themselves have not received from God’s hand with insults—just as the fox in the fable tried to steal the cheese from the crow’s beak with flattery—if only they could, when they write the following:

> *O deceitful art, hated by the good, how pleasantly you destroy those captured by your sweetness! You are a wicked Siren to the mindless.*
<note>original: "Ars fallax invisa bonis dulcedine captos / Iucundè vt perimis? dementibus improba Siren:"</note>

<margin>
25. He killed Busiris.
</margin>
The other things that same author belches out bear witness to his ignorance and his "dog-like" eloquence <note>The author is likely referring to "Cynic" rhetoric (from the Greek 'kynikos' meaning dog-like), implying a biting, snappish, and disrespectful style.</note> rather than to any learning in the secrets <term>arcana</term> or any benevolent will. It is clear, even without anyone pointing it out, that the person of Antaeus is a fiction. For he is a "Son of the Earth"—meaning he is of most obscure origin, without a father or mother—born from the brain of the Poets. He was said to easily equal twenty other men of ordinary stature and was compared to a massive tower. Mention of him is also made in the administration of the offices of Egypt, along with Busiris, Hercules, Prometheus, and Mercury; these were the governors left in charge of Isis by Osiris when he was about to set out for India. 

However, Antaeus signifies the "stone-making power" <term>virtus lapidifica</term> of transforming his mother into himself whenever he touches her. This power arises whenever the total amount of the "fixed" substance exceeds the total amount of the "volatile" substance, as we have discussed copiously elsewhere. <note>In alchemical theory, the "fixed" is the solid, stable part of a substance, while the "volatile" is the spirit or vapor; for the "Philosopher's Stone" to form, the fixed must overcome and "fix" the volatile.</note> Later, having set out for Egypt, Hercules killed Busiris (the son of Neptune and Libya) along with his sons, because Busiris used to sacrifice strangers to his father Neptune.

### Book 5: Of the Egyptian-Greeks
<meta>catchword: this</meta>

We have already mentioned Busiris <note>Busiris was a legendary king of Egypt who, according to myth, sacrificed all foreigners to the gods to end a famine until he was killed by Hercules.</note> earlier in Book 1; Isocrates wrote his praises, but Virgil in his *Georgics* (Book 3, line 5) calls him unworthy of praise when he says:

> *Or the altars of the unpraised Busiris?*
<note>original: "Quis aut Eurysthea durum, / Aut illaudati nescit Busiridis aras?"</note>

<margin>26. He also killed the son of Tithonus. 27. He freed Prometheus from his chains. 28. He broke the horn of Achelous.</margin>

Strabo, in his 17th book, says that there was never any King or tyrant named Busiris. He records that Hercules, while passing through Arabia, killed the son of Tithonus, who was most cruel toward strangers. Soon after, Hercules set out for the Caucasus Mountains and the lands of the Hyperboreans <note>A mythical people living in the far north "beyond the North Wind."</note>; there, with his arrows, he pierced the eagle—the daughter of Typhon and Echidna—which was devouring the liver of Prometheus. He then freed Prometheus, loosening his chains of wild olive. Following this, he wrestled in Calydon with Achelous <note>A river god often depicted as a shapeshifter.</note>, who had taken the form of a bull. Hercules broke his horn; to get it back, Achelous gave Hercules the "horn of Amalthea" (the daughter of Harmodius). Hercules filled this horn with all kinds of fruits and consecrated it to Jupiter <note>This refers to the origin of the Cornucopia, or Horn of Plenty.</note>. 

We have already discussed Busiris. Tithonus is imagined by some to be the brother of Laomedon and the father of Memnon, the lover of Aurora <note>The Goddess of the Dawn.</note>, and he belongs to the same class of symbols as the others. Prometheus is depicted as being bound to the Caucasus by Mercury at the command of Jupiter, because he had brought fire—lit from the light of the sun and carried in a hollow stalk—down to men, and because he refused to accept the gift of Pandora, as Hesiod relates. It is said an eagle daily ate his liver, which was always regrowing, until the bird was shot by Hercules. 

We have frequently mentioned what kind of figure Prometheus is, as well as his lineage and the meaning of his name. We understand the **Eagle** to represent **volatile matter** <term>materia volatili</term> <note>In alchemy, "volatile" refers to substances that easily vaporize or sublimate, often representing the "spirit" or "soul" of a substance that must be captured or fixed.</note> which penetrates into the innermost parts of a substance. The Philosophers <note>The "Philosophers" is the standard term for alchemists in these texts.</note> mention the Eagle in many places, interpreting the "Eagle" as if it were "Water" <term>aqua</term>. For example, Senior <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century Arabian alchemist known in the Latin West as "Senior."</note> uses the figure of the **ten eagles**, as do others. They provide a reason for this: just as the feathers of an eagle easily take up gold if they are gilded, so too this "water" easily becomes golden. Indeed, they say the eagle’s feather corrodes other feathers just as the eagle itself devours other birds; such is the nature of the **Philosophical Water**. 

Regarding this, **Basil Valentine** <note>A legendary alchemical author, supposedly a Benedictine monk, though likely a pseudonym for Johann Thölde.</note> says: *A swift bird from the South tears the heart from the breast of a powerful beast from the East.* This Eagle is pierced by the arrows of Hercules.

Hercules slew Cacus, the son of Vulcan, because of his theft; for unless a proper tempering of fire is present, evil occurs (which is what "Cacus" <note>original: "Cacum"; the author links the name of the giant Cacus to the Greek word *kakos*, meaning "bad" or "evil."</note> sounds like), and a theft or spoilage is committed against the philosophical cattle <note>Likely referring to the refined materials of the alchemical work, which are "stolen" or ruined by improper heat.</note>. The first reason by which the destruction of Troy is seen to be akin to a legend is this: because all the founders of Troy are legendary <note>original: "fabulosi"</note> and draw their origin from the genealogy of fictitious Gods—such as Tros or Laomedon, for whom Neptune and Apollo (at the command of Jove, because they, along with the other gods, had wished to bind Jove, or because Jove had killed the Cyclopes with his arrows) devoted their labor to building the walls for a set price. > *You will look upon Ilion, and the walls strengthened with high towers,*
> *built by the song of Apollo’s <note>original: "Phœbea," referring to Phoebus Apollo.</note> lyre.*

**Virgil** records that those walls were once fashioned by the hand of **Vulcan**. If this is so, as we have begun to suspect, it was done by Vulcanian arts <note>That is, metallurgy or alchemy involving the use of fire.</note>, which do not exist without fire. **Neptune**, who is considered the god of water, brought aid to Vulcan; for we commonly have need of water and fire in human affairs, so much so that we can perform almost nothing without them. Hence, those who were "interdicted from water and fire" <note>A Roman form of legal banishment or exile from the community.</note> were stripped, as it were, of civil life and the means of social interaction among men. Thus, in that craft <note>The "Great Work" of alchemy.</note> which **Homer** undoubtedly learned in **Egypt** and passed down to posterity, at least fire and water are required—namely **Vulcan** and **Neptune**, or their gifts. For as **Ares and Calib** <note>Likely referring to alchemical authorities or symbolic names for Iron/Mars and Steel/Chalybs.</note> say: "In our whole work, Mercury (who represents water) and fire are sufficient for you in the middle and at the end." For he himself <note>Laomedon, the father of Priam</note> is imagined to have built Troy—so famous and populous a city—whose very son witnessed its destruction; as if it were possible, speaking politically, for a very great city to be founded by a single man, which could be of such strength that it could resist so powerful a Greek army for so long. For a royal seat frequented for a long period of time contributes most to the growth of great cities, besides other advantages of the region. Hence, hardly anything begins as great from its start, but that which is meant to last very often proceeds from a small origin. 

Since it is commonly said, "what is made quickly, perishes quickly": thus Troy is imagined to have been founded by Laomedon and to have grown into such a great city so quickly that it is presumed not only to have been most populous and powerful, but also that in it all the more subtle arts—craftsmanship and painting—were said to have been invented. This could not have happened in such a small space of time, namely the reign of a single king. But just as it was raised to the sublime peak of dignity, so it was soon reduced to ashes, by one and the same author, so that the poet truly said of it: *There is a field where Troy once was* <note>original: "Est campus, ubi Troia fuit"</note>. <margin>
A wondrous story concerning the antiquity of language.
</margin>
Furthermore, it is established from the history recorded by Herodotus that a certain king (an Egyptian) <note>This refers to Pharaoh Psamtik I, who conducted one of the first recorded linguistic experiments</note>, when there was a dispute among neighboring nations about the antiquity of languages—each claiming their own to be the oldest—gave a newborn boy to a certain shepherd living in the wilderness to be raised. He commanded that no one should utter a word in the boy's presence, so that he might observe which word he would pronounce first of all. And since he was nourished on goat’s milk, when the shepherd approached the boy—who was now hungry—after a year and a half, he began to cry out, *beccum, beccum*, as if he desired to eat. When this was reported to the king, an inquiry was made into what *beccum* meant, and it was found that *Beccum* in the Phrygian language signifies bread, which the boy had requested. And so the glory of the antiquity of language remained with the Phrygians. But the Egyptians responded with an objection, saying it was no wonder that the word *beccum* was the first uttered by that boy, as he would have often heard it repeated by his nurse-goat <note>the sound "bec" mimics a goat's bleating</note>, and therefore he had learned it before all other sounds of words. The third reason is that the causes concurring in the siege and destruction of Troy are fictional and fabulous. If the apple and the egg were removed—as if they were post-wedding feasts, or delicacies and desserts <note>original: *repotia seu bellaria & mensæ secundæ*</note>—or if it were imagined that those two things did not exist or were not so, the whole Trojan expedition would be subverted.

[If one considers that] Ganymede was snatched from Laomedon for shameful lust <note>original: *ad incæstum*. The myth of Zeus kidnapping the Trojan prince Ganymede to be his cupbearer</note>; [if one removes] Juno, Pallas <note>Athena</note>, and Venus, whose quarrel held the torch before the war; [and if one removes] Peleus, Thetis, the goddess Eris <note>original: *Erin*; the goddess of Discord who threw the Golden Apple</note>, and the rest, no cause will remain for why the Greeks should rush to arms against the Trojans. Why would Aeneas and Ulysses—the former favored by Venus, the latter harassed by the wrath of Juno <note>In the *Aeneid*, Juno is the primary antagonist of Aeneas, though the author here associates her wrath with Ulysses as well</note>—be tossed upon such great waves for so long a time? 

But we have already demonstrated above what was originally understood by the gods and goddesses of the nations, and why they entered into human superstition; we have already removed them from our consideration. What then? If the dream of Hecuba <note>Queen Hecuba dreamed she gave birth to a flaming torch, interpreted as her son Paris, who would burn Troy</note> was nothing but a dream—meaning it has no legal weight—are not all things that depend upon it similarly dreamlike? This includes the exposure of Paris, his upbringing, the judging of the quarrel <note>The Judgment of Paris</note>, the promise of a woman, the expedition to Greece, and the abduction of the mistress or adulteress from which the burning of Troy followed. 

We have already shown in various places that everything said regarding Helen as the primary cause of the Trojan War, and her brothers the Argonauts, is a fable. This is especially clear from the calculation of the vast span of time in which they are said to have lived. However, so that the Pagans <note>original: *Ethnici*</note> might resolve this difficulty, they have convinced themselves—and insist to us through their writings, if only we would believe them—that Helen was entirely immortal. 

<margin>4. Reason: From Time, which is indefinite according to the Era or undisputed persons.</margin>

Thus Servius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> says regarding Book 2 of Virgil's *Aeneid*: "Time indicates," he says, "that Helen was immortal. For it is certain that her brothers were with the Argonauts; the sons of the Argonauts fought against the Thebans; and their sons, in turn, waged war against Troy. Therefore, if Helen had not been immortal, she could not have undoubtedly endured through so many ages." Thus says Servius. We, however, deny that she was immortal unless they can prove it by some other argument. Therefore, she did not endure; and everything said about Helen and the Trojan War fought for her sake is recognized as a fable. This is supported by the fact that he <note>the poet/mythographer</note>, along with others, records that Helen was first entrusted by Theseus to Proteus in Egypt—whom some imagine was a king of Egypt, as discussed above <note>This refers to the "Palinode" of Stesichorus or the version in Herodotus where the real Helen stayed in Egypt while a phantom went to Troy</note>.

The fourth reason is from <term>Time</term> <note>the use of chronology as a tool for historical criticism</note>, to which no certain writer can assign the truth. Virgil, following Varro <note>A prolific Roman scholar</note>, writes that the siege of Troy occurred three hundred years before the founding of the city of Rome; which...

# Book 6: Of the Egyptian-Greeks

However, this has been proven by no writer of the ancient age. <margin>Julius Hyginus <note>original: "Iul: Higinus"; a Latin author and friend of Ovid known for his work on myths</note> criticized many things in Virgil, as found in Book 10, Chapter 16.</margin> This is not established from Homer, because he did not record a specific interval of time from any fixed point or chronological era; instead, he placed all the people he described—whether gods, goddesses, nymphs, heroes, or heroines—indefinitely. Thus, it is clearly evident that they are all fictitious and, as it were, float in an immense ocean, unable to be identified by any fixed circumstances. <margin>Aulus Gellius <note>a 2nd-century Roman author of the "Attic Nights"</note>, Book 7, Chapter 21.</margin> Therefore, those who come after Homer and mention a specific time when the destruction of Troy occurred must produce true authors as evidence, otherwise they themselves become the creators of that fiction.

Thus Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, widely considered ancient Rome's greatest scholar</note>—who, according to Cassius, attempted to reduce the theology of the Pagans to a logical system, whether civil, poetic (as Augustine records in *The City of God*, Book 6, Chapters 2-5), <margin>He lived 40 years after the Trojan War and 160 years before the founding of Rome; this is based on the assumption that Troy was destroyed 300 years before Rome was founded.</margin> or fabulous, or physical and natural—borrowed the time of the Trojan expedition from Homer and was undoubtedly the first to express a certain number of years since it happened. This number he invented from his own brain, just like most of the other things for which he is most solidly refuted by Saint Augustine in the cited passages. Livy and others followed him and confirmed this for the Romans as a certainty, though it never actually happened in reality.

Indeed, even concerning Homer himself—when he lived, where he was from, or where he was buried—there are many controversies among writers and nothing is certain, as Thomas Waleys <note>original: "Thomas Valois"; a 14th-century English Dominican who wrote a standard commentary on Augustine</note> notes regarding Book 3, Chapter 2 of Augustine's *City of God* with these words: <margin>Who he was, where he was from, and when he lived has remained unknown. See Aulus Gellius, Book 17, Chapter 21 and Book 3, Chapter 11. Homer's homeland is unknown.</margin>

> At what time Homer existed is quite
> uncertain because of the disagreement among writers
> who mention his time; however, they all agree on
> this: that he lived before Romulus <note>the legendary founder and first king of Rome</note>,

as Augustine speaks of him in Book 22, Chapter 6 of *The City of God*, as well as Eusebius and Jerome in their chronicles, and Aulus Gellius in Book 9. Eutropius states that Homer lived in the time of Agrippa Sylvius, the king of the Albans <note>the Alban Kings were a legendary line of rulers in central Italy who preceded the founding of Rome</note>, who was succeeded by Aremulus Sylvius reigning for 9 years, who was succeeded by Aventinus Sylvius reigning for 34 years, who was succeeded by Procas Sylvius reigning for 22 years. He was succeeded by Amulius, in whose seventh year Romulus was born; and thus Homer preceded Romulus by 82 years. Furthermore, Cicero, in his speech *For Archias*, shows that seven cities claimed Homer as their own citizen.

# Book 6: Of the Hieroglyphics

<page-num>252</page-num>

<margin>Aulus Gellius <note>a 2nd-century Roman author known for his "Attic Nights"</note>, Book 3, Chapter 11: Seven cities compete for the lineage of the famous Homer: Smyrna, Rhodes, Colophon, Salamis, Chios, Argos, and Athens. <note>original: "Septem urbes certant de stirpe insignis Homeri, Smyrna, Rhodos, Colophon, Salamin, Chios, Argos, Athenæ."</note></margin>

...[Gellius] enumerates the people of Smyrna, Chios, Salamis, Colophon, and others. There are some, says Aulus Gellius, who say he was an Egyptian; Aristotle records that he was born on the island of Io. Thus, all things concerning Homer are left uncertain, even though some have used plausible conjectures regarding his era. If, therefore, it is not established with absolute truth from Homer or another writer even more ancient than him when that famous destruction of Troy occurred, it does not forbid it from being a fable—indeed, it truly proves it to be one. For times must correspond to times, just as events to events and persons to persons, if the truth is to shine forth. This will be clearer through examples: it is known from history which kings were reigning in Egypt and in what year Moses was born. Likewise, we know who ruled the world when Christ was born, and what happened under the emperors who preceded or followed him; or under which consuls Corinth was destroyed, Carthage overthrown, and countless other events. Hence, it is impossible that, if Troy had been destroyed, there would not exist a certain memory of the time and the persons, which would have extended even to those who followed.

<margin>The noble families of Rome were attached to authors who descended from the gods, so that they might appear more noble.</margin>
Moreover, the fact that Homer wrote that Aeneas, a fugitive from Troy, sought Italy, served the Roman writers greatly in amplifying the authority of their city. They derive Romulus—at least on his mother’s side—from the descendants of this same Aeneas (if it please the gods! <note>The author likely uses this phrase "si dijs placet" sarcastically here</note>), assigning him a father far more noble than any man, namely the god Mars himself. And since Aeneas is said to have been born of the mother Venus, they gladly recognized in Romulus a maternal lineage from Venus and a paternal lineage from Mars. It is as if it were a magnificent thing to have a city founder born outside the human custom, whom they therefore later numbered among the gods as well. As Augustine mentions in Book 22, Chapter 6 of *The City of God* <note>original: "de civ: dei"</note>, quoting Cicero, he torments the Pagans <note>referring to non-Christians of the Roman world</note> with these words:

> *Concerning Romulus, however—that he founded Rome and reigned in it—it is heard and read, not because it actually happened, but because it was prophesied beforehand; or that it is held as a belief that he was received among the gods, which literature records but does not prove as a fact. Indeed, it is shown by no signs of miraculous events that this truly happened to him. For even that she-wolf, the nurse of the two brothers, which is seen as if it had emerged as something great...* <note>original: "De Romulo autem... Nullis quippe rerum mirabilium signis... Lupa quippe illa fratrum duorum nutrix..."</note>

...such a portent, or of such magnitude, as to prove someone a god? Certainly, even if that she-wolf was not a prostitute <note>original: "meretrix". Not only this, but the same Romulus ennobled his newly-begun kingdom by establishing an Asylum there—a sanctuary for a most daring gathering of men—and expanded and stabilized it by the abduction of the Sabine women <note>The "Rape of the Sabine Women," a legendary mass abduction of young women by the early settlers of Rome.</note>. To this city, Mars and Venus (as Trojan household gods and protectors) are said by the pagans to have always been favorable. Against these myths, Augustine disputes in all those books of *The City of God*, and most firmly refutes them along with paganism and false, fashioned gods. 

*He says in Book 3, Chapter 3: I am perhaps thought to mock these fables, and not to treat a cause of such weight seriously. Let us not believe, therefore, if you please, that Aeneas is the son of Venus; behold, I grant it. Nor that Romulus is the son of Mars. But if we believe the one, why not the other? Is it lawful for male gods to mingle with human women, but for human men to mingle with goddesses a crime? A harsh, or rather unbelievable condition; that what was allowed to Mars by the right of Venus in their sexual union, is not allowed to Venus herself by her own right. But both claims are established by Roman authority.* 

And soon after in Chapter 4: *Someone might say: Do you really believe these things? Truly, I do not believe them. For even their most learned man, Varro, almost confesses—though not boldly, nor confidently—that these things are false.*

### Book 6 of the Hieroglyphics

->And in the same place [St. Augustine writes]: But whether Venus could have given birth to Aeneas from her union with Anchises, or Mars could have fathered Remulus <note>The text uses "Remulum," a variant of Romulus, the legendary founder of Rome.</note> from a union with Ilia, the daughter of Numitor, let us leave undecided. These are his words:<-

It is therefore a wonder that, in such great light of the Christian faith, it is still believed and accepted as truth that Troy was founded and destroyed in the manner described, and that from its remains the Roman kingdom emerged like a new Phoenix <note>A mythical bird that burns itself and is reborn from its own ashes; used here as a metaphor for Rome rising from the ruins of Troy.</note> rising from the ashes. This is surprising because all those stories about Troy are fables involving the "greater gods" of the nations. Indeed, if someone believes that Troy existed or stood without the conditions or destruction tied to these gods, they will certainly not satisfy the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnici". Referring to the practitioners of ancient Roman and Greek religion.</note>. Instead, such a person will be like one attempting to protect a house built in the air, without columns, from the damage of the winds. For the gods of the nations are established as the very foundation of that entire Trojan construction and destruction; without them, there would be no Troy, and no authors to build or destroy it.

Hence, those who truly embrace the Christian faith yet still presuppose or believe that Troy was built or destroyed by so many gods are entirely blind and deprived of the light of reason. For while we are truly faithful Christians, we conquer and uproot the legend of Troy even by our silence; and conversely, if we assert its reality alongside the Pagans, we silently assent to their gods and renounce Christianity.

<margin>5. Reason: From the Location.</margin> The fifth reason is taken from the place itself, which never existed. On this point, it should be known that some take "Troy" to mean the province in which the city of Ilium was located; others take it to be the city itself—an opinion which has prevailed—holding that "Ilium" refers to the citadel, "Phrygia" to the region, and "Troy" to the city. Regarding the region, there is no doubt it once existed (as we have often mentioned and it still exists today, though called by another name), but concerning the city of Troy, it is disputed.

We do not deny that a place can perhaps be identified where Troy is presumed to have stood, but this became known only through Homer's description. He, like other poets, wrote wonders about certain places: mountains, seas, springs, rivers, forests, and islands—how gods were born in them, what memorable things they achieved there, on which rock they sat, and many such things. All of these, the Pagans [hold] in their minds...

### Book 6. Egyptian-Greeks.

...blindness of mind <note>The text begins mid-sentence; the full phrase is likely "blindness of mind" (mentis caecitate).</note>, they accepted and embraced these things as true, especially those for whom the Poets imagined a certain god to be a Fellow-Countryman <note>original: "Sympatriota," a term meaning someone from the same country or city.</note>, as we mentioned before regarding the people of Thebes, Rhodes, Delos, and others. But even if the locations remain—serving as monuments and traces of the events remembered by the Poets—it does not follow that the deeds attributed to the gods are true. For the Poets, while they were inventing everything—namely the characters (whether gods or men), the eras, and the deeds—they made them seem plausible and realistic; however, they could not or should not have invented the locations as if they were speaking of another world. Since these places are immobile, unchanging, and everlasting, the human mind would have investigated where those places were said to be; if it had not found them in the world, it would have immediately recognized the story as a fable.

On the contrary, when the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnici."</note> heard a specific place named, they were not concerned about the characters, their deeds, or the timeline, because those three elements seemed changeable and, as it were, invisible. They did not deny such gods as the Poets invented, but accepted them as lustful, adulterous, incestuous, and marked by every crime, led by a certain insane persuasion. Thus, it was permitted for Poets to invent things about the gods and to perform whatever they pleased in theatrical spectacles, yet this was in no way allowed regarding humans. St. Augustine, in Book 2, chapter 13, disapproves of this practice:

*The Greeks,* he says, *think they rightly honor theatrical performers, since they worship the masters <note>The gods.</note> who demand these theatrical games; the Romans, however, do not allow theatrical performers to dishonor even the common tribes, much less the Senatorial assembly. In this dispute, a reasoning of this kind resolves the core of the question: The Greeks propose: If such gods are to be worshipped, surely such men <note>The actors who portray the gods' scandalous deeds.</note> are also to be honored. The Romans assume: But in no way are such men to be honored. The Christians conclude: Therefore, in no way are such gods to be worshipped.*

And in the following chapter 14: *Then we ask, why are the Poets themselves, the composers of such fables, prohibited by the Law of the Twelve Tables <note>The ancient foundation of Roman law, which included strict punishments for slander.</note> from damaging the reputation of citizens, while they hurl such shameful insults at the gods? Why are they not held as dishonorable as the actors? For what reason is it right that the authors of poetic fictions and shameful [insults] against the gods...*

### Book 6 of the Hieroglyphics

*...should the actors be mocked <note>The text begins mid-sentence; the full context likely asks whether actors should be shamed while the poets who write their parts are honored.</note>, while the authors are honored? Or perhaps the palm <note>A symbol of victory or highest praise.</note> should rather be given to the Greek Plato, who, when he was establishing through reason what a city-state ought to be, judged that Poets, as enemies of the state, should be driven out of the city. He took offense at the insults directed toward the gods, and did not want the minds of the citizens to be darkened and corrupted by fictions.* 

So far, Augustine has spoken. Since these words are most true, who but a total Pagan <note>original: "Ethnicus"</note> would admit those gods, or the effects attributed to them by the Poets in certain places that truly exist? It does not escape us that both ancient and modern Geographers assign a certain location to Troy, where it is presumed to have stood; and there are those who testify that the Turks living in those regions report that marbles are still dug out from the underground ruins of Troy to be used for decorating houses. However, there is no doubt that these signs are highly uncertain; and if they are real, they can only testify to buildings that once stood there, not to the specific Troy built by gods and destroyed by the Greeks. 

For what magnificent work could have remained under the earth if Troy really stood then, when that age knew humble cottages and huts <note>original: "mapalia"; a term often used for nomadic dwellings or simple hovels.</note> rather than palaces and marble houses? This is especially true since the walls are said to have been built by the lyre of Apollo <note>A reference to the myth that Apollo and Poseidon built the walls of Troy with divine music.</note>, and in the short time Troy is written to have stood, such great buildings as the poetic fame suggests could not have been constructed. 

Furthermore, it is well known that the city of Troas—from which the inhabitants are also called Trojans, and which Saint Paul mentions in his sacred writings <note>Referring to the city of Alexandria Troas mentioned in the New Testament (Acts 16, 20; 2 Cor 2).</note>—stood in that place around the time of Christ. But who will affirm for certain that this city was the remains or a colony of that other ancient Troy? Who can say the marbles excavated there were not from this more recent city rather than that most ancient one? Who would not instead guess that this city was built long after Homer’s time according to his descriptions? We have seen this happen in countless other cases, so that Homer rightly earned the name of a prophet <note>original: "vatis"</note> among the Pagans. For the things he invented, they either embraced as having happened, or imitated as things to be done. 

They claim that Phrygia was named after Phryxus, who, as the stories go, arrived in Colchis with the ram that Mercury <note>The Roman name for the Greek god Hermes; the ram's fleece became the "Golden Fleece."</note> had made of gold, traveling either through the air or through the waters. Since he lived there, he gave his name to the region. Apollonius also mentions this ram in his second book.

### Book 6. Concerning the Egyptian-Greeks.

**The Argonaut [poem] says in these verses:**

> *As I think has long since reached your ears,*
> *How Phryxus reached the kingdom and walls of Aeëtes:*
> *A ram carried him, which the Cyllenian <note>A title for the god Mercury, who was said to have been born on Mount Cyllene.</note> soon made golden,*
> *Even now that golden fleece is hung from an oak tree,*
> *A small hide that sometimes rustles gently in the breezes.*

It is clear, therefore, that Colchis and Phrygia are regions very close to one another, and the name of one is attributed to the other, and vice versa. This indicates nothing other than that both fables—the one concerning the golden fleece of Phryxus (from whom Phrygia is said to be named) and the one concerning the Trojan expedition (which is handed down as having taken place in Phrygia)—were invented and introduced to describe one and the same thing. Just as there is almost one single meaning for both allegories, so too the same characters are invented for both, though in such a way that the sons or grandsons of the Argonauts were present at the Trojan War, and some of the Argonauts themselves. This war is established as being a hundred years more recent than the voyage of the Argonauts; nevertheless, as we have reported before, Castor and Pollux, along with Helen and Clytemnestra—born from two eggs in a single birth—were present at both events. 

A single ram, I say, explains that entire war and what its nature was; it was not, as the saying goes, about "goat's wool" <note>original: "de lana caprina"; a Latin idiom referring to a trivial or useless argument.</note> but about the skin of a golden ram which Mercury had gilded. This ram made both Phrygia and Colchis famous, and we have already dealt sufficiently with its explanation. It is a wonder how the Mythologists twist themselves in explaining what should be understood by the ram of Phryxus; they bring forth twenty different meanings for it, not one of which fits the nature of the matter. Just as they are all erroneous and deviate from the truth, so they mutually cancel one another out. 

They say it was called a golden ram because the counsels of the wise are to be thought of as golden. But this is "nothing to the point" <note>original: "nihil ad rhombum"; a Latin idiom meaning the argument misses the mark entirely.</note>, since that declaration is not even worth noting in lead, let alone in red ochre or ink <term>rubrica ... atramento</term> <note>Red ochre (rubrica) was used for law headings and ink for the text; the author implies the theory isn't even worth writing down.</note>, so that it might enter the eyes and minds of the wise. Midas made the same place or land of Phrygia famous by his "golden wish," which we mentioned in Book 2 along with the golden fleece; and Ovid writes in the *Metamorphoses* concerning the Pactolus <note>A river in Lydia (modern Turkey) famous for its gold-bearing sands, which myth says turned to gold when Midas bathed in it.</note> of Midas:

### Of the Hieroglyphics. Book 6.

...having been returned [to his normal state] by a gold-bearing washing, he <note>Referring to King Midas, who according to legend washed away his "golden touch" in the river Pactolus.</note> relates it in this manner:

> *The King entered the ordered waters; the golden power tinged*
> *The river, and passed from the human body into the stream.*
> *Even now, when the seed of the ancient vein is received,*
> *The fields are stiff with gold, pale from the soaking clods.*
> <note>Original Latin: "Rex iussæ succedit aquæ, vis aurea tinxit / Flumen, & humano de corpore cessit in amnem. / Nunc quoq, cum veteris percepto semine venæ / Arva rigent auro madidis pallentia glebis."</note>

Even if this method of coloring <note>The "dyeing" or transformation of the water into gold.</note> does not accord with the laws of nature, it nevertheless sufficiently declares what the ancients wished to hint at by it: namely, the same thing as through the Golden Fleece, the occupation of Troy, the abduction of Ganymede, and similar tales. Hence King Midas is handed down as the wealthiest man of his time; he who, refuting Phoebus <note>The god Apollo.</note> when he judged Pan the victor in a singing contest on Mount Tmolus (a gold-bearing mountain of Phrygia), was given the ears of an ass by Phoebus. Therefore, let Tmolus and the river Pactolus, the Ram of Phryxus, and Midas all be witnesses that Phrygia abounded in veins of gold, and thus gave rise to the narration of many fables.

To these we shall add Ganymede, likewise a Phrygian, who is said to be the son of Laomedon, King of the Trojans, carried up into heaven by Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus.</note> in the form of an eagle, so that he might serve him cups in place of Hebe. Under this fable, Cicero, in the first book of his *Tusculan Disputations*, suspected something secret was contained, when he said: 

<margin>
Homer transferred human affairs to the Gods.
</margin>

*“Nor do I listen to Homer, who says Ganymede was snatched by the gods because of his beauty, so that he might serve cups to Jove: that is no just cause for such a great injury to be done to Laomedon. Homer was inventing these things and transferring human affairs to the gods.”* <note>Original Latin: "Nec Homerum audio, qui Ganymedem à dijs raptum ait propter formam, vt Iovi pocula ministraret... Fingebat hæc Homerus & humana ad deos transferebat."</note> By these words Cicero confesses that Homer invented what he wrote about the abduction of Ganymede; so too we know that Homer did in his entire work—not only in this one instance—but directed each and every thing toward a different goal than the words sound. 

Others attempt to refer this deed of Jove to literal history, saying that Jupiter was a king of Crete and a most foul man, who both abused boys and snatched the virgins of foreigners. They claim that Tantalus, king of the Phrygians, snatched Ganymede (the son of Tros, king of the Dardanians) for his pleasure so that Jupiter might use him, according to Orosius <note>Paulus Orosius, a 5th-century Christian historian known for his "History Against the Pagans."</note> in Book 1. But it appears from all circumstances that these things were devised by others and rest upon no truth. Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author who often critiqued pagan myths.</note> also in Book 1 feels thus about Jove: *“What [did] Jupiter...”*

### Book 6. Of the Egyptian-Greeks.

**...piter** <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods.</note>, who in formal prayer is named "Best and Greatest," is he not discovered to be almost a parricide from his very first cause and boyhood? For he expelled his father from the kingdom, not waiting for the end of a decrepit old man due to his own greed for ruling. When he had taken his father’s throne through force and arms, he was provoked to war by the Titans; having conquered them, he consumed the rest of his life in debaucheries and adulteries. I omit the virgins whose honor he diminished, for that is usually judged tolerable <note>A sarcastic remark reflecting the views of the author's source.</note>; yet I cannot pass over Amphitryon and Tyndareus, whose homes he rendered full of disgrace and infamy. Indeed, it was an act of the highest impiety and crime that he snatched away a royal boy <note>Ganymede.</note> for his lust. For it seemed too little to him that he was so stained and foul in overcoming the modesty of women, unless he also did injury to his own sex. So says Lactantius <note>Lucius Caelius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author who criticized pagan mythology to prove the superiority of Christianity.</note>.

But it is sufficiently clear from what has been said before that Jupiter was neither a man, nor a God, nor a King of Crete. This is because he was celebrated with many monstrous fictions and allegories by the Egyptians long before the Greeks knew anything of that religion, which was first brought to them by Orpheus. We have sufficiently proved that neither he, nor his parents or ancestors, nor his brothers, sisters, sons, grandsons, or descendants, ought to or can be counted among gods or men. What is related concerning Ganymede looks toward **chemical hieroglyphics** <note>Alchemical symbols or metaphors.</note>. In these, Ganymede is not interpreted as the winter season sending rains (as the cupbearer of Jove, or the air), nor as the celestial sign of Aquarius; rather, he represents that which is carried upward by the eagle—that is, the **fixed** substance which is raised to the highest dignity by the **volatile** substance <note>In alchemy, "fixed" refers to a solid substance that resists fire, while "volatile" refers to a substance that evaporates or transforms easily; the "Eagle" often symbolizes the process of sublimation or distillation.</note>.

<margin>6th Reason. From the six conditions or fatal requirements without which Troy could not be conquered.</margin>

*The sixth reason is the firmest of all, and is drawn from the Conditions or Requirements without which Troy could not be besieged. For six things are celebrated as entirely "fated," which it was necessary to have concur, and which the Greeks had to seek out before they could emerge as victors over the Trojans. The first of these was the prophecy of the seer Calchas, who pronounced that Troy could not be taken without Achilles, nor without his son Neoptolemus. The second was that the Palladium <note>A sacred wooden statue of the goddess Pallas Athena that protected the city.</note> would have to be stolen from Ilium. The third was that one of the bones of Pelops <note>A legendary king; his shoulder bone was said to be made of ivory.</note> must be held at Troy before it could be conquered. The fourth was that the ashes of Laomedon <note>The father of King Priam and founder of Troy's walls.</note> must be snatched from the gate.*

# Book 6 of the Hieroglyphics

Fifth, that the work of the arrows of **Hercules** <note>The legendary hero known for his strength and twelve labors; his poisoned arrows were required to win the Trojan War.</note> would be necessary; Sixth, that the horses of **Rhesus**, king of Thrace, would have to be driven off before they could drink from the river Xanthus. At first glance, these things would appear to be mere fables, were they not repeatedly mentioned by **Homer** and those authors who, following him, recalled the Trojan disaster. But how could such diverse things, seemingly foreign to the purpose, contribute to the capture of a city or the destruction of a nation? Why are these things said to benefit the Greeks and harm the Trojans, unless perhaps by some magical force or supernatural power? We read in the records of the Holy Scriptures how the walls of **Jericho** <note>original: "Hierochuntis"</note> were cast down by the Israelite people at God’s command, through circling them and the repeated sound of trumpets,

<margin>Joshua ch. 6</margin>
and the way was opened for the victorious Israelites; but we do not remember such a thing happening among the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicos." The author distinguishes between the divinely-ordained miracles of the Bible and the "fables" of the Greeks.</note>. This [the fall of Jericho] is held to have most truly been done by the Lord of Hosts; those other things are fashioned as if they had occurred. The former was handed down by the most sacred scriptures, the latter by the fables of poets. Truly, so that it may become more clear that these things are not only fictitious, but why they were eventually devised, we shall inquire more broadly into each one and its circumstances. The first was the presence of **Achilles** and his invincible valor against the Trojans.

<margin>
1. Requirement: Achilles and Neoptolemus. Secrets.
</margin>

Now, Achilles is fashioned as the son of **Peleus** and **Thetis**: (Peleus signifies "mud," just as Thetis signifies "water") <note>The author uses etymology to link the parents of Achilles to the elements of earth and water, a common technique in alchemical interpretation.</note>. For Peleus, as **Isaacius** <note>Likely Isaac Tzetzes, a 12th-century Byzantine commentator on Greek myths.</note> left in writing, following the advice of his father **Chiron**, seized Thetis while she was hiding in the form of a cuttlefish in **Magnesia**, a place in Thessaly. At the celebration of their wedding on Mount Pelion (where our **magnesia** <term>Magnesia: in alchemy, this refers not just to the location, but to the "base matter" or prime substance needed to create the Philosopher's Stone</term> lies hidden, and was originally named from it), all the gods came, except **Discord**. She, being angry at this, threw a golden apple into the midst of them all with this inscription: "Let it be given to the Fairest." This apple <note>The author plays on the Latin word "malum," which means both "apple" and "evil."</note> was the beginning of every evil for the Trojans. For at this wedding, two seeds were sown, or the principal causes for the destruction of Troy were provided: first, Achilles was generated from these two; and second, **Paris** was chosen as the arbitrary judge. He judged **Venus** most worthy of the apple, having been corrupted by her with the promised gift of **Helen**, the most beautiful woman. From this, the rages of the remaining goddesses flared up against the Trojans, both on account of Paris the judge and on account of **Aeneas**, the son of Venus; and the abduction of Helen followed.

They write that **Helen** bore several children to **Paris**, from which it is clear that she was still under fifty years of age. But how was **Pollux**, who emerged from the same egg with her, present with the **Argonauts** <note>The heroes who sailed with Jason on the ship Argo.</note> when they sought the Golden Fleece about 100 years earlier? Or how could **Achilles**, born from the marriage of **Peleus** and **Thetis**, have brought his own son **Pyrrhus** with him to **Troy**? From this it follows that Achilles set out for Troy at least 40 years after the Apple of **Eris** <note>The Apple of Discord, which triggered the judgment of Paris.</note> was thrown. If the duration of the siege is added to this, as well as the length of Helen’s life at the time of the Argonautic expedition, they total no less than 180 years for Helen’s age by the time Troy was finally defeated and the "adulteress" was recovered by the Greeks. Nor does it follow that Helen was very young even then, because she was said to be still a maiden when she was abducted by **Theseus**, though she was later restored to her parents. But we consider it superfluous to examine these points too scrupulously, since it is sufficiently clear that the matter is a fiction in itself. 

**Helinandus** <note>Helinand of Froidmont, a medieval chronicler and poet.</note> relates that **Jupiter** loved **Thetis**, but when he was warned not to father anyone by her who might expel him from his kingdom, he gave her as a wife to **Peleus**, the king of the **Peloponnese**, brother of **Aeson**, and uncle of **Jason**. When all the goddesses were present at their wedding except for **Discord** (Eris), she became angry and threw a golden apple into the midst of the goddesses with the inscription mentioned before. **Fulgentius** <note>A late antique mythographer who interpreted myths as moral allegories.</note> maintains that through these three goddesses, the poets intended to signify three types of life: specifically, through **Venus**, the voluptuous life; through **Juno**, the active life; and through **Pallas** (Athena), the contemplative life. However, while we do not deny that these moral meanings fit very well in a secondary sense, it is not likely from all the circumstances that these were the primary things being said about them. 

From the aforesaid, it is therefore established that **Achilles** is the son of **Peleus**—that is, of <term>mud</term> <note>original: "cæni." For it is necessary that he be so, because he must be chosen by the philosopher to complete his work <note>The "Great Work" of alchemy.</note>. Without those ancestors, he would scarcely be of a noble character. But let us hear of his instruction and education, as well as his selection. After Achilles was born from the goddess **Thetis**, because she knew that he would be an invincible Hero in war, she therefore took him from the dark...

->### Book 6 of Hieroglyphics.<-

his mother <note>original: "matris" — the word is split across pages 261 and 262.</note> accustomed him to enduring every hardship. <margin>Ulysses as a craftsman strong in counsel.</margin>

*“We say, therefore, that he who does not possess a natural genius and a soul subtly investigating natural principles, the foundations of nature, and the crafts which can follow nature in the properties of its actions, will not find the true root of this most precious science.”*

->### Hieroglyphics, Book 6<-

**Thetis**, as you will recognize from her names and omens, is the mother of **Achilles**. In the form of a cuttlefish <note>original: "sepiæ"</note> hiding in the sea, **Peleus** coupled with **Thetis**. *The genus of the cuttlefish is a well-known aquatic creature which, when it is captured, stains the water with ink;* the location of this event is **Magnesia**; from which our **Achilles** is called "**Magnesia**" by some writers. Regarding this, **Flaminius** <note>likely referring to a commentator on alchemical texts</note> writes, citing **Democritus**: *For whitened Magnesia does not allow bodies to be broken, nor the shadow of Venus* <note>In alchemy, "Venus" often refers to copper or the lower, unrefined states of matter</note> *to be brought in.* And shortly after: *What is Magnesia but the whole compound?* And again: *Behold beautiful Magnesia, and marvel at how she brings forth through a single multitude.* **Dardaris** also mentions her among the crowd of philosophers. Furthermore, *know that the body of bronze is ruled by Magnesia.* **Mosius** says: *The Mercury* <note>original: "Argentum vivum"</note> *of the Cambar* <note>an Arabic-derived alchemical term often referring to a specific state of mercury or sulfur</note> *is Magnesia.* **Pythagoras** says: Therefore, you must not set aside that Magnesia without its mercury: for when they are composed together, it is a most powerful composition, which is one of the ten. **Pandulphus**, **Belus**, **Astratus**, **Rarson**, and many others in the crowd of philosophers have made mention of the same, though we omit their specific sayings here.

Indeed, the same **Pythagoras** defines the entire art thus: *And it should be known that the knowledge of this art is nothing other than vapor and the sublimation of water, and the joining of Mercury and Magnesia to the body.* Nor does it matter that some think this name was given to it out of envy <note>Alchemists often used "envious" names—deliberately confusing terms—to hide secrets from the uninitiated</note>. Regarding this, **Rarson** says: *This is indeed our greatest secret, which the envious have called Magnesia for the sake of the secret itself. Therefore, cook this Magnesia diligently in its own vessel, until the whole thing coagulates and contains itself.*

Once you have obtained this **Magnesia**, or **Achilles** (or **Pyrrhus** <note>another name for Neoptolemus, Achilles' son, meaning "The Red-Haired"</note> who arose from it), let him be fostered under the fire by the industry of his mother. Let him be educated by his grandfather **Chiron**, who instructed so many Heroes, and among them his cousin **Jason**, so that he may truly become our **fire-natured** <note>original: "Pyrifous"</note> one and our **salamander** <note>The salamander was a legendary creature believed to live in and endure fire; in alchemy, it represents a substance that is stable at high heat</note>. Only then is it permitted to proceed to the occupation of **Troy**.

<margin>What is understood by the destruction of Troy.</margin> By the siege of **Troy** and its reduction to ashes, **Homer** understood nothing other, *mystically and occultly*, than the period and circuit of the philosophical vessel. In this vessel, **Helen** and **Paris**—the principal Matter—are contained, tightly enclosed, by the surrounding, vaporous, and digesting fire. **Helen** herself is that for which the struggle occurs, in whose lap **Paris**, the idle adulterer, lies hidden. For in a single subject there is a double power, both acting and suffering, **masculine and feminine**, with which there concurs—

Regarding its origin, there have been various opinions. We embrace the story passed down by **Apollodorus** <note>A 2nd-century BCE Greek scholar and mythographer</note> in Book 3, who says that when **Ilus** founded **Ilium** <note>Another name for the city of Troy</note>, having followed a multicolored cow, he prayed to the gods that some sign might appear to him. At that moment, the **Palladium** <note>A sacred wooden statue of the goddess Pallas Athena, believed to protect the city that possessed it</note> fell from the sky. It was three cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm; thus the statue was about 4.5 feet tall</note> in length and appeared to walk of its own accord, holding a spear in its right hand and a distaff and spindle <note>Tools used for spinning wool, representing feminine domestic labor</note> in its left. To this **Ilus**, an answer was later given by the Oracle: that the city of **Troy** would remain safe for as long as that **Palladium** was kept inviolate. **Pherecydes** <note>An early Greek mythographer from the 6th century BCE</note> asserts that all images not made by human hands, but cast down from heaven to earth, were called **Palladia**, as if there were many of that kind. This one, of which we speak here, they say fell from heaven into **Pessinus** <note>original: "Pelsinuntem"</note>, a city of **Phrygia**, which obtained its name from that fall, as **Dio** and **Diodorus** believed. Others, to explain this, devise different causes. Some refer it to the contest of **Pallas** with **Minerva** <note>In some myths, Pallas was a childhood companion whom the goddess Athena (Minerva) accidentally killed; the statue was made in her memory</note> as an image of fear impressed upon the breast of **Minerva**, which **Palladium** was in later times brought to the **Trojans**. **Ovid** narrates in Book 6 of the *Fasti* <note>A Latin poem explaining the origins of Roman holidays and customs</note> that in the time of King **Ilus** of the Trojans—who was the fourth descendant of **Dardanus**, from whom the Trojans are called **Dardanides**—the aforementioned **Palladium** fell from heaven onto the highest citadel of Troy. **Apollo** was consulted on this matter, and he replied that as long as Troy held the **Palladium**, its empire would stand. The Trojans, therefore, kept the **Palladium** in the citadel with the greatest diligence until the time of King **Priam**,

### Book 6 of the Egypto-Greeks ###
->271<-

Did not someone once imagine that **Homer** vomited a great foam from himself, while all the other minor Greek poets reclined nearby to lick up his spit? For through these streams, diverted from that fountain, superstition and monstrous opinions regarding the gods were carried into the minds of the Greeks, later the Romans, and the nations of the entire world.

This **Palladium**, because it was entirely fictitious, has provoked many doubts—not only regarding its origin, as we previously discussed, but also whether it was seized by the Greeks, or if instead **Aeneas** carried it away along with the other Trojan gods to Italy. **Ovid**, in Book 6 of the *Fasti* <note>A poem explaining the Roman calendar and its festivals</note>, leaves the matter in doubt but asserts that in his time the **Palladium** was in Rome within the Temple of the goddess **Vesta**. **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, the famous Roman historian</note> agrees with this in his account of the Second Punic War.

It is said to be a thing of fate <note>original: "fatale"</note>, such that if it were moved, the seat of power <note>original: "imperium"</note> would move with it. For this reason, such objects were called "sacred things of fate." It is said that three cities perished while possessing it: first **Troy**, then **Lavinium**, and finally **Alba Longa**. This last city was founded by **Ascanius** <note>The son of Aeneas</note>, from whom the Albans descend; it is said to have been the mother-city of Rome, but was eventually destroyed by **Tullus Hostilius** <note>The legendary third king of Rome</note>.

Yet the more common opinion is that the **Palladium** was snatched from the Trojan citadel by **Diomedes** and **Ulysses** <note>Two Greek heroes of the Trojan War</note> and brought to the Greeks. For these men, as **Virgil** records in Book 2 of the *Aeneid*—and as **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo</note> mentions in *The City of God* (Book 1, Chapter 2)—"having slain the guards of the highest citadel, seized the sacred image, and with blood-stained hands dared to touch the goddess’s virginal headbands" <note>original: "caesis summae custodibus arcis corripuere sacram effigiem, manibusque cruentis Virgineas ausi divae contingere vittas"</note>.

**Dictys of Crete** <note>A legendary chronicler of the Trojan War</note> narrates that **Antenor** the Trojan—a traitor to his own country—after conspiring with the Greeks for the betrayal of **Troy**, persuaded **Theano**, the priestess of the temple of **Minerva** (or **Pallas**) where the **Palladium** was kept, to hand the statue over to him. She did so, and **Antenor** then delivered it to the Greeks. In a similar fashion, both this Cretan and **Dares the Phrygian** <note>Another legendary historian of the war</note> report that **Aeneas** was complicit in the betrayal of the city of **Troy**, even though **Virgil** attempts to excuse **Aeneas** from this charge of treason by claiming he was unaware of the plot.

Then, after the destruction of the city, they say a great contest arose over the **Palladium** between **Ajax** and **Ulysses** (just as there was a contest for the armor of the fallen **Achilles**), with both of them seeking the statue and citing their own merits. **Agamemnon** favored **Ulysses**, and

From him also **Dares the Phrygian** and **Dictys the Cretan** <note>Legendary authors of "eyewitness" accounts of the Trojan War, now considered later forgeries</note>, who seemed to have written historical accounts of the Trojan War to seek glory for their own people, took their material; yet neither was actually present at the war, though they falsely boast of it. <margin>What the Palladium denotes.</margin>

We shall briefly add: It has been sufficiently explained above what is signified by the Palladium, and since both its name and form are derived from this <note>likely referring to Pallas/Athena</note>, it is easily apparent what **Homer** wished to sketch out: namely, that wisdom and the highest subtlety of talent <note>original: "ingenij ſubtilitatem"</note> ought to reside in the craftsman <note>term: <term>artifex</term> (the skilled artist or creator)</note>, so that, relying on this, he might be successful in perfecting his work. For in this whole allegory, **Ulysses** is held to be the craftsman endowed with the sharpness of reason, by which he accomplishes all the most difficult business. His first labor was regarding the discovery of **Achilles** and leading him to Troy; the second was to investigate, with a more subtle inquiry of the mind, by what means Troy might be occupied—specifically by seizing the Palladium. Therefore, it is useless to ask about purely fictional things, such as where it came from, whether from heaven or from the imagination of **Minerva**, and where it remained. Rather, it is assigned to **Ulysses**, who is strong in prudence, and not to **Ajax**, who excels in strength; this is because the subtlety of the craftsman is required here, not the magnitude of labor or force, which concerns Hercu-

Tantalus is called by some the son of Jupiter and the nymph Plota, and by others the son of Jupiter and Plutus. When this man had once received the gods as guests and prepared a sumptuous banquet for them, he placed his slaughtered son Pelops among the dishes; and this, as some believe, was done for the magnificence of the feast, as if he were offering them the most precious thing of all, his own son. However, when the gods recognized this, they abstained from those foods, except for Ceres alone, who, being almost out of her mind due to her grief over her stolen daughter Proserpina <note>Also known as Persephone, abducted by Pluto/Hades</note>, thoughtlessly ate the shoulder. Then the remaining gods, taking pity on the son, threw him back into the cauldron and, having boiled him again, restored him to life. But since the shoulder was missing, which...

### Book 6 of the Hieroglyphics ###

->274<-

...Ceres <note>The goddess of agriculture, often identified with the Greek Demeter</note> had eaten, the gods are said to have replaced it with ivory. For this reason, Lycophron <note>A Greek poet known for his obscure and riddling style</note> called Pelops "twice-pubescent," because he was restored by the gods to a younger state than he had been before. Tantalus was cast down to the underworld because he had contaminated the feasts of the gods with human slaughter and violated the laws of hospitality. He is said to always have a most lavish banquet prepared before him, which he nevertheless cannot touch, being tortured by hunger. Others have said he is vexed by a perpetual thirst, for while water rises as far as his chin, it retreats whenever he attempts to touch it. Ovid <note>A famous Roman poet, author of *Metamorphoses*</note> recorded another cause for this punishment—namely his loquacity—because he had revealed the secrets of the gods to mortals, writing:

> *He seeks water in the midst of waters and catches at fleeing fruit,*
> *Tantalus; his talkative tongue gave this to him.*
> <note>original: "Quærit aquas in aquis et poma fugacia captat / Tantalus, hoc illi garrula lingua dedit."</note>

Pelops is said to have been the son of this Tantalus. He obtained Hippodamia, the daughter of Oenomaus, the King of Elis and Pisa, by winning a chariot race. Countless suitors before him had failed and been killed in this contest, and a temple to Mars <note>The god of war</note> was meant to be built from their skulls. Pelops won with the help of Myrtillus <note>The king's charioteer, whom Pelops bribed and then betrayed</note>, whom Pelops also later murdered; they record that he was purified of this slaughter by Vulcan <note>The god of fire and craftsmanship</note>. The myths tell that Pelops, after he was cooked <note>Referring to the feast where Tantalus served him to the gods to test their omniscience</note>, was loved by Neptune <note>God of the sea</note>, as Pindar says. He is said to be buried at Letrina, which was a city in Elis. This story of Tantalus serving his son to be eaten by the gods is a poetic fiction. The poets may have invented this either to insult him (as they did with similar stories about Sisyphus, Ixion, Busiris, and the like) and thus attributed an eternal punishment to him, or perhaps it was due to his impiety or talkativeness. Indeed, it was more likely for the latter reason, just as they tell of Ixion <note>Who was punished for trying to seduce Hera and revealing divine secrets</note>. As for what secrets of the gods he might have revealed to mortals, it is easily seen from the banquet and the feast he set before the gods, from which only Ceres tasted. As we have said above, the Eleusinian Mysteries <note>Secret religious rites of ancient Greece</note> and all the most hidden ceremonies were dedicated to Ceres among both the Egyptians and the Greeks, the secrets of which no one was permitted to reveal. Thus, it could be established that these stories imply that he made those mysteries public. But...

### Book 6 of the Egyptian-Greeks ###

->275<-

Whether Tantalus was punished for his lack of restraint in speech <note>Referring to the myth that Tantalus betrayed the secrets of the gods</note>, or for some other reason, it is beyond doubt that this entire narrative contains a fable and allegory, and that it refers to those very same Hieroglyphic traditions which we mentioned before. For just as Osiris was restored by Isis, Bacchus (or Dionysus) by the Nymphs, Jason by the nurses of Bacchus, and Aeson by Medea—all of whom are said to have been "cooked" <note>In an alchemical context, "cooking" or decoction refers to the purification and transformation of a substance through heat</note> and returned again to youth—so too did Pelops recover both life and youth at once after being cooked by Ceres or the gods. Since we have already said enough about these matters above, the same should be understood regarding *Pelops*. He is said to have been purified from slaughter by Vulcan <note>The god of fire and smithing, representing the transformative power of the forge</note>, and loved by Neptune <note>The god of the sea</note>; the nature of these gods is already sufficiently known.

*Regarding this Pelops, Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola* <note>A prominent Renaissance philosopher and nephew of the famous Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note> *mentions him in Book 2, Chapter 2 of "On Gold" in these words:* "Thus, I say, some interpret the field or the ram to be named after Atreus so as to suggest to the readers the described power of gold-making. For Callisthenes of Olynthus <note>A historian and relative of Aristotle</note>, both a disciple and kinsman of Aristotle, left it written that the wealth of Atreus and Pelops came from metals." *And in Book 3, Chapter 1, he says:* "Nor were there those lacking who attributed the riches of Tantalus also to the chemical composition described on lamb skins; from which the kingdom of the son Pelops and the descendants of Pelops was propagated far and wide. Thus it did not seem absurd that Thyestes, the younger son of Pelops, sought the lamb—that is, the gold-making composition inscribed on the lamb's skin—which the elder Atreus held among his secrets; and Thyestes extorted it from his brother's wife after an act of adultery was discovered, from which followed the tragedy of hatred and the most bloody banquet." <note>This refers to the "Golden Lamb" of Atreus, which granted the right to rule; Pico interprets it here as a coded alchemical recipe</note> The most ancient poets, as well as Cicero, Seneca, and Papirius, have mentioned this matter, though under an obscure veil.

These are his words. But if the truth of the matter and the fables clinging to each of these persons are considered, they will all be seen to lead back to Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, who was the father of Tantalus, who was the father of Pelops, who was the father of Thyestes and Atreus. From these, Thyestes fathered Aegisthus by his own daughter Pelopeia; Atreus fathered Agamemnon and Menelaus. Atreus served his brother Thyestes his own sons to be eaten; Aegisthus slaughters Atreus and Agamemnon and takes Clytemnestra as his wife; but Orestes killed his mother together with Aegisthus, as was narrated above. All of which provided the occasion for fashioning allegories about Pelops...

### Book 6 of the Hieroglyphics ###

->276<-

...they gave: It is recorded that his bone <note>Referring back to the ivory shoulder of Pelops mentioned on the previous page</note> was of remarkable size, which was obtained by Ulysses as well, along with the rest. But why was this said to be useful or necessary for the seizing of Troy? Without doubt, it is because the craftsmen <note>The "artifices" or alchemists</note> wished to indicate that a certain earthy substance is required for the work, which is, as it were, dead and a remnant of the metallic body, just as a bone is a remnant of the human body. For just as bones in the body of an animal or a human sustain the flesh, humors, vessels, and spirits—serving as the base and foundation of the house—so too in the Philosophical Work <term>Philosophical Work (Opus Philosophicum): The process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term> one fixed element contains all volatile (or non-fixed) elements and binds them together so that they may rightly be called a single substance. 

Hence, in the *Rising Dawn* <note>original: "Aurora consurgens," a famous medieval alchemical manuscript</note>, it is said in chapter 20: *That the tincture comes from the nature of flying things; and that which firms and fixes the spirit itself is fixed, perpetual, and fire-resistant, and is named the Sulfur of the Philosophers, or ash extracted from ash.* As the Elder <note>original: "Senior," referring to the alchemist Senior Zadith</note> says: *That which is fixed fixes fugitive things.* And shortly after: *Earth fixes, water whitens, air penetrates, fire colors.* Likewise: *Earth is left behind in that same place, so that the other three elements may be able to take root in it; if earth itself were not there, the elements would have no foundation upon which to build the new storehouse of treasures.* 

The author of the *Counsel of Conjunction* <note>original: "Consilium coniunctionis"</note> quotes Cratiano: *Fire in the air becomes light; from bone comes lime.* He intends the drying out of that shining moisture so that it may be turned into ash, of which Aziratus says: *And how precious is this ash! Air in the egg becomes spirit.*

<margin>4. Requirement: The Ashes of Laomedon.</margin> Hence also the fourth requirement <note>According to prophecy, several conditions had to be met for Troy to fall; the author interprets these alchemically</note> was the ash of Laomedon, which was to be snatched from the Scaean gate. For since ash is made from bone, as authors say and as is evident through experience, bone and ash are two substances necessary for the Philosophical Work. Regarding ash, they have mentioned it in innumerable places. Bonellus says in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: *That nature,* he says, *from which moisture has been taken away, appears like a dead thing when it is left through the nights; and then that nature needs fire until the body and its spirit are turned into earth, and then there becomes a dust like a dead man in his tomb. When these things are finished, God restores the spirit and soul to it, and with all infirmity removed, our nature is strengthened and improved.* It is therefore necessary to burn that thing without fear until it becomes ash, which ash is fit to receive the spirit, soul, and the infused tincture.

### Book 6. Egyptian-Greek Secrets. ###

->277<-

*Look, you sons of doctrine, at how painters are unable to paint with their colors until they turn them into ashes and pulverize them: similarly, Philosophers <note>Referring to alchemists, often called "Philosophers" in this period</note> are often unable to compose medicines for their patients unless they are broken and pulverized. But if you rule that ash itself with subtlety, many things will proceed from it, because it, like a human being, possesses a body and a spirit. The Guardian, and many others, indicate—as is clear to those who read them—that in the chemical art <term>Chemical Art (artificio chymico): The practice of alchemy or early chemistry</term> nothing can be achieved without ash. For two bones and ash are of great power here; yet the ashes (as well as the bones) of a specific individual are required, namely those of Laomedon. He, as the King of Troy, is said to have built the walls with Apollo and Neptune—or even Vulcan—as his workmen, whom we mentioned before. He is said to have been slaughtered by Hercules, as we explained under his 14th labor; thus Laomedon, the founder of Troy, was deprived of life because of that very city. For when he would not give the agreed-upon payment to the aforementioned workmen, he was harassed by a sea monster <note>original: "Ceto"</note>, from which his daughter Hesione was freed by Hercules; but when he would not give the promised horses to Hercules either, he was killed, and his ashes were preserved in a certain Scaean gate. These ashes also seemed necessary for the destruction of Troy, and therefore they were secretly carried away from there by Ulysses. Thus, authors often report that the end of the Philosophical work testifies to its beginning, and vice-versa, that it begins with one and ends with one.*

<margin>5th Requirement: The Arrows of Hercules.</margin>
*The fifth requirement for Troy was the arrows of Hercules. Hercules, while dying on Mount Oeta between Thessaly and Macedonia, gave his arrows to Philoctetes as a gift, and commanded him, after receiving an oath, that he should not reveal the location of his body's remains to anyone. But when the Delphic oracle later warned the Greeks that Troy could not be captured without the arrows of Hercules, or without the remains of his body, Philoctetes was found. When questioned about Hercules, he denied knowing anything; and when he was pressured, he remained silent but pointed to the place with his foot. Ulysses received these arrows from Philoctetes and brought them to the Greeks. They say these arrows had been infected with poison; when Chiron <note>The centaur, known as a master of healing and tutor to heroes</note> once handled them, admiring their length, one fell on his foot, from which he received a lethal wound, though he is said to have been healed by the centaury herb <note>original: "centaurea herba"</note>. No one fails to recognize that these things are fictions; the arrows of Hercules were given to Philoctetes,*
