### Book 6 of the Hieroglyphics ###

->278<-

...just as the club is to Mercury; with the club, Hercules fought those monsters at close range, and with arrows from a distance. With the fixed and resistant club, he struck down and softened them; with the fleeting and volatile arrows, he pierced them and slowed their flight. Every Philosopher <note>In this context, a "Philosopher" refers to an alchemist</note> requires these two instruments or methods of operation, as has been demonstrated often above; just as they require two "waters," one of which fixes the other while the other dissolves it in mutual exchange. Therefore, little can be accomplished at Troy without the Herculean arrows: for the greater labor is spent in halting that which is fleeting and volatile, as if "fixing" it with arrows (hence the term <term>Fixation (fixio): The alchemical process of making a volatile, vaporous substance stable and resistant to fire</term> used by the Chemists). This is seen in **Apollo** piercing the **Python**, **Diana** slaying **Orion**, **Atalanta** the boar, and similar stories which we have discussed in their proper place.

The sixth and final requirement is held to be that <margin>6th Requirement: The horses of Rhesus must be led away.</margin> the horses of the King of Thrace, after he was slain, had to be led away before they could drink from the **Xanthus** river; unless this was rightly performed, Troy could not be occupied. We might rightly judge these things to be ridiculous and very much like the fables usually told to children by their nurses, were they not handed down by so many great writers, such as Homer and his followers. What do bones, ashes, and arrows have to do with occupying a city? What is the significance of horses being led away before they drink from a specific river? 

Yet we have seen from what was said before that these things were not devised without cause. Now, the Xanthus was a river in the region of Troy, whose power is celebrated for staining any animals that drink from it with a yellow color; for <note>original: "Xanthus"</note> denotes "yellow" <note>From the Greek *xanthos*, meaning yellow or golden-brown</note>. This color was perhaps seen as undesirable in the horses; therefore, they had to be prevented from drinking the water of that river. Thus they recall that **Neptune** brought the horses **Xanthus** and **Balius** to the wedding of **Peleus** and **Thetis**, which are believed to have come to **Achilles** by hereditary right. 

But it might seem a wretched thing, were it not a fable, that a King had to be slaughtered just for the sake of leading away horses—and indeed a <margin>A King slaughtered for horses.</margin> Thracian king, fierce and warlike, who could be so easily overcome by **Ulysses** alone, or with a few companions, without any resistance. Was it easier to kill the King of Thrace and seize his goods by force than the Trojan Phrygians? For though the Trojans were held to be weak, yet in occupying them...

### Book 6 of the Egyptian-Greeks ###

->279<-

...so many years are said to have been consumed; these things seem contrary to nature and reason if we consult history: for one does not hunt hawks with doves, but doves with hawks; nor do we hunt dogs with hares, but the opposite. But if indeed these things are reduced to their true **Hieroglyphic** sense, they will not be absurd, but possible and necessary before Troy can be occupied. And if the sayings of the **Philosophers** <note>The "Philosophers" are the alchemists; their "work" is the transmutation of matter.</note> are well regarded, we notice that they warn the craftsmen to see that they do not acquire redness instead of whiteness, or whiteness instead of blackness at the beginning of the work; for a reddish or yellowish color at the start is not suitable, but is considered damnable among the Philosophers. And these are those six memorable requirements without which Troy could not be occupied or destroyed. To these, a seventh

### Book 6 of the Hieroglyphics ###

->280<-

<margin>The sacrifice of Iphigenia.</margin>
...We have experienced similar examples in voyages successfully completed in our own time. Thus, the story of Iphigenia, daughter of Agamemnon, offered to Diana as a sacrifice because of the evils plaguing the army, is entirely a fictional matter and akin to a fable. Just as everything contained in the entire *Iliad* and *Odyssey* is allegorical—partly explaining the physical and secret works of nature, and partly political, instructing kings and public or private persons in many things. For this reason, Homer was held in such high esteem by **Alexander the Great**, who placed the book under his pillow at night and called it a "royal traveling companion" <note>original: *regium viaticum*</note>. He was likewise esteemed by other great and learned men of every age, so much so that the highest skill of the human intellect seems expressed in Homer's work—unless one were to focus on the many evils he heaps together with the good, namely the adulteries of the gods, their thefts, murders, robberies, and other such things. It is unlikely that such a great man truly attributed these to the gods; rather, he brought them forth with poetic license and an allegorical manner of writing, so that the wise might separate the kernel from the husk <note>original: *nucleum á cortice*</note>, and the good from the evil, turning it to their own use.

<margin>The fourfold use of Homer's work: 1. Hieroglyphic.</margin>
Therefore, we assign a fourfold use to Homer, as also to Orpheus. The first is **Hieroglyphic**, secret, deep and hidden, and primary, looking toward the most secret works of nature (which we have already discussed). Only philosophers and those initiated into the true <term>Chemistry</term> <note>In this context, *Chymia* refers to Alchemy, the Hermetic "Great Work" of understanding and manipulating the hidden forces of nature.</note> look into and admire this; others neglect it and, under the shadowy covering, do not notice it.

<margin>2. Political.</margin>
The second is **Political**, ethical, moral, historical, and economic; it is secondary, instructing kings, leaders, magistrates, and every individual in morals and common life. Many have noticed this use and respected it as if it alone held something of the divine.

<margin>3. Poetic.</margin>
The third we leave to the **Poets**, who uniquely embrace his fables, fictions, and traditions concerning gods, heroes, and other matters.

<margin>4. Grammatical.</margin>
The fourth we assign to the **Grammarians**, who observe the ornament, the trappings, and the flow of speech, interpreting them for others. Hence Homer (who is most falsely considered a beggar, when he was a man of the greatest political standing and most experienced in managing great affairs—qualities that do not belong to a beggar, but to one excelling in intellect and the gifts of fortune) [inspired] so many Grammarians...

He defends Homer's depictions of immoral gods as a "husk" intended to hide deeper truths about nature and statecraft.</summary>

### Book 6 of the Egyptian-Greeks ###

->281<-

...grammarians throughout Greece, it was said that **Alcibiades** even struck a certain man with his fist for biting at <note>or "criticizing"</note> Homer, adding this biting jest <note>original: *scommate*</note>: "Will you call him a beggar, or a vain man, who feeds so many of his own interpreters and makes them rich?" From so many reasons and arguments produced and explained thus far, it appears clearly enough that the **Trojan Expedition** has little or nothing of historical truth in itself, but a great deal of allegory. It was introduced for the sake of a secret understanding <note>original: *intellectum arcanum*</note> rather than its common literal sense. Nevertheless, we do not deny that a second, third, and fourth use—as we have just said—can be attributed to it. For nothing forbids mixing a bit of truth with allegories and fictions, although, conversely, it is not becoming to thrust fictional things into true matters. For just as leaven, even in the smallest portion, when mixed into a mass of pure wheat flour <note>original: *similagineæ*</note>, renders the whole thing sour and fermented, so too do even a few false or fictional things render a true history suspect and deprive it entirely of its credit. Thus, if the poets, such as **Orpheus** and **Homer**, perhaps mixed some truth into their fables and allegories regarding places, things, or persons, it does not follow that the stories are true, or should be accepted and understood exactly as they sound, as many of the Heathens <note>original: *Ethnicis*</note> have done. Therefore, if someone happens upon such truths in the sayings of these poets, it does not make their fictions true, except to the most thoughtless of men. Hence, even if **Troy** had been a city in the most ancient times and was destroyed, it would not have happened in the manner described. For the things handed down by the poets, or by the historians who followed them in time and style of writing, are such that they ought deservedly to be called into doubt and reduced to their origin—namely, the allegorical one—just as we have done. 

It remains now to briefly run through the return and the wanderings of **Ulysses**, since he, as has been said, is the persona of the **Craftsman** <note>original: *Artificis persona*</note>, as powerful in intellect as **Hercules** was in strength. Therefore, if all things are well considered, whatever was famously achieved at Troy will be seen to have been performed by his counsel and labor. ### Hieroglyphics, Book 6 ###

->282<-

...with these words: "No other servant would be better, believe me, whether there is a need to kindle a fire or to chop wood." <note>original: "Non alius potior fuerit, mihi crede, minister, Siue ignem succendi opus est, seu ligna secanda." This is a Latin translation of Homer’s *Odyssey* 15.321-322.</note> For in these things, the greater part of Ulysses' labor is spent in the philosophical art. Thus, Ulysses himself is said to have built his raft very quickly by his own labor, without the help of craftsmen. He obtained those six fatal requirements <note>referring to the *fatalia*, specific conditions or objects prophesied as necessary for the fall of Troy</note> mentioned before, without which the city could not be occupied; by his eloquence and prudence, he ruled the whole army. After him came **Achilles**, and in his place **Neoptolemus**; then **Helen** with **Paris**. The other characters are added to conceal the artifice: **Agamemnon** as the commander, **Menelaus** as the claimant <note>or the one driving the action</note>, **Ajax** as one who relies much on his hands <note>physical strength</note>, **Diomedes** as the companion of Ulysses, **Sinon** the traitor, **Thersites** the scold, and so with the others.

<margin>The wanderings of Ulysses concerning his return to his homeland:</margin>
With Troy now finally subdued by art and by war, conquered and overturned, **Ulysses** desired to return to his homeland, just as the other Greeks did. For thus **Ovid** says of him:

> *The wisdom of the Ithacan is not in doubt, but nonetheless he prays*
> *that he might see the smoke from his ancestral hearths.*
> <note>original: "Non dubia est Ithaci sapientia, sed tamen optat / Fumun de patrijs posse videre focis." From Ovid, *Epistulae ex Ponto* 1.3.33-34.</note>

Regarding the reason why he fled, which we mentioned above, we add nothing here. First of all, then, he was carried by a storm to the shore of the **Cicones**, a people of Thrace. Afterward to the **Lotus-eaters** in Africa, where, when his companions had tasted the fruit of the lotus, they forgot their homeland and did not return to the ships at all. From there to Sicily, to the cave of **Polyphemus**, whom he blinded along with twelve companions. After that to the island of **Aeolus** and the **Laestrygonians**, the most monstrous peoples of Campania; soon he held his course to the island of **Aeaea**, where the sorceress **Circe**, daughter of the Sun, turned his companions into beasts. By her he fathered **Telegonus** and **Ardea**. Afterward he descended to the underworld, consecrating a pillar to **Pluto** and **Proserpina**, so that he might learn there from the prophet **Tiresias** what things he had to do. Then, carried to the **Island of the Sirens**, he stopped up the ears of his companions, which had been smeared with wax, and ordered himself to be bound to the ship's mast. Crossing from here through **Scylla** and **Charybdis**, not without some loss of his companions, he reached Sicily again, where the daughters of the Sun guarded their father's flocks,

### Book 6. Egyptian-Greeks ###

...whom, when his companions were being slain, almost all perished in a shipwreck. Ulysses himself, having seized the mast of the ship and clinging to it, was tossed by the waves of the sea for nine days until he was carried to the island of **Ogygia**. There, he was received with hospitality by the Nymph **Calypso**, staying for seven years; he is even said to have fathered sons by her. Then, by the command of the gods, he set sail from there, but his ship was broken again near **Phaeacia** through the instigation of **Neptune** because of the blinding of **Polyphemus** <note>The Cyclops, son of Neptune, whom Ulysses blinded</note>. He swam to the port of the Phaeacians and, being naked, hid himself there among the leaves of the trees. After he later received clothing from **Nausicaa**, the daughter of **Alcinous**, he was led by the aid of **Pallas** <note>The goddess Athena</note> to **Arete**, the wife of Alcinous. From her, he received garments and companions as a gift, and he was set down in **Ithaca** with many treasures while he was sleeping. There, having assumed the habit of a beggar, he returned to **Penelope**. She is said to have borne him a son, **Polyporthus**, after the defeat of Troy, in memory of his father's valor, since that name signifies a "destroyer of the city." <note>original: "Polyporthum... cum id nomen populatorem vrbis significet." From the Greek *Ptoliporthos*, a common epithet for Ulysses.</note> And these are the wanderings of Ulysses concerning his return to his homeland, which appear to have extended beyond a decade. Since the Trojan siege lasted just as long, Ulysses lived for twenty whole years away from his homeland, entangled in many errors and misfortunes. Having finally overcome these, he obtained the name of "city-destroyer" through the son born to him. These things are well enough known in themselves, being entirely fabulous and fictitious, produced by the Poet to demonstrate allegorically <note>original: "polytice" - likely a reference to the many-sided or "political" (social/human) application of the myth</note> what errors and evils human life is exposed to, and also what things the practitioners <note>the "artifices" or alchemists</note> are subject to before they reach the final goal. For he who has not wandered is said not to have yet begun. As **Bacasser** says in the *Assembly*: <note>Bacasser is a speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), a foundational alchemical text.</note> *The right way,* he says, *is not discerned except through error, and nothing generates more grief in the heart than an error in this art and work.* Concerning these diversions and difficulties of the art, since the commentaries of others exist and daily examples attest to them more than enough, we add nothing further to their demonstration here.

Therefore, whether Troy stood and was truly destroyed, or whether it is merely a fiction (the same is to be understood regarding the labors of **Hercules**, the sacred contests, and things pertaining to the gods), it remains the same to us, since nothing is sown or reaped for us from that fact; but if, on the other hand...

# Book 6 of the Hieroglyphics #

->284<-

Which side we ought to agree with, a thousand signs will prove that none of these things were real, although the Pagans assert them in almost as many books as if they had actually happened. If, however, we consult all the writers on these matters to see where they drew such great and numerous things from, we must return to the six previously mentioned authors of all Pagan religion—or rather, idolatry: **Orpheus**, **Linus**, **Musaeus**, **Melampus**, **Homer**, and **Hesiod**. But if we ask where *they* obtained them, we will notice that all these things take their origin partly from the **Egyptians**, and partly from their own brains in imitation of Egyptian doctrine. The Egyptians, in turn, received all their teachings from **Isis**, and she from **Mercury** and **Vulcan**, as we have already reported. 

If, however, someone is nevertheless led by their own persuasion to affirm that all those things should be said and understood regarding true and certain persons, and thinks that history is inherent in the fables themselves, we do not strongly oppose them—provided they concede to us in turn that an **Allegory** can be hidden beneath true history. That is to say, the most secret matters, intended to be handed down figuratively, are not rarely covered under the veiled form of true teaching. If anyone seeks an example of this, let them inspect and judge the books of that great **Physician of Amiens** <note>original: "Ambianensis Medici." This refers to Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a celebrated French physician whose work "On the Hidden Causes of Things" (*De abditis rerum causis*) sought to reconcile traditional medicine with deeper natural secrets.</note> regarding the hidden causes of things. Let them decide whether, under that bark—which seems very hard to many—he does not hide another kernel; whether he does not intermingle the most secret works of nature and art with the theorems and precepts of common Medicine gathered from other authors, so that his true intention is recognized only by the most sharp-sighted. 

So too those most ancient writers—in whose time even the name of **Alchemy** <note>original: "Chymia"</note> was not yet widespread—even if they handed down certain true things in their writings, it is nevertheless clear that most of what they brought forth was fictitious, and these fictions far outweigh the historical truths in their significance. Under these fictitious and allegorical tales, who can prove that those Alchemical secrets do not lie hidden? We have so far sufficiently extracted these from their darkness and placed them in the light for all who can understand. In this kind of writing, setting aside all other considerations, if someone attempts to reduce even those fables to literal truth, and considers all the authors together to have been ignorant of Alchemy, nor [perceives] any Alchemical sen...

# Book 6. Egyptian-Greeks #

...once hidden in his own writings, let him use his own judgment as he pleases, as much and wherever he wishes; nevertheless, he will be bound to concede to us as much as is permitted to himself and others by the **right of retaliation** <term>Latin: *Lex Talionis*. This is the legal principle of "like for like." Here, the author argues that if other scholars are allowed to interpret myths as they wish, he should be granted the same freedom.</term>.

And now, just as **Natalis Comes** <note>Natalis Comes (Noël Conti) was a 16th-century Italian mythographer whose work "Mythologiae" was the most influential handbook of classical mythology in the Renaissance.</note> gives thanks to God under the mythology of the **Sun** with these words: *“That a clearer and more abundant explanation of the fables has been reserved for my own times is why I should give immortal thanks to ALMIGHTY God the Redeemer. By His favor, it has been granted to me to reveal these foolish ramblings of the ancients—which contain nothing truly religious—and to demonstrate that they are merely fictions created to explain philosophical matters.”*

In the same way, with equal devotion of spirit, heart, and voice, we also give as many thanks as we can conceive in our minds to that same **TRIUNE GOD**. For He has most mercifully granted to us the means to trace the allegories, fables, and mysteries of the Egyptians, the Greeks, and all antiquity back to their true origin. These were once held to be the most secret of secrets <note>original: "arcana arcanissima"</note>, even as they are now. They were not devised concerning common things known to the world, but about those things which by their own right ought to be hidden. From these stories, the idolatries, darkness, and errors of so many nations have overflowed like most abundant springs. Yet, we have been able to reconcile them into a single line of truth and an unmovable point of harmony—an irreproachable harmony which is the very property of truth.

Since all these things converge in nothing other than that truly golden matter called the **MEDICINE OF THE SOUL AND THE BODY**, may the supreme, best, greatest, and uniquely **Thrice-Greatest** <term>Trismegistus: A title meaning "thrice-greatest," usually associated with the legendary Egyptian sage Hermes Trismegistus, the purported founder of alchemy. Here, the author boldly transfers the title to Jesus Christ.</term> physician of soul and body, **JESUS CHRIST**, grant that we may use this medicine for the glory of His name and for the benefit of ourselves and our neighbors for a very long time, and after this life, grant us eternal life. May He, who is the **STONE** torn from the high **MOUNTAIN** without hands <note>A reference to the prophecy in Daniel 2:45. In alchemical literature, this "stone" was frequently equated with the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, and the **cornerstone** rejected by the greater part of the world (or the Gentiles) but claimed by us, be blessed forever: AMEN.
